tieu_de: Verse for Opening the Sutra
noi_dung:
Verse for Opening the Sutra

The Buddhadharma is deep and profound,

Hard to encounter in hundreds of thousands of eons.

Now that I see, hear, receive and uphold it,

I vow to understand the Tathagata's true meaning.

tieu_de: Penetrate All Dharmas by Reciting Avalokiteshvara
tom_tat: From limitless kalpas past until now, we are born only to die, and die only to be born again. Through hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, we have never encountered an Avalokiteshvara Dharma assembly. That is why our bad habits…
noi_dung:
Penetrate All Dharmas by Reciting Avalokiteshvara

From limitless kalpas in the past until now, we are born only to die, and die only to be born again. Through a span of time stretching hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, we have never once encountered an Avalokiteshvara Dharma assembly. That is why our bad habits and faults have not lessened in the slightest, while our ignorance and afflictions grow greater every day! Now that we have encountered a Dharma assembly of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, we can say it is because the good roots we planted in limitless kalpas past have now ripened that we are able to join such a wonderful and inconceivable Dharma assembly as this. Without good roots, without virtuous conduct, one could never have the chance to join an Avalokiteshvara Session. Therefore, all of you should treasure these seven precious days—do not give rise to discursive thoughts, do not waste time. If you keep indulging in discursive thoughts, then joining this Dharma assembly is as good as not joining, for you will gain no benefit at all!

Although this Dharma assembly only began two days ago, I know that some people have already seen the Bodhisattva, seen light, or seen inconceivable states appear; and some are even about to open the Five Eyes. Therefore, those who have not yet gained any benefit should feel ashamed, and should not assume that because they themselves have gained nothing, others must be the same—that is not so at all!

One could say that Gold Mountain Monastery is a place that "sifts sand in search of gold"—whoever truly wishes to cultivate cannot leave Gold Mountain Monastery, for finding a place to genuinely cultivate is no easy matter. Everyone at Gold Mountain Monastery is a cultivator with resolve for the Way; even in extremely harsh and difficult circumstances, they remain vigorous in applying their skill in cultivation.

There are eighty-four thousand Dharma-doors for cultivating the Way, and you should understand at least a little of each, instead of knowing only one single door. If you have some general idea of every Dharma-door, gradually you will penetrate them all. If you understand only one Dharma-door, it is hard to fathom the "deep as the ocean" state of the Buddhadharma; you would be no different from "a fool peering at the sky through a bamboo tube," convinced that the sky is only as big as the tube's mouth! If you put down the bamboo tube, you will see how vast the sky truly is. Therefore, in studying the Buddhadharma, do not limit yourself to a single Dharma-door—you must penetrate all dharmas and understand all dharmas.

Right now we are reciting the name of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, and that too is a part of the Buddhadharma. If you have never practiced this Dharma-door, you must come and try it for yourself; do not refuse to cultivate without even trying! If you can complete these full seven days of reciting Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's name, you will surely reap great benefit for both body and mind. So do not let this opportunity slip by; do not pass up this rare chance before your eyes!

A Bodhisattva cultivates the Six Paramitas and the myriad practices. The Six Paramitas are:

Giving. Giving means we ourselves give to others—not that we want others to give to us.

Patience. Through this Avalokiteshvara Session you will find out

whether or not you have the capacity to endure. One who can endure will surely complete this Avalokiteshvara Session to perfection. One who cannot endure will spend the whole day giving rise to discursive thoughts, such as: "In a little while I'll go to that restaurant and eat my fill," or: "What good does staying here reciting Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's name do me? It's useless! I'd better hurry home!"

Without the ability to be patient and to endure, you cannot cultivate the Way! Whether you wish to practice sitting meditation, Buddha-recitation, or reciting Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's name—all are fine, for these Dharma-doors are one and the same, with no difference at all. Whichever Dharma-door you cultivate, with patience you will attain accomplishment. Without patience, you cannot cultivate any Dharma-door! A person lacking patience always feels that this is wrong and that is wrong, that nothing is ever right; how could such a person cultivate anything?

The Way fundamentally has no view of self, no attachment to "I"; therefore, whoever clings to self can never cultivate the Way! Someone says: "I want to investigate Chan!" You want to investigate Chan? Then you need patience all the more!

Moral discipline. To uphold the precepts is: "Commit no evil, practice all good."

Vigor. Vigor means diligence, not laziness or laxity.

Samadhi. Right now we recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's name, praying that Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva will help us attain samadhi.

Wisdom. Once samadhi is attained, wisdom arises. Thus these six practices are all interrelated.

Someone says: "I like to specialize in samadhi." Then let me now tell you how to cultivate samadhi. Once you have stepped into the Chan Hall, no matter what happens, you may not leave the Chan Hall even half a step! Someone asks: "What if I get sick?" If you're sick, then just be sick! Sick or not, you still investigate Chan as usual!

"But what if I die?" Even dead, your corpse may not be carried out of the Chan Hall! If a meditator dies, the body is tucked beneath an empty sitting bench, and even if it putrefies it must stay there—it may not be taken outside. The dead may not leave the Chan Hall either!

Someone says: "Isn't that just like being in prison?" Do you think you aren't in prison right now? Everyone is locked inside a prison of their own, only they do not realize it! Your own nature wants to get out but cannot get out; wants to return but cannot return. Once out, you cannot come back; once back, you cannot get out again—can that be called "freedom"? Each person's body is itself a prison; only, you have not yet understood this!

During a Chan Session, once you have entered the Chan Hall you may not step out of its doors again. Whoever goes out gets a beating—the fragrant board whistling down on head and back. That is during a Chan Session. It is the same during an Avalokiteshvara Session—no one may leave the Buddha Hall! Whoever disobeys will be beaten, for—who told you to come here in the first place!?

Someone says: "I came because I read the announcement." But the announcement never said that once here you could leave as you please! If you want to go, fine—but first you must pay for everyone's meals before you may leave; otherwise, you cannot go. Why? Because if you leave, others will see you and follow your example. You leave, she leaves, he leaves too, and soon everyone has left—that is "destroying the Way-place." So to avoid the offense of "destroying the Way-place," you must pay for everyone's food. If you cannot afford it, best not to leave!

You all have good affinities with one another, which is why you have come together to Gold Mountain Monastery. Without good affinities, there would be no way you could even set foot past Gold Mountain Monastery's threshold. Having good affinities, do not hesitate to befriend one another in this Avalokiteshvara Dharma assembly. Support one another and advance forward together. Forward to where? To wherever the depths of your hearts wish to go. Each of us should help others. Why do I say this? Because I fear you may take a wrong turn and get lost!

(Avalokiteshvara Session, March 15, 1976)

tieu_de: Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva Is Our Elder Brother
tom_tat: Every day we recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's name, but what does “Avalokiteshvara” mean? “Avalokita” means contemplating the sounds of the world. “Avalokita” also means looking—not looking outward, but looking into the minds of living beings, to see…
noi_dung:
Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva Is Our Elder Brother

Every day we recite the name of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, but what does "Avalokiteshvara" mean? "Avalokita" means contemplating the sounds of the world. "Avalokita" also means looking—not looking outward, but looking into the minds of living beings, to see whose mind is free of scattered discursive thoughts. With no more discursive thoughts and the mind empty, that is enlightenment. Hence it is said:

"Gathered together from the ten directions,

We study together the Dharma of non-action."

Reciting the name of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva is also a dharma of non-action. "Non-action" means doing nothing, yet leaving nothing undone—that is, it teaches us not to give rise to discursive thoughts.

When you recite "Nam Mô Quán Thế Âm Bồ-tát", Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva also recites you—the two sides recite each other, just as when you fondly remember your kin, your kin also remember you. We and Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva have, from limitless kalpas past until now, been kin in the Dharma, relatives in the Buddhadharma. Kin since when? Counting from the time of Amitabha Buddha! Amitabha Buddha is the Teaching Host of the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the West, and he is also the teacher of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva. Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva helps Amitabha propagate the Pure Land Dharma-door. We are none other than fellow disciples of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva. Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva is the eldest brother to all living beings who have not yet been reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and so living beings are his younger siblings. Put that way, it is clear that he and we are very close kin. Therefore, whenever we remember our elder brother, our elder brother also remembers us. We are Avalokiteshvara's younger siblings, and Avalokiteshvara is our elder brother.

Someone says: "How can Avalokiteshvara possibly be my elder brother? Isn't that going too far?" Not only does Avalokiteshvara regard us as younger siblings, he regards all living beings as his youngest siblings besides. If it were not so, why would he contemplate sounds and rescue the suffering? Why is it that whenever living beings meet with difficulty, he comes to their rescue? It is because he regards living beings as his own flesh and blood that he fears no hardship and goes to rescue all suffering beings in this Saha world. Therefore, do not forget your elder brother in the Dharma—each time we recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's name, Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva at once fondly remembers us.

When we recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's name, it is we who are calling out to our elder brother. When Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva calls our names, it is he who is calling his younger siblings—that is, the Bodhisattvas of the future, the Buddhas of the future.

Seeing Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva in this way, we must all the more recite the name of our own brother in the Dharma with sincerity and earnestness, and not let this opportunity slip by. When reciting Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's name, do not hang your head down; hold your head up, expressing a valiant and vigorous spirit. Do not look droopy and drowsy. When Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva sees your vigorous spirit, he will say to you: "Quickly take my hand!" And then he will lead you to the world of Ultimate Bliss.

Someone idly wonders: "Why is it that Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva just looks and looks from morning to night, while I am not allowed to look at anything?" Your "looking" and Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's "looking" are very different! Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva looks inward, while you look outward. Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva contemplates his own nature. His mind-nature is like a radar screen on which all living beings appear. Whatever discursive thoughts living beings have, he knows them all. He looks at the radar screen within, unlike the way you look. Because living beings are so far from him, even with a thousand hands and a thousand eyes, to look upon limitless beings would still not be enough hands, not enough eyes. Therefore he returns the light and reflects it inward, and turns the hearing around to listen to his own nature. He contemplates the own-nature of living beings to see who is suffering, and then he goes to rescue them. But you look outward, forgetting your own fundamental wisdom. Hence your looking and his looking are completely different.

Someone else thinks: "Master! I don't believe what you teach! Why don't I believe it? Because you say we are siblings with Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, yet he is a sage and we are common beings; how can common beings be siblings with a sage? That is unreasonable, so I don't believe it." Very good! You may disbelieve; what you say has its logic. But that logic belongs to the knowledge and views of common beings, for you have not deeply entered the Sutra Treasury and so lack wisdom as vast and deep as the sea.

The Avatamsaka Sutra teaches: "The Bodhisattva reflects thus: From beginningless kalpas past until now, I and living beings have been brothers, parents, sisters, husbands and wives to one another." That you say you do not believe is simply because you do not clearly understand the principle taught in the Avatamsaka Sutra.

Moreover, not only does the Bodhisattva see living beings this way—even the Buddha regards living beings as "all men are my fathers, all women are my mothers." If the Buddha regards living beings as his parents, then what is unreasonable about my saying that Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva regards living beings as his siblings? That you say you do not believe is just because you lack wisdom and knowledge. Or perhaps your view is too narrow, and so you have become deluded and disbelieve what I say.

Why does the Buddha wish to save living beings? Because he holds that "all men are my fathers, all women are my mothers." Since his fathers and mothers are suffering in the cycle of the six paths of rebirth, no matter what, he must rescue them and enable them to leave suffering and attain bliss.

Every day we recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, we bow to Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva; yet when he appears before us, we do not recognize him. So we living beings are truly pitiful! Why is it that Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva appears before us and we do not know it? This is a test for us. When you recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's name, you must learn to become like him. Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva has great kindness, great compassion, great vows, and great power; therefore, when reciting Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's name, we must learn to have great kindness, great compassion, great vows, and great power—if anyone treats us badly, let our minds be unmoved; if anyone scolds us, we must bear it in silence; if anyone beats us, we must endure it; and even if someone kills us, we must accept it, taking it as repayment of a debt! What is "repaying a debt"? For example, had we never scolded anyone in the past, no one would scold us now; had we never beaten anyone, no one would beat us now. Why is it that someone comes to scold, beat, or even kill us? Because in the past, when we were deluded, we scolded, beat, and killed others; therefore in this life we must settle those old debts in full. In the past, deluded, we owed debts and did not repay them. Today, understanding the Way, we must sincerely repay those debts in full. Once we have repaid all our debts, we will see Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva and become his kin in the Dharma.

So, having recited Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, whomever we meet, we must not go looking for their faults. If we keep picking at others' faults, our own suffering is not yet ended, and we have not yet cut off suffering at its root. Therefore, clearly recognize every state you meet, and penetrate to the root of every matter. In studying the Buddhadharma, you must know how to apply the Buddhadharma. If you do not know how to apply it, then no matter how long you cultivate, the Buddhadharma remains the Buddhadharma, and you remain you. When you know how to apply it, you merge into one with the Buddhadharma, with nothing separating you.

Patience is the most essential dharma. You must be able to endure what is hard to endure. For example, you dislike being scolded, yet when someone scolds you, gladly endure it. Though you dislike being beaten, when someone beats you, gladly bear it. You do not want to die, for human life is precious; yet if someone wants to kill you, regard them as liberating you from a lifetime of karmic obstacles—they are truly a Good Knowing Advisor. Friends! In studying the Buddhadharma, we must turn our attitude around and study; in cultivating the Way, we must turn our attitude around and cultivate! What does turning our attitude around mean? It means gladly doing what we formerly disliked doing, and never imposing on others what we ourselves dislike.

If you are just like ordinary people: unable to see through, unable to let go, unable to cut off attachment to "self" and to "dharmas," tightly holding the four discriminating views of self, others, living beings, and a life—then you will have endless trouble and vexation. If you know how to take a step back, everything naturally becomes calm, like a still sea and a clear sky. In studying the Buddhadharma, do not chase after what is lofty and recondite, for:

"The ordinary mind is the Way,

The straightforward mind is the Way-place."

(The ordinary mind—the mind without desires—is the Way;

The straightforward heart is the Way-place, the place of cultivation.)

That is why in cultivation we need an upright and straightforward heart.

When reciting Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, do not be greedy. Do not think: "If I recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's name, I'll get rich!" That can never be! When you are free of greed, wealth may come; once greed arises, you will gain nothing. When reciting Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, do not show off: "I've been here and there to join Avalokiteshvara Sessions. You've never joined one, so you're not my equal!" Do not give rise to such discursive thoughts, and do not crave fame, gain, or comfortable enjoyment.

When reciting Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, recite in an ordinary way; do not seek after anything. Do not imitate those who recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva while thinking: "I am childless; I pray Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva will give me a son." Some pray for a daughter; many young men recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva praying for a pretty girlfriend, and many young women recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva praying to meet a boyfriend—none of these can be had that way! When reciting Avalokiteshvara's name, sweep all such impure thoughts away. Do not harbor greed, anger, or delusion. For instance, when you put on clothes each day, do not mind whether they are fine or not—warmth is enough. When you eat each day, do not crave delicacies. If you harbor such thoughts, you are no longer reciting Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva with a true mind. If you sincerely recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, why would you still think of fine food and fine clothes? You should have forgotten all those things long ago! There is only one way: forget everything, and then we can merge into one with Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva.

Within the mind of every living being there is already an Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva. Right now, as we recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, we are reciting the Avalokiteshvara within our own minds. Someone says: "I look into my mind, but I can't find my mind anywhere!" If you had no mind, you wouldn't need to recite Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva at all. For that very absence (your having no mind to find) is Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva. Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva is precisely the absence of mind, because he never gives rise to discursive thoughts, nor has greed, anger, or delusion. He never schemes over what fine clothes to wear today, what delicious dish to eat, or what offerings to enjoy. He is attached to nothing and seeks nothing. What he does is rescue living beings, vowing that all beings may leave suffering and attain bliss, end birth and death, and accomplish the Buddha Way. He seeks nothing from living beings. He hopes living beings can truly understand the Buddhadharma and completely rid themselves of greed, anger, and delusion.

When reciting Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, do not chatter idly all day: "No breakfast in the morning, no tea at night—this is too miserable! I can't stand it anymore; quickly pack up and run!" Cultivating that way is utterly worthless!

(Explained on March 16, 1976)

tieu_de: Instructions for the Amitabha Session
tom_tat: In the Saha world, everyone loves pleasure and hates suffering. Beings in the hells love suffering and hate pleasure. Hungry ghosts love anger and hate compassion. Animals, fond of stupidity…
noi_dung:
Instructions for the Amitabha Session

In the Saha world, everyone loves pleasure and hates suffering. Beings in the hells love suffering and hate pleasure. Hungry ghosts love anger and hate compassion. Animals, because they loved stupidity and hated wisdom, fell into animality.

Although people love happiness and hate suffering, they do not know how to be free of suffering. In the heavens, everyone loves pleasure and hates suffering. Meanwhile, for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, their state has neither suffering nor pleasure. They have completely forgotten both states of suffering and joy. Most living beings are upside down—taking right for wrong and wrong for right, black for white and white for black. In the end, do living beings know they are upside down? They do! Yet though they know, they still do wrong; though they clearly understand a thing is irrational, they insist on doing it; though they know what is right, they refuse to do it.

For example, some people go off to drink tea right in the middle of Buddha-recitation. Drinking tea also has its set time; it cannot be done casually, anytime and anywhere. Using Buddha-recitation time to drink tea is laziness. "Reciting the Buddha is too tiring; I'll go drink a cup of tea and rest a while"—that is being lazy. If you sincerely recited the Buddha, how would you still think of drinking tea? You would long ago have completely forgotten about drinking tea, let alone drinking milk, for you must forget everything! One who truly recites the Buddha does not even know whether he has eaten, let alone drinking tea?

Someone says: "Reciting the Buddha that way is too dangerous, because it makes you forget even whether you've eaten!" Yet this is precisely the skill of those who truly apply effort—whether they have eaten or not, they do not know; whether they have dressed or not, they do not remember; whether they have rested or not, they are unaware. Forgetting everything! Daytime? Don't know! Nighttime? Don't know. Above, no sky is seen; below, no earth is seen; in between, no people are known—everything is empty. When all things are empty, how could you still remember drinking tea or drinking milk?

At Gold Mountain Monastery there is a monk who dares not drink milk. For after drinking milk, sexual desire arises and cannot be controlled; therefore he does not drink milk. We eat and drink to sustain life, taking food as medicine. Without eating we would starve, so we eat to stay alive—it is not that we need nourishing foods to pamper the body. When food is too rich, there is great trouble.

One who practices the Buddha-recitation Dharma-door must remember at all times to recite only the single phrase "Nam Mô A Di Đà Phật", without ever stopping. Recite it awake, recite it asleep. You must recite the six-syllable honored name "Nam Mô A Di Đà Phật" so that nothing can interrupt it—even a sword could not cut it off. The power of Buddha-recitation must be firm, surpassing even the hardness of vajra. When no means at all can destroy your recitation of "Nam Mô A Di Đà Phật", only then is it called "Buddha-recitation samadhi."

Not only Buddha-recitation is so, but Sutra recitation and mantra holding are the same. In that state, even if you wanted to give rise to discursive thoughts, you could not. Cultivation is no easy matter. Look at Master Heng Sure: why doesn't he drink milk? Because he knows the harm in milk! As soon as he drinks cow's milk, the "cow nature" at once flares up. And when that "cow nature" (sexual desire) flares up, it is fiercer than a tiger!

Ordinarily, if the body lacks no nutrition, there is no need for rich supplements. Eating rich foods brings all kinds of trouble. Hence, "excess is just like deficiency"—going too far and falling short are both unwholesome.

Living beings in this Saha world—every movement, every act is greed, anger, and delusion. Cultivating worldly dharmas, beings use greed, anger, and delusion to cultivate. Cultivating world-transcending dharmas, they still use greed, anger, and delusion to cultivate. Thus, as they cultivate they crave enlightenment—sitting in Chan for two and a half days and already wanting to become enlightened, practicing not yet three days and demanding spiritual powers, reciting the Buddha only a few days and demanding Buddha-recitation samadhi. Just see how enormous their greed is! These are all expressions of hungry ghosts.

We should treat cultivation as our own duty, with no need for greed—in time, merit and virtue will be perfected, and the fruit of Bodhi will naturally ripen. Cultivation would already have succeeded, but just because you are too greedy, in the end you cannot "digest" it. Like eating rice: you must chew one mouthful at a time; if you cram a whole bowl into your mouth at once, your mouth full, how can you eat? You can neither chew nor swallow. Eating is a very simple example. Hence the saying: "The greedy bite off more than they can chew."

In cultivation, you must cultivate as if cultivating nothing at all. Do not give rise to greed, nor calculate what you will become or what you will get. You want enlightenment, you want spiritual powers; but how could you attain results so quickly? When a seed is sown in the ground, you must wait for it to slowly grow tall; and when the time is full, it will ripen. The ancients taught:

"Grind an iron rod into a needle;

With enough effort, it naturally becomes."

Do not fear wasted effort; when the time is full, even iron will be ground into a needle—with effort in grinding iron, the day comes when it becomes a needle.

In cultivation, the essential point is to eradicate all bad habits and faults. What are bad habits and faults? Fondness for tea is a fault, fondness for milk is a fault, fondness for giving rise to scattered discursive thoughts is also a fault. If you crave comfort, your skill will win no sympathetic response. In applying effort, do not fear suffering, hardship, or fatigue—only then will cultivation succeed. Here I must apologize to you, for I love to joke, so those of you who are plump, after hearing my talks, please do not go on a diet to shed fat and slim down. Otherwise, I fear you will be "putting a head on top of your head"—doing useless things and creating all kinds of afflictions for yourselves.

Today, the whole world is everywhere filled with natural and man-made calamities. Everywhere has turned dark, without light, showing that humankind's very existence is gravely threatened. That murderous atmosphere is truly unprecedented. You have heard of the atomic bomb, the hydrogen bomb, nuclear weapons, and now there is the laser besides. Should such weapons ever be used, all humanity would surely perish. Thus the entire globe is now shrouded in a dark, sinister aura, and dark evil karma blankets the land. The only way to dispel such calamities is for us to rely on the Buddhadharma in our cultivation. Wherever there are people truly cultivating, there calamities will lessen. If many people join together in cultivation, the collective strength can eradicate calamities, dissolving that cruel, poisonous aura into an air of peace and auspiciousness. For this, everyone must truly practice, genuinely walking the Way according to the Buddhadharma.

Recite the Buddha with sincerity. With each recitation of the Buddha, a beam of light appears in empty space. If you sincerely and earnestly recite the Buddha, that beam of light will shine throughout the great trichiliocosm, and can dissolve all pollution, violence, and calamity, making the atmosphere of the great trichiliocosm wholesome.

The City of Ten Thousand Buddhas is a luminous place in this world, radiating light throughout the universe. If you give rise to discursive thoughts even while at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas, you still earn merit—greater merit, in fact, than the greatest merit you could earn in the outside world. Why do I say this? Because everyone at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas turns toward goodness, so even their discursive thoughts are mostly good ones; rarely do they think of evil. Thus you could say the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas is the sun and moon of the world, shining everywhere and bringing all beings purity and coolness.

All who dwell at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas planted many good roots long ago. They once vowed to improve the world and dissolve all calamities. Therefore, dwelling at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas, you must walk the proper path in cultivation—in every act and every word. Do not follow along with bad or vulgar people. Those who live at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas are all good, upstanding people. Those with fierce temperaments and evil minds, sooner or later, will be unable to stay and will leave the monastery of their own accord.

The City of Ten Thousand Buddhas, rising from the earth in the West, is where Buddhists of the whole world will gather in the future to cultivate and study the Buddhadharma together, making Buddhism ever more radiant. Whoever can leave home and cultivate the Way at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas will certainly become a Buddha in the future. Why? Because:

The tower by the water sees the moon first.

(Whoever dwells in the tower beside the lake will see the moon's reflection first.)

If you come to the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas early, you will become a Buddha early.

Whoever comes later will become a Buddha later.

Many people come to the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas but feel they cannot stay, because they find little going on here, the rules too strict, and nothing fun. But you should know: chasing outer pleasures, you will lose true joy. In life, seeking what is false, you lose what is true. To find what is true, you must first let go of what is false and hollow. You cannot both cultivate the world-transcending Way and cling to ordinary worldly dharmas—like stepping into two boats at once, wanting to sail north of the river yet also south. That cannot be done!

In this Buddha-recitation Session, you must "deeply enter through a single door"—focusing on one Dharma-door—relying only on a true, sincere, and reverent heart in practicing Buddha-recitation, without wasting even a minute. Know that a moment of time is a moment of life. Without effort, your offenses only grow. With true effort, your good roots grow. Therefore, sincerely and earnestly recite the Buddha; only then will your time not be wasted, and only then will your life have true worth.

(Explained in winter, 1979, at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas)

tieu_de: Rules of the Chan Session
tom_tat: In 1959, the Dharma Realm Buddhist Association was founded. Its predecessor was the Sino-American Buddhist Association. From its founding until now, every year the Association has held many Buddha-recitation…
noi_dung:
Rules of the Chan Session

In 1959, the Dharma Realm Buddhist Association was founded. Its predecessor was the Sino-American Buddhist Association. From its founding until now, every year the Association has held many Buddha-recitation Sessions and Chan Sessions; yet those Sessions have all been conducted in silence, so very few people know that Buddha-recitation Sessions or Chan Sessions are held at Gold Mountain Monastery. That is because we do not advertise or seek publicity, nor do we seek after external conditions—we simply cultivate genuinely. If anyone hears that a Chan Session is being held and wishes to join, they are still welcome. But we absolutely do not solicit or call on others for support, saying: "Gold Mountain Monastery is holding a Session, and there are several 'no-mind cultivators' practicing there. Come make offerings and your merit will be limitless." From the beginning until now, we have never trumpeted ourselves that way!

In China, whenever a Chan Session is held, the offerings from donors can cover expenses for a whole year, sometimes with surplus besides. During a Session, a great many laypeople resolve to make offerings to form good affinities, supplying the monastery with goods such as rice, noodles, oil, soy sauce, dried foods, and so on.

In America, Buddhism is still in its infancy, so we must transform the mistakes of the past and head toward perfection. There is a saying: "A good beginning is half the work done." We do not use tactics to gain offerings. Had we used the tactics and methods used in China, we might have been more successful!

Why do we not seek offerings? Because first of all we must cultivate sincerely and accord with the arrangement of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. When the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, the eightfold division of gods and dragons, and the Dharma-protecting good spirits see us applying effort in cultivating the Way, they will naturally bring about sympathetic response. If we do not cultivate genuinely, then even if people come to make offerings, we should feel deeply ashamed, for:

If the three minds are not ended, even water is hard to digest;

If the Five Contemplations are understood, even gold is easily digested.

(If the past, present, and future minds are not ended, then even a glass of water offered by a donor cannot be digested.

But if the principle of the Five Contemplations is understood, then even gold and iron are easily digested.)

If we have not yet severed the three minds (the past mind, the present mind, and the future mind), then even a glass of water offered by a donor cannot be digested. But if we clearly understand the principle of the Five Contemplations, then even gold and iron are easily digested. What are the Five Contemplations?

Reflect on how much labor went into producing this bowl of rice.

Consider whether your own virtue is complete or deficient in accepting this offering.

Guard your mind, keeping it far from error, whose roots are greed, anger, and delusion.

Regard food as medicine, taking it to cure the withering of the body.

Accept this food only in order to accomplish the karma of the Way.

Tonight the Chan Session begins. The Chan Session at our Gold Mountain Monastery is very different from Chan Sessions in monasteries in China. Their Chan Sessions are really "eating sessions," because every night they eat steamed buns! Even Gold Mountain Monastery in Zhenjiang and Gaomin Monastery in Yangzhou are no exception. A great many meditators make a point of attending Sessions at monasteries that serve evening buns. Wherever the buns are good, they go. They do not judge the quality of the Chan Session, only whether the buns are big or small, tasty or bland. Thus some monasteries are famous for their big, delicious, fragrant buns. I say this with no intent to slander monastics who cannot let go of food and drink—it is simply that such things really happen.

This Gold Mountain Monastery has no custom of eating buns—not even a small bite for a snack.

In China, during a Chan Session a great many laypeople come to make offerings to the meditators. After one hour of sitting, a layperson comes to offer four longans. After the next sitting, someone else offers two peanut candies or a piece of pastry. In short, after every hour of Chan someone comes with offerings, stirring greed in those "mindless cultivators," who eat until their bellies bulge and can no longer sit still. At this monastery such things will not happen; that is the difference.

Each morning, sitting begins at two-thirty, followed by walking meditation—continuously until midnight, when we rest. You must practice asceticism, train bitterly. You must do what no one else can do. But if you do not hang the two words "birth and death" before your eyes, and instead complain you haven't slept enough, then sit there entering the "sound-sleep samadhi"—if that is how it is, you will never accomplish anything.

You must join the Session "heedless of death, forgetting life." You must truly apply effort in the Session. You must reap the results you are meant to reap—only then is it of use. Do not "drift with the waves," doing whatever others do. Seeing someone sit, you sit; seeing someone sleep, you sleep—that will not do; it only wastes time and does you no good at all.

In the past I joined Chan Sessions in many places. Nowhere was I ever struck by the incense monitor (the one who patrols and strikes drowsy meditators awake with a stick). Why? Because I never dozed off. By day I sat in the Chan Hall, by night I also sat in the Chan Hall—all twenty-four hours of the day I sat in the Chan Hall, knowing nothing of rest or snoring. Not even a second did I waste—at every moment I applied the skill I had to apply, at every moment I kept my skill raised up.

All of you here are people of deep good roots, intelligent, possessed of wisdom. You must treat this cultivation as truly important; do not go through the motions. In this Chan Session, someone must become enlightened. If no one becomes enlightened, then when the Session ends, each of you will take a beating of a hundred blows! If you feel you can bear a hundred blows, then you need not become enlightened; if you cannot bear it, then strive to become enlightened! If anyone fears a beating, right now, before the Session begins, you may withdraw! Once you have joined, you must stay from beginning to end—no quitting halfway. By the rule of the Chan Hall, you have already bid farewell to life and death—if anyone dies, the corpse is simply tucked beneath the sitting bench and may not be carried outside. All the more, when no one has died, you may not quit halfway.

Right here you must draw the line between life and death. If not alive, then dead; if not dead, then alive:

Unable to cast aside death, you cannot exchange it for life.

Unable to cast aside the false, you cannot realize the true.

(If you cannot throw away death, you cannot trade it for life.

If you cannot throw away the false, you cannot realize the true.)

That is the threshold of Gold Mountain Monastery. So in this year's Chan Session, you must be utterly vigorous. No matter what, you must recognize your own "original face." If you do not recognize your "original face," no one may think of slipping out Gold Mountain Monastery's great gate! If you sneak away, you will be "put in prison"! That, roughly, is the rule of this year's Chan Session; I hope you will all comply!

(Explained on January 6, 1974, at Gold Mountain Monastery, San Francisco)

tieu_de: Investigate the Hua-tou: Using a Discursive Thought to Subdue Discursive Thoughts
tom_tat: In the Chan Hall we do not recite the Buddha's name; during a Buddha-recitation Session we do not investigate Chan. Now, we must “walk in Chan, sit in Chan, stand in Chan, lie down in Chan”—in short…
noi_dung:
Investigate the Hua-tou: Using a Discursive Thought to Subdue Discursive Thoughts

The Chan Session is about to begin.

In the Chan Hall we do not recite the Buddha's name; during a Buddha-recitation Session we do not investigate Chan. Now, we must "walk in Chan, sit in Chan, stand in Chan, lie down in Chan"—in short, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, we investigate Chan.

In the past, one who investigated Chan never gave rise to a single thought; that is called "no thought":

When not a single thought arises, the whole is revealed.

When the six senses suddenly stir, it is covered by clouds.

(When not a single thought arises, the whole (the true mind) appears.

When the six senses suddenly stir, (the Buddha-nature) is covered by clouds.)

To investigate Chan is to investigate "not a single thought arising." It was not until the Ming dynasty that people adopted the method of "investigating the hua-tou." Nowadays every Chan Hall investigates the hua-tou. There are many kinds of hua-tou, such as "Who is reciting the Buddha's name?" or "Before my parents gave birth to me, what did my face look like?" or "What is 'nothing'?" and so on.

To investigate Chan is to give rise to no discursive thoughts at all. For example, when investigating "Who is reciting the Buddha's name?" you keep reflecting, seeking to find who it is that recites the Buddha's name. But in fact this too is just a discursive thought; it is only that we use one discursive thought to control all other discursive thoughts. This method is called "using the false to control the false, using poison to counter poison." Even reciting "Amitabha Buddha" is "using the false to control the false"; that is, the thought of reciting the Buddha is false, not real. And even the thought investigating "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name" is false—but this one discursive thought has the power to control all other discursive thoughts. That is the principle of investigating Chan.

One who investigates Chan "kills the Buddha when a Buddha comes, kills the demon when a demon comes," attached to no state at all. When your investigation reaches the point where "above, you do not know there is sky; below, you do not know there is earth; in between, you do not know there are people; outside, you do not know there are things; within, you do not know there is mind," then you will merge into one with the Dharma Realm and may suddenly become enlightened. Remember: do not be swayed by the dust of sound (outer conditions), do not look east and gaze west, and do not let your mind waver and scatter!

When your Chan investigation reaches "no self, no others, no living beings, no life," you will sever the root of birth and death and will meet Shakyamuni Buddha face to face—only then will you know the wonder of investigating Chan.

From limitless kalpas until today, we are truly fortunate to have met the Dharma-door of "joining a Chan Session." Therefore we must be especially single-minded, sincere and earnest, and apply effort vigorously; do not squander precious time, do not idle away thoughts on food, clothing, or lodging, for "a moment of time is a moment of life"—time and life are equally precious:

An inch of time, an inch of gold;

An inch of gold cannot buy an inch of time.

An inch of gold lost is easily regained;

Time once gone is hard to find again.

Meaning:

An inch of time is an inch of gold,

Yet an inch of gold cannot buy an inch of time.

An inch of gold lost is still easily found,

But time slipped away is hard to seek again.

This poem speaks of the preciousness of time in ordinary days—how much more precious is time during a Session.

No one knows in which minute or second they will become enlightened; therefore, make use of every second and minute—do not waste them. I hope all who join this Chan Session will be valiant and vigorous, never lax or indulgent. Only by enduring every hardship will you attain bliss. To bear what others can hardly bear, to endure what others can hardly endure—that is the spirit of cultivating the Way!

(Explained in September 1975 at Gold Mountain Monastery)

tieu_de: Cultivate Genuinely; Do Not Be Lax
tom_tat: Gold Mountain Monastery was formerly called the Buddhist Lecture Hall, located on the fourth floor of an apartment building in San Francisco's Chinatown, established by the Dharma Realm Buddhist Association. The first summer…
noi_dung:
Cultivate Genuinely; Do Not Be Lax

Gold Mountain Monastery was formerly called the Buddhist Lecture Hall, located on the fourth floor of an apartment building in San Francisco's Chinatown, and was established by the Dharma Realm Buddhist Association. The first summer study session was held here in 1968. At that time a great many people came from Seattle to join that 96-day session. The study schedule was very demanding, with no rest each day; only Saturday afternoons were free, for laundry or personal matters.

During that session I lectured on the Shurangama Sutra, planning to finish before the session ended. At first I lectured once a day, but after a while I saw we would not meet the deadline, so I increased it to twice a day. Gradually, still fearing we could not finish, I raised it to three times a day; and in the end it became four times a day. And so, in that summer session the Shurangama Sutra was completed, with its perfected merit dedicated to all beings.

After the Shurangama Sutra lectures ended, five young American men and women sought to leave home. These were the first Americans to leave home and receive the Complete Precepts—three Bhikshus and two Bhikshunis.

Afterward, every year there has been a summer study session. A great many people came to study the Buddhadharma, and many left home to become Bhikshus and Bhikshunis. Though the numbers were not large, for Gold Mountain Monastery—which values quality, not quantity—genuine cultivation and study of the Buddhadharma is what matters: even one person is not too few, let alone that there were more than one or two!

Each month Gold Mountain Monastery publishes a bilingual Chinese-English magazine—Vajra Bodhi Sea. This magazine presents the essential meaning of the Buddhadharma so that Westerners can understand the origins of Buddhism and gain a correct understanding of the Buddhadharma, and no longer regard Buddhism as superstition, idol worship, negativity, pessimism, or a "parasite" on society. This magazine shows people that Buddhism means freedom and equality, with the goal of promoting world peace, and that everyone alike is a disciple of the Buddha—with absolutely no barriers of race, nationality, or territory. Since its beginnings, Buddhism has never caused a war, because the very first precept of Buddhist morality is No Killing—not only must one not kill people, one must not kill even animals; on the contrary, one frees and protects all living creatures—and so no wars are ever caused!

Gold Mountain Monastery is like a place that "sifts sand in search of gold"—if you are "gold," then when you come to Gold Mountain Monastery you will feel as if it were your own home. Here, no one chats, so it is very convenient for reading—studying the Buddhadharma day after day, disturbed by no one—truly an ideal setting! Though Americans are many, how many sincerely resolve to come here to study the Buddhadharma, to hear Sutras and learn the Dharma? Thus, becoming a Buddha depends on the individual, not on the group. In this world, whatever is rare is precious—though the number studying the Buddhadharma at Gold Mountain Monastery is small, to this world it is incomparably precious! In the future, once you have penetrated the Buddhadharma, you can go everywhere to propagate it, benefit beings, and lead all beings to soon accomplish the Buddha Way—that is what I expect of you!

In this summer session, everyone must treasure time and let none of it go to waste. There is a saying:

"An inch of time is an inch of gold,

But an inch of gold cannot redeem an inch of time."

Time, then, is the most precious, the most important thing. All of you joining this year's summer session, strive to learn the Buddhadharma; do not let time slip by in vain—you must surely learn some true principle.

There is something I wish to tell you. Truly I did not want to say it, but now I cannot remain silent. What is it? Those who have left home must know self-respect: do not think too lowly of yourselves, yet do not be arrogant and conceited either; always reflect and examine yourselves—if you have made any mistake, correct it at once; if you are faultless, advance further; absolutely do not be careless, lax, or indulgent.

Once you are my left-home disciples, whenever I see a fault in you I will surely point it out so you may know and correct it. If I did not speak, I would truly be failing you. Once I have spoken what I have seen, whether you listen or not, whether you reform or not—that is your affair. I only fulfill a teacher's duty, with a clear conscience. Do not wait until you have fallen into the hells to blame your Master: "Oh! Why didn't my Master teach me more strictly at the start? Had he taught me more carefully, more sternly, how could I have fallen into the hells?"

Now I have said what I wished to say; those of you who have left home must remember: you must not disturb or interfere with the freedom of others, nor affect their actions. If you yourself do not wish to cultivate, so be it—but do not obstruct the cultivation of others; if you yourself do not uphold the precepts, do not hinder others from upholding them; if you yourself do not foster virtue, do not block others from refining their virtue! Whoever harbors such thoughts and conduct must reform at once, "turning evil into good." Those who have left home must watch over themselves every second, every minute—every word, every deed must always accord with the precepts. You must be earnest, never indulgent or undisciplined; you may not do whatever you please. There is a saying:

Without rules, no square or circle can be made.

(Without standards, nothing square or round can be formed.)

Thus, when the Buddha was about to enter Nirvana, he instructed Venerable Ananda: "Take the precepts as your teacher!" That is what those who have left home must engrave upon their hearts.

When eating, we must remember the Three Recollections and the Five Contemplations, for:

A single grain of rice from a donor

Is heavy as Mount Sumeru.

Having eaten it, if you do not cultivate,

You will repay it wearing fur and horns.

(A single grain of a donor's rice

Weighs as much as Mount Sumeru.

Eat it and fail to cultivate,

And you will repay it bearing fur and horns.)

It is that dreadful, that dangerous, all of you! This is called "losing the human body right beneath the kasaya robe"! Therefore, those who have left home, wherever they are, must strictly uphold the precepts—until birth and death are ended and the mind of sexual desire is severed, never for a moment be lazy, lax, or indulgent. Samantabhadra Bodhisattva teaches:

"A day has passed, and life likewise decreases,

Like a fish in shallow water—what joy is there in that?

Great assembly!

Be vigorous and diligent, as if your head were ablaze;

Remember impermanence always, and never be lax!"

We who have left home must treasure every second and minute; remember that:

"An inch of time is an inch of gold, yet an inch of gold cannot redeem an inch of time."

Time is so precious that we must not waste it. Everyone must apply effort in cultivation, ever more vigorously, if accomplishment is to be hoped for. Those who truly apply effort have no time for gossip about others' rights and wrongs, no time for scattered busyness that interrupts cultivation. On this point, I hope everyone will take heed.

When I see people unwilling to cultivate, I feel boundless grief—for have they not failed to carry out the vows they made at the very start, when they first left home to cultivate? Can those who have left home yet whose "minds think one thing while their mouths say another" be worthy of the Sangha Jewel? I hope you will all know self-respect!

tieu_de: Using Electrotherapy to Purify the Air
tom_tat: The Chan Dharma-door directly points at people's minds: see the nature, become a Buddha. It is also the Sudden Teaching, which comes about through diligent cultivation of the Gradual Teaching. Hence the saying…
noi_dung:
Using Electrotherapy to Purify the Air

The Chan Dharma-door is the dharma of directly pointing at people's minds, seeing the nature and becoming a Buddha; it is also the Sudden Teaching. The Sudden Teaching comes about through diligent cultivation of the Gradual Teaching. Hence the saying:

"Though the principle is suddenly awakened to, practice is cultivated gradually."

(Though the meaning may be understood in an instant, practice must proceed step by step.)

Right now, walking, standing, lying down, and sitting are all gradual practice. Wait until some day you truly understand, and you will suddenly become enlightened. That is "sudden." In fact, "sudden" is inseparable from "gradual"; "gradual" is precisely what aids "sudden."

Usually, cultivators each claim the dharma they practice is the finest, number one. If it were not number one, they would be unhappy, and they would refuse to cultivate. If you truly understood, then all dharmas are the Buddhadharma and all are unattainable (ungraspable); hence there is nothing worth clinging to.

Chan is a way of harmonizing body and mind. "Harmonizing the body" means keeping the body from agitation. "Harmonizing the mind" means keeping the mind from giving rise to discursive thoughts, ever pure. Once the mind is pure, all of empty space and the entire Dharma Realm lie within your own nature. Your own nature contains all things, embraces all things, and is precisely our Buddha-nature of old.

From limitless kalpas until now, life after life, we have been so deeply tainted by wrong views that it is not easy to understand the mind and see the nature. For this reason we "join a Chan Session." "Joining a Session" is called "setting a fixed period to win realization"—that is, fixing a definite time and a definite course for applying effort, seeking to attain penetrating clarity.

If you wish to truly penetrate and understand, first you must learn to act as if you knew nothing at all. In the Chan Hall, in applying effort, what method do you use? The method of "not knowing"—above, not knowing there is sky; below, not knowing there is earth; in between, not knowing there are people. From morning to night, what are you doing? Don't know! What food are you eating? Don't know! What clothes are you wearing? Don't know! As if in a stupor, knowing nothing at all. There is a saying:

Nurture great clumsiness, and only then is there skill;

Learn to be as a fool, and only then is wonder seen.

That is, if you can become like the stupidest person in the world, only then will marvelous skill arise. At that point:

Penetrate one, and penetrate them all;

Understand one, and understand them all;

Awaken to one, and awaken to them all.

(Penetrate one thing, and penetrate all things.

Clarify one thing, and clarify all things.

Awaken to one thing, and awaken to all things.)

Then you will penetrate all things and become thoroughly enlightened. What have you learned? Don't know—just like a fool. Yet right then, wonders appear.

When joining a Chan Session, you must set aside petty cleverness and sly shrewdness. Do not suppose you know and understand everything. To suppose you know everything is not true understanding of the Buddhadharma. There is a saying:

"Great wisdom appears as folly."

(One of great wisdom looks as if dull-witted.)

Outwardly they seem to understand nothing, yet in fact they understand everything. That is called "hazy on small matters, clear on great ones." Whoever is like that is one of great accomplishment.

In the Chan Hall, when the assembly runs, we run; when the assembly sits, we sit—east, west, south, north, we need not know. Then we will truly understand, truly comprehend. Understand what? Understand the "scenery of our homeland." Comprehend what? Comprehend our own "original face."

In the Chan Hall, apply effort in cultivation, speak fewer useless words, and waste no time.

"An inch of time is an inch of gold,

But an inch of gold cannot buy an inch of time."

Sitting in Chan is truly most precious. No one knows in which minute or second you will become enlightened, so seize every minute and second and let none slip by. If you go to the restroom, return to the Chan Hall at once and keep sitting. At the dining hall, finish eating and return to the Chan Hall at once; finish your tea and return to the Chan Hall at once. In short, do not miss your chance at enlightenment, for no one knows when that moment will be. In other words, circling, running, or sitting in Chan are all fine chances for enlightenment—let none slip by.

In the Qing dynasty, Emperor Yongzheng once invited Abbot Tianhui of Gaomin Monastery to Beijing to discuss the principles of Chan. The emperor asked whether he knew the tenet of National Master Yulin, and he could not answer. The emperor then ordered him to remain in the Chan Hall and find the answer within seven days, or lose his head. For six days he could not find the answer. On the last day, in extreme urgency, he ran round and round the Chan Hall. Running back and forth made him dizzy, and he crashed headlong into a pillar, raising a bump on his head! In that very instant his mind turned suddenly bright, and he found the answer. He then went to see the emperor. Emperor Yongzheng knew he had grasped National Master Yulin's tenet. From then on began the custom of circling (running incense) in the Chan Hall.

The Chan Hall has walking incense, running incense, sitting incense, and investigating the hua-tou. Walking incense means stepping briskly. Running incense means jogging slowly. Sitting incense means sitting in Chan. Investigating the hua-tou means turning a question over in the mind—as in investigating "Who is reciting the Buddha's name?" Wholeheartedly investigating that phrase, investigating to the point of single-minded unity, unstained by a single mote of dust—that is the moment of enlightenment. These are all methods to prevent and halt discursive thoughts. Only without discursive thoughts can there be awakening. The purpose of sitting in Chan is enlightenment. After enlightenment comes transcendental wisdom.

Thus the Patriarchs studied the method of "using poison to counter poison," using the investigation of the hua-tou to control discursive thoughts—that is, using one question to control all other questions. What hua-tou to investigate? Investigate "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" When you find out "who," when you thoroughly understand "Who is reciting the Buddha's name?"—only then do you truly penetrate. Penetrate what? Penetrate the need to stay far from all that is upside down and contentious.

The Heart Sutra teaches:

"Far apart from upside-down dream-like thinking, and reach Ultimate Nirvana."

This process requires a bout of bitter effort to succeed. If I speak too much, I will interrupt your skill. Best that you follow the rules, and truly apply effort in cultivation.

One thing you must understand is that in the "Three Character Classic" there is a line:

"What is precious is concentration."

(What is precious is singleness of purpose.)

Whatever you do, if you can focus wholeheartedly, the outcome will be success. Likewise, when investigating the hua-tou, think only of that one phrase—think of it morning and evening, while eating and sleeping, while walking and sitting; until you have pondered it to the point where "seas run dry and rocks split open," never give up. In other words, "unenlightened, never rest." Thinking of a single question alone is the truth; thinking of too many questions is discursive thought.

Two lines of verse are truly full of meaning:

If one sits still for but a brief moment,

It surpasses building seven-jeweled stupas as many as the Ganges' sands.

(If one sits in stillness for a single instant,

It exceeds building seven-jeweled stupas as many as the Ganges' sands.)

That describes the merit of sitting in Chan: if a meditator can still the mind for even a short while, that merit exceeds manyfold the merit of building stupas—as many as the Ganges' sands—of seven jewels. For raising countless stupas is at most an offering to the Buddha's sharira; but sitting still for an instant can fashion the Buddha's true body. Hence sitting still for an instant surpasses building many seven-jeweled stupas.

If sitting still for a moment holds such merit, then sitting day after day holds merit beyond reckoning. If in a brief span you give rise to no discursive thoughts and the mind is pure, gradually you will become "limpid and ever still."

Sitting still in the Chan Hall, your merit is not only limitless—for all humankind, that merit is also limitless. Someone asks: "How can my merit be shared with humankind, with the whole world?" People of today's world, scrambling for fame and gain, create a soaring murderous aura—selfish and self-serving, each scheming against the other—turning the world dark and gloomy, filled with poison. Humankind's strife grows ever fiercer, ever more dangerous, ever graver. If we find no way to rescue the world from the crisis enveloping it, surely one day the earth will explode! Why explode? Because science is now so advanced that the great powers are researching ever swifter weapons of murder, racing to build nuclear arms, laser beams, and the like.

Once war breaks out, such weapons will turn the earth to ashes. That will truly be humankind's last day.

Applying effort in cultivation in the Chan Hall, invisibly we can destroy that murderous aura and spare the world its crisis. How to destroy it? The air has been polluted by poisons, and directly or indirectly those poisons affect the health of beings, threatening the lives of all. Just look: nowadays strange illnesses grow ever more numerous, leaving doctors helpless. That is because the air is polluted, no longer fresh and clean—everywhere nothing but poison. We who cultivate the Way must use a kind of electrotherapy to dissolve the poisons in the air. What is "electrotherapy"? It is sitting still, from which the light of wisdom radiates. This light of wisdom is precisely an electric current. That current travels through space and detoxifies, turning turbid air into pure air. That is called healing the world's ills by electrotherapy.

Now someone doubts whether this principle is feasible: "How can sitting still dissolve poisons in the air?" Let me tell a story: in the Song dynasty there was a great man of letters named Su Dongpo. At that time there was also a Chan Master named Fo Yin. The two were friends in the Way, often visiting each other, as shown by this couplet testifying to their close friendship:

Coming and going, the monk is always Fo Yin.

Back and forth, no guest but Dongpo.

(Going out or in: Master Fo Yin is ever near.

To and fro: if not Dongpo's company, whose else?)

Once Su Dongpo composed a verse:

I bow my head to the God among gods;

His light shines upon the great chiliocosm.

The eight winds cannot move him;

Seated upright upon the purple-golden lotus.

(I bow to the God among gods (that is, the Buddha);

His light shines upon the universe.

The eight winds blow him not;

Firmly seated on the golden lotus throne.)

Su Dongpo sent it to Chan Master Fo Yin for comment, and the two fell into dispute over it. Now let us take the line "His light shines upon the universe" to illustrate a principle. This light is precisely electrotherapy, shining upon the entire great chiliocosm and dissolving its poisons. This light can dispel the turbid air of the universe, cleansing it utterly until not a trace of poison remains.

If you can radiate light shining throughout the universe, then your share of poison will dissolve. If others can radiate light shining throughout the universe, then their share of poison will be dispelled. If everyone can radiate light shining throughout the universe, then everyone's poison will be dissolved.

If all people join hearts and forces, using electrotherapy to heal the world's ills, then polluted air will steadily lessen and fresh air will steadily increase. Gradually the atmosphere will become wholly pure. Know that turbid air is poison, while fresh air is wisdom.

Why is the air polluted today? Because most people do not know how to cultivate, do not know how to use electrotherapy, so the air grows ever more turbid. We who cultivate the Way must take up the duty of making the air pure. Not only must we ourselves vigorously cultivate Chan, we must also encourage friends and kin to sit in Chan. The merit of sitting in Chan is limitless, with inconceivable benefit for body and mind. If they do not believe, tell them to try the experiment—sooner or later they will gain inconceivable benefit. Strive in sitting Chan. When your light shines throughout the great chiliocosm, the poisons in the air will naturally all be destroyed.

Take heed! You need only halt discursive thoughts, and you can radiate the light of wisdom. This light can shine throughout the great chiliocosm and purge the poisons in the air. You will reap limitless merit benefiting all humankind. What benefit? The power to dissolve the poisons polluting the air, so humankind no longer suffers calamity from grave illnesses. That is precisely indirect benefit to everyone.

tieu_de: Demons Come to Help You Cultivate the Way
tom_tat: I once said: “If one can sit still for a brief moment, it surpasses building seven-jeweled stupas as many as the Ganges' sands.” Someone sitting in the Chan Hall idly thinks…
noi_dung:
Demons Come to Help You Cultivate the Way

I once said: "If one can sit still for a brief moment, it surpasses building seven-jeweled stupas as many as the Ganges' sands." Someone sitting in the Chan Hall idly thinks: "Sitting still for a moment holds more merit than building seven-jeweled stupas"; then thinking back and forth, he cannot sit still for even an instant, and so gains not a shred of merit! Why? It is like mistaking the finger for the moon—seeing only the finger pointing at the moon without seeing the moon—and then claiming limitless merit! Limitless? You are just sitting there with limitless discursive thoughts!

Then he says: "I can radiate light shining throughout the universe! I can radiate light shining throughout the universe!" That state needs no thinking from you, no announcing from you—it needs your practice. Only if you can truly become pure and enter samadhi can you radiate light shining throughout the universe. Unable to enter samadhi, idle fancies do no good at all. Thinking back and forth is all discursive thought, eighty-four thousand miles from reality.

Someone else thinks: "How can I enter samadhi? How can I become enlightened?" If you harbor such discursive thoughts, then by no means can you enter samadhi or become enlightened. Why? Because you are applying effort only skin-deep, not applying effort in prajna wisdom. You are altogether seeking outward. Never seeking inward, you will never find it.

Be electrotherapists to help this world. Rescue the beings living in this polluted air so they can become Buddhas in fresh, clean air. Now you must sit in stillness, without so many discursive thoughts, and I hope you clearly understand this. I have already explained to you the electrotherapy that makes the air pure. Try it and see how it works?

Today is the second day of the Chan Session—have you "set out on the road" yet? "Setting out" means taking the road of Right Enlightenment, the road of Bodhi. Have you raised up the phrase "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name" yet? Have you let go of discursive thoughts yet? If you have not yet raised up "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" then hurry and do it. Train like "a cat stalking a mouse," patiently watching for the mouse. Be like "a mother hen hatching her eggs," wholeheartedly mindful of the chicks about to hatch. Be like "a dragon guarding its pearl," carefully and single-mindedly holding the precious pearl tight. Only by applying effort at all times can accomplishment be hoped for.

We practice "eating one meal a day, sleeping without lying down"—an ascetic practice I dare say is the finest in the world. Especially during a Chan Session: sitting twelve hours a day, circling six hours. Such bitter practice requires meditators to eat their fill. Thus in China, whenever a Chan Session was held, every night each person was given two big steamed buns, and everyone loved it. But here we have no such custom. So at lunch, eat a little extra—eat your fill, to have strength for circling or running.

Buddhist precepts stipulate "eating once at midday"—that is, eating only one meal a day, at noon (twelve o'clock). Later this changed to "not eating past noon"—after twelve noon no meals are taken, though morning porridge for breakfast is allowed. Since it is not eaten after noon, this is no violation of the precepts.

During a Chan Session, if you do not eat enough you will lack the strength to sit in Chan, to circle, or to run, and so may retreat. Why? If you investigate Chan into the night, your stomach will growl and scold you for being so selfish—knowing only how to cultivate, caring only about enlightenment, ignoring it and making it suffer. It asks what kind of Way you cultivate, without even a shred of compassion. Then it refuses to cooperate with you, and you easily retreat in resolve, no longer wanting to cultivate, wasting all your former effort. Hence during a Chan Session you must eat your fill to have the energy to seek liberating wisdom.

Today I will tell you the story of "Eating Buns During a Session." This is a true story, not made up. At Tiantong Monastery in Ningbo, China, there was an abbot named Miyun. He was a Good Knowing Advisor with the Clear Eye. The Venerable Weina was also a Good Knowing Advisor with the Clear Eye. But the Venerable Weina's compassion was vast, while the Abbot's compassion was narrow. Abbot Miyun's style was "a Mahasattva who minds nobody's business," while the Venerable Weina stood for "a Bodhisattva who loves minding people's business." Since the two held different views, their conduct clashed.

During the Session, everyone sat vigorously in Chan, seeking liberating wisdom. One night, this compassionate Venerable Weina saw that the assembly, too hungry, had no spirit left for sitting. Some were sunk in stupor, some with scattered minds, and if not dozing then "slumped sitting." Normally a sitting person measures about three feet tall, but with stomachs too empty to sit straight, they hunched over, barely a foot tall—hence "slumped sitting." Once this set in, no one could keep sitting. Seeing this, the Venerable Weina took pity and, wishing to preserve the assembly's strength, entered samadhi and used his spiritual powers to slip into the kitchen and steal some scorched rice, distributing a little to each person. When the sitting ended, everyone opened their eyes to find a piece of scorched rice on their laps, and quietly ate it all up. For "people are iron, rice is steel"—once eaten, everyone regained their spirits. While circling, no one felt tired. No longer like before, when empty stomachs made circling impossible and they had to sit aside to rest.

After the compassionate Venerable Weina stole scorched rice two days running to feed the assembly breakfast, on the third day the Abbot discovered the theft and expelled him from the monastery.

It happened thus: on the morning of the third day, the monk in charge of the kitchen found that yesterday's scorched rice had vanished, and suspected the rats had eaten it. Since it was his duty, he reported it to the Abbot for instructions. The Abbot said: "Very well, catch that rat!" That night the Abbot entered samadhi to contemplate, and discovered that the Venerable Weina had stolen the kitchen's scorched rice while in samadhi. He then hid the Venerable Weina's physical body beneath a sitting bench. When the Venerable Weina left samadhi, his "house" (his body) was nowhere to be found. Searching everywhere, at last he found his body lying beneath a bench, and pulled it out. The Abbot then said: "What are you doing? You are quite the big rat. You dare steal scorched rice from the kitchen? Do you know you have violated the precepts? Whoever violates the precepts must be expelled! Tomorrow you must go. We can keep you here no longer!"

The Venerable Weina said: "Venerable Sir, expel me if you must, but I beg one thing of you, and hope you will grant it."

The Abbot asked: "You are about to leave—what more do you ask?"

The Venerable Weina said: "Meditators must eat their fill before they can apply effort in cultivation. If they do not eat enough, they surely cannot cultivate. That is why I slipped into the kitchen to steal scorched rice for the assembly—not for myself. I hope the Abbot will be compassionate and give each person two buns every evening. If so, I will bow to you in gratitude. Once I am gone, I will have no more regrets!"

The Abbot thought it over and saw the sense in it: "Very well! I will grant your request." From then on, whenever a Chan Session was held, each person received two buns in the evening.

The Venerable Weina then asked the Abbot: "Venerable Sir, where should I go?"

The Abbot replied: "Go to Sichuan province and build a Way-place. The Dharma protectors there have affinities with you."

Then the Venerable Weina used his spiritual power of unimpeded travel to reach Sichuan. Seeing two tall cassia trees with lush branches and leaves, he sat in Chan between them. Many Dharma protectors and laypeople saw him sitting beneath the trees, recognized him as a true cultivator, a virtuous high monk, and so built a monastery beneath the two cassia trees, naming it "Two Cassia Hall." There he transmitted the Dharma and accepted disciples. Later, a great many Chan investigators became enlightened, and he became the founding Patriarch.

Investigating Chan is like drinking water—hot or cold, only you know. When your skill is steady, you know it yourself; when your skill is not yet mature, only you know that too. Whoever's skill is steady and mature must keep striving without pause. Whoever has gotten nowhere must not be lazy. During the Session you must let go of everything. There is a saying:

"Take it up, and let it go."

"Take up" what? Take up the phrase "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?"

"Let go" of what? Let go of all discursive thoughts. Only by letting go of discursive thoughts and scattered thinking will wisdom arise. Unable to let go of discursive thoughts, your effort will bear no fruit.

During these seven days you must be valiant and vigorous, without a trace of laziness or a shred of doubt. Apply effort together. When your effort reaches "seeing neither self nor others," you will become enlightened. When your effort reaches "neither form nor emptiness," you will merge with the Tathagata. If you have not yet understood the state of "neither form nor emptiness," you should truly be ashamed.

Why does effort fail to correspond? Because habits and tendencies from limitless kalpas past are far too deep; thus the mind wishes to head for the Bodhi road while the body refuses to advance, always wanting to retreat. Know that the heavier your habits, the deeper your karmic obstacles, the more you must let go of discursive thoughts. Letting go of discursive thoughts is not hard—you need only forget yourself, and discursive thoughts vanish at once. Only because the "I" remains can you not forget yourself.

Cultivating in the Chan Hall, you must cultivate so that "above, you do not know there is sky; in between, you do not know there are people; below, you do not know there is earth." Sky, earth, and people gone, east, west, south, and north dissolved—then not a single thought arises, and the whole true mind appears. You will attain "the great function of the whole."

Giving rise to discursive thoughts all day, your skill will never correspond. So you must apply effort to where not a single thought arises. Walking, not knowing you are walking; standing, not knowing you are standing; lying down, not knowing you are lying down; sitting, not knowing you are sitting. Of walking, standing, lying, and sitting, knowing nothing at all:

Eating rice all day, yet not swallowing a single grain.

Wearing clothes all day, yet not putting on a single thread.

Then you merge into one with empty space. Merging into one with empty space, you suddenly interpenetrate; abruptly you will understand all things. That is the state of sudden enlightenment.

Sudden enlightenment comes from ordinary effort—applying effort to the point of correspondence, then suddenly becoming enlightened. Without ordinary effort there can be no sudden enlightenment. Like a child after birth: hearing speech day after day, one day it naturally learns to speak. When it utters its first words, it is much like our moment of enlightenment. When it starts to walk, that first step too may be compared to our enlightenment. How does it take that first step? Because day after day it watches adults walking back and forth, and the scene perfumes its mind, until it naturally toddles forth. Our effort must be the same—apply effort today, apply effort tomorrow. Continuing thus, when the skill ripens, with no more ideas arising and discursive thoughts wholly ceased, you will become enlightened.

Enlightenment through day-by-day effort, hour-by-hour effort, until the skill ripens and enlightenment suddenly comes—that is enlightenment through this life's cultivation.

Someone asks: "I see that fellow applies no effort at all, yet shortly after coming to the Chan Hall he suddenly becomes enlightened. Why is that?" That case is rather special. It is because, though in this life he applies no effort, in a past life he already cultivated. And not ordinary cultivation—hour after hour, minute after minute he cultivated, falling short of enlightenment by just a little. Thus in this life, meeting the right conditions, he at once becomes enlightened.

Though sudden enlightenment is instant enlightenment, it requires good roots nurtured in past lives. Like farming—sow in spring, till in summer, and only in autumn reap the harvest. If in spring no seed is sown, how could autumn hold a harvest? There is a saying:

"As you till, so shall you reap."

We who cultivate the Way must be the same—whether enlightened or not, valiant and vigorous, striving forward. Hoping that in a final moment we will gain the result and recognize our "original face."

Why can we not recognize our "original face"? Because the mark of self (the "I") is not yet removed, and selfishness not yet ended. If the mark of self were gone and selfishness ended, you could recognize your "original face" at once.

If you do not wish to recognize your "original face," that is no problem—cultivate or not, it makes no difference, for you have no hope at all. But one who cultivates the Way must surely have hope. The hope of clearly knowing where you came from and where you are going—of knowing where you were born from and where you go after death. If you wish to know what your "original face" is like, you must not fear suffering, hardship, or difficulty—only then can you return to the origin and attain the "indestructible vajra body."

What do we do in the Chan Hall? We forge the "indestructible vajra body." Once it is the "indestructible vajra body," this body surely knows no more suffering, no more pain. So if we keep fearing suffering and pain, we can never accomplish the "indestructible vajra body." This indestructible body is forged through training.
