And the work we are doing here is precisely forging the "indestructible vajra body"—training this body to be firm, never to decay.

Hearing this, someone thinks: "I cultivate not for this 'stinking skin bag.' What use is forging it into indestructibility?" Not wrong! Your reasoning is quite right; but the "indestructible vajra body" I speak of is not this "stinking skin bag." What is it then? It is the "indestructible vajra body" of the own-nature—also the Dharma body and the wisdom life—precisely the "indestructible vajra body" of the originally pure own-nature.

Remember: cultivating the Way is no easy matter. As soon as you wish to cultivate the Way, demons come to disturb you. These demons come not from one place alone, but from all directions. Some are sickness demons, some are affliction demons; there are heavenly demons, human demons, ghost demons, and monster demons besides. The demons come from where you least expect or know, shaking your resolve for the Way and making you retreat in practice. They use every means to lure, intimidate, and threaten you, forcing you to retreat, lose your samadhi power, and quit cultivating altogether.

When your sitting reaches a fair level, demons will come to test your Way-power. Sometimes they transform into handsome men or beautiful women to seduce you—if your mind is unmoved, you pass the test; if your mind moves, you will fall. This is of utmost importance—remember it well! One false step, and the regret lasts a thousand lifetimes!

When states appear to test the cultivator, we must examine whether the state is true or false. By what method? Very simple: recite "A Di Đà Phật", single-minded and undisturbed, without discursive thoughts. If the state is false, it will slowly fade away. If the state is true, the more you recite, the more clearly it appears. Whoever sits in Chan without knowing this method will go astray and fall under demonic influence, and their Way-karma will dissolve. Others, supposing they have entered demonic states, will miss their chance at enlightenment.

When young I heard it said: "To cultivate the Way is to meet demons." I did not believe it, and arrogantly declared: "No demon frightens me! I fear no monsters or ghosts at all!" I thought saying so was harmless, nothing to fear. Who knew that before long demons truly came to disturb me. What demon? The sickness demon! That time I fell gravely ill, unconscious for seven or eight days, knowing nothing at all. Only then did I know my skill was insufficient and I could not pass the test. Monsters and ghosts, heavenly demons and outside ways—none frighten me; only the sickness demon—I could neither subdue it nor endure it. Therefore, one who cultivates the Way must not boast or preen, claiming to fear nothing. If you are smug and self-satisfied, trouble comes at once!

How should one who cultivates the Way be? Humble and cautious, as if walking on the edge of a deep abyss or treading on thin ice. At all times utterly careful, highly alert—only then can you cultivate the Way. In short, "speak little, sit much"; that is the root of cultivation.

Whose aid enables the cultivator to accomplish the Way-karma? The demons'! Just as a blade must be whetted to be sharp, the cultivator shines forth the light of wisdom thanks to demons' help. So regard demons as Dharma protectors. Hence the saying:

Meeting matters, awake to matters: transcend the world. Meeting matters, confused by matters: fall and sink. (Seeing matters, understanding them: transcend the world; Seeing matters, deluded by them: suffer a fall.)

If you can awaken, meeting each state with penetrating understanding, you will transcend the world. If you cannot awaken, deluded by whatever you meet, you are bound for the hells. So one who cultivates the Way does not fear meeting demons—only fears lacking samadhi power. Demons come to help you, to test you, to see whether you have skill and samadhi power. If you have skill and samadhi power, then no matter what demon it is, none can shake your spirit.

In cultivation, always hang the words "the question of birth and death" before your brows, always thinking of how to end birth and death. Know that nothing is more important than "the great matter of birth and death." If birth and death are unresolved, you will not know why you were born or where you go after death. So until you have truly penetrated "the question of birth and death," you must apply effort vigorously; otherwise you will forever be bound by the wheel of birth and death, never to be liberated.

On the path of the Way, hold this "question of birth and death" in mind, and regard the demons as Dharma protectors helping your cultivation. Whoever scolds you or beats you is helping you cultivate. Whoever gossips about you or makes things hard for you is also helping you cultivate. In short, when adversity comes, simply go along with it and endure. Regard them all as friends come to aid you, and afflictions will end. Once afflictions end, wisdom arises. With true wisdom, no demon can shake your mind.

Why are we shaken by demonic states? Because our wisdom is not yet perfected. With wisdom imperfected, whatever we meet deludes us and we fail to see clearly—the marks of self, others, living beings, and a life all arise, and afflictions rise along with them. With true wisdom, such problems would never occur!

tieu_de: Patriarch Bodhidharma Comes to China
tom_tat: In the ninth month of the first year of Putong (520 C.E.), under Emperor Wu of Liang, Patriarch Bodhidharma sailed from India to China. He landed at Guangzhou, came ashore, and went to Jinling (Nanjing)…
noi_dung:
Patriarch Bodhidharma Comes to China

In the ninth month of the first year of Putong (520 C.E.), under Emperor Wu of Liang, Patriarch Bodhidharma sailed from India to China. Landing at Guangzhou, he came ashore and went to Jinling (Nanjing) to hold discourse with Emperor Wu of Liang. Because the emperor's disposition was not in tune, the Patriarch left Jinling and headed north toward Luoyang. Passing the place where Dharma Master Shenguang was lecturing on the Sutras, he stopped in along the way to listen. Discovering that Dharma Master Shenguang's eloquence was unobstructed—so much so that "flowers rained from the sky and golden lotuses welled up from the earth"—he knew Shenguang was a worthy Dharma vessel. At the time, Master Shenguang, seeing an Indian monk come to hear his lecture, could not restrain his pride; when the lecture ended, he gave Bodhidharma a wink.

The Patriarch asked him: "Venerable Master, what are you doing here?"

Master Shenguang replied: "I lecture on the Sutras."

The Patriarch asked: "What Sutra do you lecture?"

Master Shenguang, annoyed, retorted: "Where do you come from?"

The Patriarch answered: "I come from India."

Master Shenguang asked: "Then do they not lecture on Sutras in India?"

The Patriarch replied: "Of course they lecture on Sutras, but they lecture entirely on the 'wordless true Sutra.' " (the Sutra without words).

Master Shenguang asked again: "What is the wordless true Sutra?"

The Patriarch answered: "The wordless true Sutra is a Sutra of only blank paper. The Sutra you lecture is black words on white paper. So what is the use of your lecturing?"

Hearing this, Master Shenguang grew irritated and said: "I lecture on Sutras to teach people to end birth and death."

The Patriarch asked: "On what basis do you teach others to end birth and death? You yourself have not yet ended birth and death!"

Master Shenguang thought to himself: "This black-faced monk must be a demon king in disguise, come here to slander the Triple Jewel. I must test his dharma power!"

Then Master Shenguang took his iron-bead rosary (an iron-bead chaplet, a demon-quelling weapon) and struck the Patriarch hard in the face. Caught off guard, the Patriarch was struck and lost two front teeth. The Patriarch (already a sage) thought to himself: "Wherever a sage's teeth fall to the ground, that place will suffer drought for three years." Out of compassion for beings, he at once swallowed both teeth into his belly; hence the saying:

"Knocked-out teeth are swallowed with blood." (Swallow broken teeth together with blood).

Without a word, the Patriarch turned and walked out of the monastery, then stepped upon a single reed to cross the Yangzi River, arriving at Shaolin Monastery on Mount Song in Henan. There he sat facing a wall for nine years, contemplating Chan potentials.

As for Master Shenguang, he was most pleased with himself, thinking he had won, never knowing that the Patriarch acted thus to practice the patience paramita. Not long after Patriarch Bodhidharma left the monastery, the Ghost of Impermanence arrived and asked Master Shenguang: "Are you Shenguang?"

Master Shenguang replied: "I am Shenguang. What is it?"

The Ghost of Impermanence said: "By order of King Yama, I invite you for tea, and to ask how many Sutras you have lectured, how many you have recited, how many remain unrecited, and how many unlectured."

Hearing this, Master Shenguang was startled out of his wits. Knowing he was about to die, he pleaded: "Is there anyone who can end birth and death and escape King Yama's judgment?"

The Ghost of Impermanence replied: "None other than that bushy-bearded, dark-skinned monk whose two front teeth you knocked out!"

Hearing this, Master Shenguang deeply regretted that he had failed to curb his temper and had driven away a sage. So he asked the Ghost of Impermanence: "May I go seek that monk and learn the dharma of 'ending birth and escaping death'?"

The Ghost of Impermanence agreed: "Very well! But you must go quickly and return at once, or I take no responsibility!"

Master Shenguang set out at once, traveling day and night without rest to catch up with Patriarch Bodhidharma. Reaching Mount Song, he saw the Patriarch sitting facing the wall, and was overjoyed. He came before the Patriarch, bowed reverently in repentance: "May the Master be compassionate and forgive this coarse disciple, who did not know you are a sage and so offended you. Pray teach me the practice that ends birth and death."

Bodhidharma glanced back, then said nothing and kept sitting. Master Shenguang knelt down—and knelt for nine straight years.

We sit in Chan, and in less than two hours our backs ache, our knees hurt, we cannot bear it—or we drift off thinking of food and soft drinks. In short, we cannot control the "monkey mind and horse thoughts" that always want to run wild. Master Shenguang, in the spirit of "seeking the Dharma forgetting oneself," knelt unbroken for nine years. Among us here, is there anyone who could kneel for nine hours? I fear not one!

One day snow fell heavily, over two feet deep, yet Master Shenguang still knelt beside the Patriarch. The Patriarch then raised his head, moved by Master Shenguang's sincere quest for the Dharma, and asked: "What are you kneeling here for?"

Master Shenguang replied: "Pray, Master, transmit the Dharma to me with compassion, that I may escape King Yama's grasp!"

The Patriarch said: "Seeking the Dharma is hardly so easy! Wait until the sky rains red snow, and I will transmit the Dharma to you!"

Master Shenguang thought to himself: "In the past, when Shakyamuni Buddha practiced the Bodhisattva conduct, for the sake of half a verse he dared give up his very life..." At that thought his resolve turned. Seeing a precept knife hanging on the wall, he took it down and severed his own left arm. Blood gushed like a fountain, turning the white snow red. He scooped up a handful of that red snow and offered it before Patriarch Bodhidharma, entreating the transmission of the Dharma.

The Patriarch said: "For the Dharma you severed your arm—truly a sincere quest for the Dharma"; and transmitted to Master Shenguang the dharma of "no establishment of words and letters, a special transmission apart from the doctrinal teaching, direct pointing at the mind, seeing the nature and becoming a Buddha." The Patriarch further named Master Shenguang "Huike."

Master Huike said: "My mind is not at peace; pray pacify my mind for me."

The Patriarch said: "Bring me your mind, and I will pacify it."

Master Huike reflected for a long while, then said: "I have sought my mind, but cannot find it anywhere."

The Patriarch said: "I have pacified your mind already!"

Master Huike was suddenly greatly enlightened and became the Second Patriarch of Chinese Chan. Later he transmitted the robe and the mind-dharma to Sengcan as the Third Patriarch. Sengcan transmitted to Daoxin as the Fourth Patriarch. Daoxin transmitted to Hongren as the Fifth Patriarch. Hongren transmitted to Huineng as the Sixth Patriarch. At this point Chan divided into two schools. Shenxiu represented the Northern school, advocating "sweeping away dust, contemplating purity," becoming the school of Gradual Enlightenment. His verse says:

The body is the Bodhi tree,

The mind like a bright mirror's stand.

Time and again, wipe it diligently;

Let no dust alight.

Meaning:

The body is the Bodhi tree,

The mind like a bright mirror's stand.

Always sweep it clean;

Let no dust cling to it.

Huineng represented the Southern school, advocating "instant enlightenment," becoming the school of Sudden Enlightenment. His verse says:

Bodhi is fundamentally no tree,

Nor is the bright mirror a stand.

Fundamentally there is not a single thing—

Where can dust alight?

Meaning:

Bodhi is not a tree,

Nor the bright mirror a stand.

From the first, there is nothing—

Where can dust cling?

Later the Southern school further divided into five houses: Guiyang, Linji, Caodong, Yunmen, and Fayan. According to Patriarch Bodhidharma's verse:

I came originally to this land

To transmit the Dharma and save the deluded;

One flower opens into five petals,

And the fruit will ripen of itself.

Meaning:

I came originally to this land

To transmit the Dharma and save the deluded;

One flower blooms into five petals,

And the fruit forms of itself.

Sure enough, by the Sixth Patriarch's time Chan had split into five houses. The Dharma was thus passed from generation to generation in China. Now the Dharma has been transmitted to America, yet no one need kneel to seek the Dharma. If you sincerely cultivate, you can attain the Dharma.

(Chan Session, December 1980)

tieu_de: The Secret to Controlling Discursive Thoughts
tom_tat: The City of Ten Thousand Buddhas holds several Chan Sessions each year, each lasting seven days. Before Amitabha Buddha's birthday there is one Buddha-recitation Session (7 days), followed by three consecutive Chan Sessions (21 days). Every year…
noi_dung:
The Secret to Controlling Discursive Thoughts

The City of Ten Thousand Buddhas holds several Chan Sessions each year, each Session lasting seven days. Before Amitabha Buddha's birthday there is one Buddha-recitation Session (7 days), followed by three consecutive Chan Sessions (21 days). Every year, those who attend the Chan Sessions stay from beginning to end, bringing their merit to perfection. This year, I hope all of you who attend will likewise remain faithful, never quitting halfway and abandoning the Chan Hall; otherwise your skill will be left unfinished, time wasted, with nothing attained.

Your sitting posture must be upright, back straight. The head must be straight—not bowed, not tilted back, not leaning left, not veering right. Then cross your legs in full lotus—placing the left foot on the right thigh, then the right foot on the left thigh—that is the standard. Because the full-lotus posture makes it easy to enter samadhi, it is also called the demon-quelling pose, the vajra pose, or the lotus pose. This posture can help dissolve karmic obstacles of limitless kalpas, end birth and escape death, and create limitless merit.

When you first sit in Chan, you must train in this basic posture. Next, adjust the body—eyes gazing down at the tip of the nose, from the nose down to the mouth, from the mouth down to the mind. That is the secret to controlling discursive thoughts. Then regulate the breath—not fast, not slow—breathing naturally. Only then do you investigate the phrase "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" After a long time, Chan investigation takes effect.

Applying effort in Chan investigation is like "a mother hen hatching her eggs." The mother hen constantly thinks of her chicks, wholeheartedly hatching the eggs. She does not hatch for five minutes and then run off, come back a while later to hatch some more, then before five minutes run off again...; for doing so, the eggs would never hatch into chicks. Chan investigation is the same—at all times effort must be unbroken. Do not fear backache, do not fear aching legs, do not fear hardship or difficulty. Single-mindedly investigate Chan. Investigate what? Investigate "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" Investigate until "rivers run dry and mountains end, waters stop and rocks appear"—only then will you become enlightened.

Chan investigation is also like "a dragon cherishing its pearl." The dragon always clasps its precious pearl, never lax or careless. Thus the pearl grows ever brighter, while the dragon guards it day and night. The Chan investigator must be the same—in every minute and second giving rise to no stray thoughts. The ancients said:

"When not a single thought arises, the whole appears."

That is, when not a thought arises, the true mind and the Buddha-nature appear. It can also be said:

"When discursive thoughts do not arise, the whole appears."

When discursive thoughts cease, the whole clearly appears. When discursive thoughts are stilled, you will have your chance at accomplishment.

The Chan investigator should not think of becoming a Buddha, pay no mind to enlightenment, nor think of attaining wisdom. Just apply effort vigorously, diligently cultivating. When the time ripens, enlightenment will come. In the Chan Hall, just sit in Chan, then circle, then sit again, then circle again, then sit again, then circle again... Continuing thus, cultivating over a long time, you will have your chance at accomplishment, for "long sitting brings Chan"—sit long and Chan will come.

Chan investigation is also like "a cat stalking a mouse." The cat must fix its attention at the mouse hole, waiting for the mouse to dart out to pounce at once. The cat cannot be lax; with a scattered mind it can pay no attention. The Chan investigator is the same—at all times holding right mindfulness fast, never giving rise to discursive thoughts. That is the most elementary entry into the Way of Chan investigation.

The cultivator of the Way should neither head for South Mountain nor climb to the North Sea to find the Way. The Way is right in your own body. If you can sit in full lotus, focusing the mind to investigate Chan, that is the Way. Do not crave what is lofty and recondite, turning the mind outward to seek the Way; for then you will never find it. If you abandon what is near to chase what is far, everywhere you go you will meet only hardship and trouble. That is asking for trouble yourself, bringing suffering upon yourself!

(Chan Session, 12/1980)

Investigating the Hua-tou

"Investigate" means to seek—to seek who it is that recites the Buddha's name.

To "investigate the hua-tou" is to study the phrase "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?

Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" There is a saying:

Great doubt, great enlightenment;

Small doubt, small enlightenment;

No doubt, no enlightenment.

(Great doubt brings great enlightenment;

Small doubt brings small enlightenment;

No doubt brings no enlightenment.)

When you have thoroughly penetrated the hua-tou "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?", that Chan investigation is itself the Vajra King's jeweled sword, cutting off all desire-thoughts until only the single thought investigating the hua-tou remains. When all thoughts cease, the resolve for the Way blazes forth.

Before a Chan Session there is usually a Buddha-recitation Session. Only when a Chan Session follows a Buddha-recitation Session is the effect fine. First recite the Buddha's name, then investigate the hua-tou "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?"

"Investigate" means to seek—to seek who it is that recites the Buddha's name. A ghost? Then what kind of ghost? A person? Which person? Me? Once dead, can I still recite? Packed into a coffin, no one recites the Buddha's name anymore! Seek and see—in the end, who recites the Buddha's name? And recites whom? Seek and see—who is it that recites the Buddha's name? Who is reciting the Buddha's name? You cannot find it? Though you searched forever, you could never find it! If you found this "Who," all discursive thoughts would vanish entirely. Why do you still have discursive thoughts? Because you have not yet found that "Who"!

Seeking this "Who" may take a whole great kalpa. When you see seasoned cultivators sitting motionless in Chan, they are seeking this "Who"! Because they single-mindedly investigate this "Who," all discursive thoughts cease, and they suddenly become enlightened. Then, in the gloomy darkness a brilliant light suddenly appears, and everything becomes clear to them. As it is said:

Deluded, a thousand books are too few;

Enlightened, even one word is too many.

(When deluded, a thousand books are still too few;

Once enlightened, a single word is already extra.)

That is the principle of investigating the phrase "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" Thus, whoever gives rise to no discursive thoughts has skill. Whoever constantly gives rise to discursive thoughts accomplishes no skill at all. That is the crux of Chan investigation.

The skill of Chan investigation lies in single-minded investigation—walking also investigating, sitting also investigating, standing also investigating, lying down also investigating. In short, at all times you must investigate Chan, missing no chance to investigate. Hence during a Chan Session we do not bow to the Buddhas, recite Sutras, ascend to the main hall, or attend formal meals. When mealtime comes, we eat; finished eating, we return at once to the Chan Hall to keep investigating. When nature calls, we go, then return at once to the Chan Hall to keep investigating. Waste not a minute or second, for who knows—in that very minute or second you might become enlightened? So seize every second, every minute!

There is a saying: "Never leave this!" Leave what? That is, never leave the hua-tou "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" Never straying from this phrase—it is precisely the sword of wisdom that severs the seven emotions and six desires. Once bad habits are wholly removed, the fundamental nature appears. When the fundamental nature appears, the fruit of enlightenment is accomplished.

While investigating Chan, face reality, overcome every circumstance, and hold fast to the tenet. Remember that suffering is the start of bliss. I often tell you:

"Endure suffering and suffering ends;

Enjoy blessings and blessings vanish!"

The ancients taught:

"Misfortune is what fortune leans upon;

Fortune is where misfortune hides."

After ill fortune, good omen often follows; beside peaceful times, mishap may lurk. Worldly dharmas are always thus in opposition. Through long kalpas past, who knows how much evil karma we have created—so now we must undergo its retribution. If you strive in effort, valiant and vigorous, repaying all karma in full, you will accomplish the Way-fruit.

Take heed! Whether the state is favorable (to your liking) or adverse (against your wishes), endure it—even what you cannot endure, force yourself to endure! Cultivating the Way is cultivating patience; there is a saying:

"Patience is a priceless jewel."

If you can patiently bear all things, you will gain true peace. Like a martial artist lacking experience—in a grapple forgetting every move, only remembering the forms after the fight, too late! Chan investigation is the same—when states come, you must endure, suffer loss, grit your teeth and bear it; past the hardship, you attain ease.

In Chan investigation, investigate thus in the morning, investigate thus in the evening. Practice Chan in the morning, practice Chan in the evening. Practicing long, you will succeed. To be patient means: though your back aches, pay no mind; though your knees hurt, ignore them—just single-mindedly investigate "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" If at all times you are thus, you will give rise to no discursive thoughts, and can gather in body and mind, bringing the mind to such purity that not a single stray thought arises. Keep the mind never apart from the hua-tou "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?"—raising it up at all times, never forgetting—that is precisely the goal of applying effort.

Investigating the hua-tou involves a single discursive thought, while scattered thinking involves countless discursive thoughts. So we use the method of "countering poison with poison"—taking the single discursive thought of "investigating the hua-tou" to control all other discursive thoughts—gradually, each discursive thought is destroyed, never to arise again. Then, whatever state comes, you are no longer deluded; discerning clearly, you can never go astray and fall under demonic influence. The ancients said:

"Better a thousand lives without enlightenment,

Than a single day possessed by demons."

(Better a thousand lifetimes unenlightened,

Than a single day entangled with demons.)

In practicing samadhi, be careful and cautious, never extreme. Be open and upright, giving ghosts and demons no chance to harm you. When you harbor scattered thoughts, you open the door for demons to slip in! Thus, investigating the hua-tou is precisely the Dharma-treasure that "drives demons away"!

(Chan Session, 12/1980)

tieu_de: States in Chan Meditation
tom_tat: Sit in Chan until within there is no body or mind, without there is no world, and near and far are all empty—only then do you reach the place of no mark of self, no mark of others, no mark of living beings, no mark of a life…
noi_dung:
States in Chan Meditation

Sit in Chan until within there is no body or mind, without there is no world, and near and far are all empty—only then do you reach the place of no mark of self, no mark of others, no mark of living beings, no mark of a life; the time when "the past mind does not exist, the present mind does not exist, and the future mind does not exist either." Reaching this state is still not true accomplishment, nor anything special. Whether you sit for one hour or ten hours, even for a whole month or ten months, it is only that your skill has slightly corresponded—just a slight state of lightness and ease. Passing through that light, easy state and continuing to investigate Chan, you will enter the state of the First Dhyana.

The heaven of the First Dhyana is called "the Ground of Joy and Bliss Born of Separation"—the state apart from the pleasures of beings. In the state of the Ground of Joy and Bliss Born of Separation, you enter samadhi very quickly. While in samadhi, breathing stops completely—neither out nor in, neither going nor coming—like a tortoise in winter drawing its head into its shell, halting outer breath while inner breathing continues. That is the phenomenon of "hibernation." The Chan investigator, entering samadhi, stops breathing, but leaving samadhi breathes as usual. Take heed! At this state do not give rise to the idle thought: "Ah! My breathing has stopped!"

Once that idle thought arises, breathing resumes at once. So vigilance cannot lapse, or you will miss the chance and have to start over.

From the First Dhyana, with vigorous practice you will enter the Second Dhyana. The heaven of the Second Dhyana is called "the Ground of Joy and Bliss Born of Samadhi"—in the state of samadhi, joy and bliss arise. Hence the saying:

Chan bliss as food, replete with Dharma joy.

(The savor of Chan as food, full of the joy of Dharma.)

Entering this state, not only does breathing stop, the heartbeat stops too. The pulse merely pauses, not ending for good, so leaving samadhi all returns to normal.

From the Second Dhyana, advancing in practice you enter the Third Dhyana. The heaven of the Third Dhyana is called "the Ground of Wondrous Bliss Apart from Joy"—apart from all coarse delights, only subtle, supremely wondrous joy remains. Entering the Ground of Wondrous Bliss Apart from Joy, not only does breathing stop and the heart stop beating, thought itself wholly ceases—just like a dead person. When thought ceases, all scattered idle thoughts cease too.

When breathing stops, the blood loses oxygen and circulation halts, so the heart does not beat and no pulse remains. Then stray thoughts are gone. Suppose breath is wind, the pulse waves, and thought water—when wind dies, waves calm, and water naturally stills. That is precisely the principle of "wind ceasing, waves calming." This is a temporary effect of entering samadhi, not a final end as in death. Whenever you wish to restore breath or pulse, they function normally again.

From the Third Dhyana, vigorously practicing samadhi you enter the state of the Fourth Dhyana. The heaven of the Fourth Dhyana is called "the Ground of Purity through Renouncing Thought," meaning the subtle joy of the Third Dhyana is renounced and the mind is pure. Breath stops, blood and pulse stop, thought stops; yet even that state must be renounced—only then does the pure True-Suchness nature appear. Do not mistake this state for something outstanding or special; it is merely the Fourth Dhyana heaven, not yet the state of realizing the Way-fruit. This is still the station of common beings, for desire is not yet severed. From this state, practicing the deviant samadhi of outside ways you will enter the Heaven of No Thought, enjoying a supremely blissful state. But practicing Right Samadhi you will enter the Five Heavens of No Return—the state of sages who have realized fruition.

Realizing the First Fruit, the stage of Srotapanna, not only are there no idle thoughts in samadhi—walking, standing, lying, and sitting are all free of discursive thoughts and attachments. Attaining the First Fruit is only severing the eighty-eight grades of view-delusions within the Three Realms. Seven more rounds of birth and death remain—realizing the First Fruit is hardly entering Nirvana. Upon realizing the First Fruit, whatever state is met, the mind is unmoved—"facing states, the mind does not stir"—with only the resolve for the Way, single-mindedly practicing Chan. Though outer states be ever so splendid and fair—pretty girls, handsome boys—they cannot move your mind. Then you no longer crave money, sex, fame, food, or sleep. Free of all craving—only then can it be called realizing fruition. A First-Stage Arhat walks without a sound, for the feet hover three inches above the ground. Why? Because fruition-sages, in compassion, fear crushing tiny insects, and so walk in empty space.

Take heed! Do not claim realization without realization, or fruition without fruition. That violates the precept against false speech, and in the future you will fall into the tongue-pulling hell. I must warn you beforehand; believe it or not as you will. Among Buddhists there are those unenlightened who trumpet themselves enlightened—unacceptable conduct. Even if truly enlightened, you should not boast: "I'm enlightened! I have the Five Eyes and Six Spiritual Powers!" Do not publicize and advertise yourselves; it is utterly meaningless.

Even Buddhas and Bodhisattvas never publicize or advertise themselves. If anyone learns that this one is a Bodhisattva or that one a Buddha appearing in the world, they at once vanish. In the Tang dynasty there were two great Masters, Hanshan and Shide. Hanshan was an incarnation of Manjushri Bodhisattva, Shide an incarnation of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. The two, Hanshan and Shide, were close fellow cultivators. As a small child, Shide was brought back by Abbot Fenggan to Guoqing Monastery to be raised and taught. Shide tended the boiler in the kitchen, each day gathering leftover food into a bamboo tube to offer Hanshan. Hanshan lived in Moonlight Cave on Mount Tiantai, coming daily to Guoqing Monastery for the leftovers. Of one heart and mind, the two often laughed and joked together, so the whole monastery took them for madmen and paid them no heed. No one knew they were Bodhisattva incarnations, sporting in the human realm to save beings in need of salvation.

One day Prefect Lü Qiuyin came to see Abbot Fenggan and asked: "Venerable Chan Master, in the past Buddhas and Bodhisattvas often incarnated into this world—do Buddhas and Bodhisattvas still incarnate into this realm today?"

Master Fenggan replied: "Of course! Only you do not recognize them. Right now at Guoqing Monastery on Mount Tiantai, the master tending the boiler in the kitchen is Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. He has a friend, Hanshan, who is Manjushri Bodhisattva. How can you say there is no one?"

Hearing this, Prefect Lü was delighted and hurried to Guoqing Monastery to bow to the two Bodhisattvas Hanshan and Shide.

The guest prefect of Guoqing Monastery received the visiting Prefect warmly. But hearing that this official wished to meet Hanshan and Shide, he was utterly puzzled, not knowing why he would want to meet these two madmen. Not understanding, he still led the Prefect to the kitchen. Just then Hanshan and Shide were laughing and chattering like two lunatics, making everyone laugh. Yet Prefect Lü most reverently bowed to them, and most reverently said: "Your disciple Lü Qiuyin begs the great Bodhisattvas in compassion to teach this deluded one!"

Shide asked: "What are you doing?"

The Prefect replied: "I heard Abbot Fenggan teach that you two are incarnations of Manjushri and Samantabhadra. So I have come specially to bow and beg you to instruct me."

Hearing this, Shide backed away saying: "Master Fenggan talks nonsense! Master Fenggan talks nonsense! Master Fenggan is an incarnation of Amitabha—why not bow to him instead of coming here to bother us?"

With that they ran out of the monastery, up to Moonlight Cave on Mount Tiantai, where both merged into the rock cliff. The Prefect was bitterly disappointed, for the two Bodhisattvas had hidden themselves in the cliff and would come out no more. He thought: "Then I shall go home and bow to Amitabha!" But when he returned to the monastery, he learned that Master Fenggan too had already passed away. Truly a case of "missing it right before one's face." Hence the saying:

"Facing Avalokiteshvara, yet failing to recognize him."

In this Chan Hall there is also an Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, but I cannot reveal him to you, lest you scare him away!

(Chan Session, 12/1980)

tieu_de: Sitting in Chan Can End Birth and Death
tom_tat: In the closing years of the Northern Song dynasty, China had a national hero named Yue Fei. His father died while he was still a child. His mother was a virtuous and wise woman. Mother and son depended on each other…
noi_dung:
Sitting in Chan Can End Birth and Death

In the closing years of the Northern Song dynasty, China had a national hero named Yue Fei. His father died while he was still a child. His mother was a virtuous and wise woman, and mother and son depended on each other to live. Yue Fei was taught reading and writing by his mother. Too poor to buy paper, brush, or ink, Yue Fei practiced writing on sand—yet later he became famed for beautiful calligraphy. Grown, he joined the army. His mother then tattooed four characters on his back—"serve the nation with utmost loyalty"—to remind him always to remember his great vow to save the country and its people.

At that time the Jin armies invaded the Northern Song, seizing Bianjing (Kaifeng) and exiling the two emperors Huizong and Qinzong to the north. Huizong was the abdicated emperor, with two sons: Qinzong and Prince Kang. Prince Kang, then in Hangzhou, ascended the throne, naming the dynasty Southern Song, calling himself Emperor Gaozong of Song, and appointing Qin Hui as prime minister. At court, the civil officials favored reconciliation with the Jin, while the military officials favored war.

Yue Fei then routed the Jin at Zhuxian (very near Bianjing) and planned to press on to the Jin capital at Huanglong (present-day Nong'an, Jilin). To his misfortune, Qin Hui, jealous of Yue Fei, used twelve false gold tablets to summon him back to the capital. Yue Fei, holding the ideals of "loyalty to the sovereign, love for the country," obeyed the imperial command and returned. Reaching the Yangzi River and passing Gold Mountain Monastery, he called upon Chan Master Dao Yue.

Chan Master Dao Yue urged him not to return to the capital, but to stay at Gold Mountain Monastery (in Zhenjiang), leave home, and cultivate—thus he might escape calamity. But Yue Fei had long scorned life and death, and held that a general's duty is to obey the sovereign's command—one may not claim that "a general in the field may sometimes disobey the sovereign's orders." So he did not heed Chan Master Dao Yue's advice. At parting, the Chan Master gave him a verse:

Before the year's end arrives,

Beware the weeping sky;

Beneath "feng," two dots—

They will murder you!

(Ere the year runs out,

Guard against heaven's tears;

Under "feng," two dots—

They plot your harm!)

When Yue Fei reached Hangzhou, Qin Hui used the three words "perhaps there is" (a fabrication) to order father and son both imprisoned. Near the day of execution, Yue Fei suddenly grasped the deep meaning of Chan Master Dao Yue's verse. That year, on the twenty-ninth of the lunar New Year season, rain poured from the sky. Sitting in prison listening to the rain, Yue Fei abruptly understood that great peril was at hand. Chan Master Dao Yue's prophecy had at last come true. "Two dots beneath feng" (two dots added beneath the character "feng") forms the character "qin"—pointing to Qin Hui. Sure enough, Yue Fei was afterward beheaded at Fengbo Pavilion.

Qin Hui then asked the executioner: "Did Yue Fei say anything before the blade?" The executioner replied: "I heard him say only that he regretted not heeding Chan Master Dao Yue of Gold Mountain Monastery, and so met this tragic end." Hearing this, Qin Hui was furious and at once dispatched He Li to Gold Mountain Monastery to arrest Chan Master Dao Yue. But the Chan Master, entering samadhi a day earlier, had already known of this affinity, and left behind a verse:

He Li comes from the South;

I head for the West.

Were the Buddhadharma not vast,

How could I escape his grasp?

Meaning:

(He Li comes up from the South;

I set out for the West.

If the Buddhadharma were not profound,

I would surely fall into his hands.)

This story proves that when a cultivator's samadhi skill reaches its peak, birth and death can be controlled—one may pass away whenever one wishes, directing one's own destiny—a most natural thing. In ancient times, Chan Masters all had such skill—free in life and death, as they wished. In the Tang dynasty, Chan Master Deng Yinfeng could pass away standing on his head. Recently, a Living Buddha at Gold Mountain Monastery passed away standing up. All through samadhi skill, they could come and go freely, bound by nothing.

(Chan Session, December 1980)

tieu_de: Cultivation Requires Patience
tom_tat: Shakyamuni Buddha, from long ago when he still cultivated blessings and wisdom, passed through three great asamkhyeya kalpas (limitless kalpas) before realizing Right Enlightenment. He…
noi_dung:
Cultivation Requires Patience

Shakyamuni Buddha, from long ago when he still cultivated blessings and wisdom, passed through three great asamkhyeya kalpas (limitless kalpas) before realizing Right Enlightenment. He:

"Never failed to do good because it was small,

Never did evil because it was small."

(Never neglect a good deed because it is small,

Never commit an evil deed because it is small.)

When Shakyamuni Buddha practiced the Bodhisattva Way, he never passed over a good deed, even one tiny as a hair, and never did an evil deed, even one small as a mote of dust. Thus, with blessings, wisdom, and merit perfected, he became the Honored One of Two Perfections (one complete in both blessings and wisdom).

Take heed! Though a good deed be small, you must still do it, for grains of dust and sand piled up can build a stupa—becoming a great good deed. Though an evil deed be small, done again and again "small piles up into great," becoming great evil, and then you can never accomplish the Way. Cultivation is:

"Do no evil deeds; do all good deeds."

Doing no evil, blessings grow ever greater. Doing all good, wisdom ever increases. And the more they increase, the more we must keep cultivating without pause—only then is there accomplishment.

Now in the Chan Hall, as you walk then sit, sit then walk, applying effort in cultivation—that is cultivating blessings and wisdom. How to cultivate blessings? That is, "doing no evil." How to cultivate wisdom? That is, "doing all good." When blessings are perfected and wisdom also perfected, you will accomplish the Buddha Way very swiftly, with no need to pass through three asamkhyeya kalpas.

Shakyamuni Buddha in the past, while cultivating, went down wrong roads many times, yet he remained patient, never yielding, ever vigorous—diligently practicing morality, samadhi, and wisdom, ending greed, anger, and delusion—and at last attained Buddhahood.

Now as we cultivate the Buddhadharma, compared with Shakyamuni we are truly fortunate beyond measure. The Buddha has passed down to us the true road; we need only follow it forward to reach the goal (the other shore, the Pure Land) very swiftly.

Shakyamuni Buddha's former incarnation was Never Slighting Bodhisattva, who specialized in the practice of patience. Meeting anyone, he would bow and say: "I dare not slight you. You are all Buddhas-to-be." Some disliked this gesture, so when he bowed they beat and scolded him.

Once, while practicing the Bodhisattva Way, as he bowed he was stoned and lost two front teeth. Yet he bore no anger, and kept up his arduous practice of bowing. Having learned from that experience, thereafter whenever he saw anyone approaching, he would bow from afar, saying: "I dare not slight you. You are all Buddhas-to-be." Said and bowed, he at once left. So though they wished to beat him, none could catch him!

Never Slighting Bodhisattva used the spirit of "No Mark of Self" (no notion of "I" or "me") to cultivate blessings and wisdom. Who taught him to practice thus? No one taught him to bow—of his own willing heart he practiced so. Beaten or scolded, he never gave rise to anger. That is precisely practicing the patience paramita.

The most essential Dharma-door for the cultivator is the dharma of patience. Meeting unfavorable conditions, you must endure, yield, and never contend with anyone. If you cannot be patient, constantly flaring in anger, then all the merit of your bitter cultivation will dissolve.

Ask yourselves: "If I bowed to someone only to be beaten, could I bear it without anger? If you can bear it, you are a disciple of the Buddha; if not, you must gather in body and mind and keep valiantly on in cultivation. Otherwise you only waste time, accomplishing nothing.

The cultivator must bear cold and heat, wind and rain, hunger and thirst, scolding and beating. Imitate the spirit of Never Slighting Bodhisattva: "However badly others treat me, I will neither anger nor resent. I will meet them with sincerity, and they will naturally be moved—enemies will become my good friends."

The cultivator must practice so as to dismantle the "I" (the mark of self). With no more "I," everything can be patiently endured. States may come, yet your mind stays unmoved. Regard yourself as empty space. Pleasant states come—still cultivate. Adverse states come—still cultivate. In other words, meeting pleasant states, do not rejoice in delight; meeting adverse states, do not fret in gloom. Whether favorable or adverse, see them all clearly. If you can be "thus, thus unmoving" (giving rise to no emotion, discursive thought, or attachment), no state can shake you. If at all times you are "clear and ever bright" (luminously illumining the causes and effects of all things), you can turn states around.

Long ago, Shakyamuni Buddha specialized in the dharma of patience, and so was called the Patient Immortal. One day, for no reason at all, King Kali severed his limbs. Yet he bore no resentment—on the contrary, he pitied the King

Kali for his delusion. So he said to the King: "When I become a Buddha, first of all I will save you to cultivate the Way." Hearing this, King Kali at once resolved in great repentance, took refuge with the Patient Immortal, and later became Venerable Kaundinya (one of the first five Bhikshus). After the Buddha realized the Way, he taught the Four Noble Truths for the five Bhikshus, turning the Dharma wheel in three turnings, and all realized Arhatship. Shakyamuni is the founding Patriarch of Buddhism. His patience was ultimate—meeting whatever came, he never angered or fretted. We, the Buddha's disciples, must study the patience-skill of our Fundamental Teacher Shakyamuni. In short, patience and endurance are the pivotal practice, never to be slighted. The ancients said:

Endure a moment, and wind calms, waves still;

Step back once, and seas widen, skies clear.

Meaning:

Endure one instant, and wind dies, waves calm.

Yield one step, and the sea is wide, the sky is vast.

Hence: "Patience is a priceless jewel." If someone smashed the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas to pieces, I would neither blame nor mind, nor ever resent it. If everyone were like this, the world would know peace.

The cultivator cannot do without patience! Only with patience can you cultivate. Without endurance, say no more. What I say today is most ordinary, simple, bland, and tasteless—yet it is precisely the wondrous and rare Buddhadharma. Though ordinary, the Way always springs from the ordinary. "The Way" (the road) is made by feet truly walking it. This dharma of non-action (formless, uncontrived) is hard to meet in hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, so do not miss this affinity. If you take it as "wind passing the ears," hearing without remembering, later regret will come too late. If you can apply what I teach today, then whatever happens, whatever states come, you will give rise to no afflictions. And if you further know how to use wisdom to judge each state, then whatever happens will naturally dissolve, without a hitch. In closing, I pray you strive in investigating Chan, investigating "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" Not yet found the "Who"? Then keep on, patiently cultivating.

(Chan Session, 12/1980)

tieu_de: Investigating Chan Is the Means to Enlightenment
tom_tat: After Buddhism spread to China, it divided into five schools: Chan, Teachings, Vinaya, Pure Land, and Esoteric. Chan is meditative concentration; Teachings is doctrine; Vinaya is moral discipline; Pure Land is the Pure Land…
noi_dung:
Investigating Chan Is the Means to Enlightenment

After Buddhism spread to China, it divided into five schools: Chan, Teachings, Vinaya, Pure Land, and Esoteric. Chan is meditative concentration; Teachings is doctrine; Vinaya is moral discipline; Pure Land is the Pure Land; Esoteric is mantra holding. This is the time of a Chan Session, so I shall speak only of Chan principle, leaving the other four schools aside for now.

Dhyana, translated as "cultivation through reflection," means constantly reflecting upon a single matter. What matter? The hua-tou. Examining "Who is reciting the Buddha's name?" is called investigating Chan. In fact, investigating the hua-tou is itself just a discursive thought; only, we use one discursive thought to subdue discursive thoughts—"countering poison with poison"—taking one discursive thought to destroy many other discursive thoughts. Skill in investigating the hua-tou takes a long time to mature; hence the saying: "Only long investigation brings Chan."

"Investigate" is like boring into wood with an auger. Until you have bored clean through, you do not stop—you cannot quit halfway, for then all former effort is thrown away. In investigating Chan, the most important thing is the ability to endure. When patience reaches its peak, not a single idle thought may arise. When "not a thought arises," you can become enlightened. There is a saying:

"Atop a hundred-foot pole, step one step further."

That is, standing atop a hundred-foot pole, you still step one step further. Then "the worlds of the ten directions wholly appear." But this Dharma-door works only if cultivated in every thought at all times—no laziness, no laxity. In the Song of Enlightenment it is said:

Suddenly awakened to the Tathagata Chan,

The Six Perfections and myriad practices complete within;

In dreams, clearly there are the six destinies,

Awake, utterly empty, not even the great chiliocosm.

Meaning:

Suddenly awakened to the Tathagata Chan.

The Six Perfections and myriad practices, whole and complete.

Dreaming, clearly there are six paths;

Awake, all empty—no great chiliocosm.

"Sudden" means instantly awakening to a principle. As it is said:

Principle can be suddenly awakened to; practice is cultivated gradually.

(Principle may be understood in an instant, but practice must proceed step by step.)

As to "practice," we must cultivate step by step; as to "principle," we must understand it at once. When suddenly enlightened, we know where the well is and go draw water; before sudden enlightenment, we hear only the pulley's rope drawing water, never knowing where the well is. This analogy explains where the Buddha-nature comes from. How is the Buddha-nature realized? Realizing the Buddha-nature has no other method—only investigating Chan and sitting in Chan.

The Six Perfections are the Dharma-doors Bodhisattvas cultivate. Giving "carries across" stinginess and greed. Moral discipline "carries across" violation. Patience "carries across" anger. Vigor "carries across" laxity and laziness. Samadhi "carries across" scattering. Wisdom "carries across" delusion. Only when the Six Perfections are perfected can enlightenment come.

We are always dreaming. As it is said:

Human life, a single dream;

Human death, a dream's span.

In dreams, glory and honor;

Awake, a poor village still.

Day after day, ever dreaming,

Unaware of the yellow-millet dream;

Dreaming on, yet never knowing—

A wasted dream indeed.

Meaning:

The living: one long dream,

The dead: a dream one long.

Within the dream, rank and riches;

Dream over, poor and bare.

Day after day, always dreaming,

Never knowing the "yellow millet" dream;

Dreaming, yet never knowing—

A wasted dream indeed.

Dreaming, we clearly see the six destinies (heavens, humans, asuras, animals, hungry ghosts, hells); only upon awakening do we see that the great trichiliocosm does not even exist. Why? Because attachment is gone. With attachment gone, the myriad things "return to the origin"; how then could there be marks of self, others, living beings, or a life? All are gone! Hearing that the four marks are all gone, some dare not cultivate, mistakenly thinking: "Cultivate to the peak and people no longer exist, beings all vanish, no liver of life remains—then what? All work ends too, and I shall be out of a job!"

Must you have work to do? Then keep right on being upside down! When cultivation reaches the end of the four marks, you will "sweep away all dharmas, leave behind all marks," realizing the True Suchness of all things. As it is said:

Not a single dharma is set up; the myriad dharmas are all empty.

(Not one dharma is established; all things are empty.)

It will not do to merely say you understand this principle—we must truly realize the state where "not a single dharma is set up, all things are empty." Then there is no more suffering, only the enjoyment of peace.

People in the world, if not clinging to fame, clutch tightly at gain; if not attached to money, then entranced by beauty—and so cannot see through (appearances), cannot let go (of attachments). They wish to see through, wish to let go, yet cannot. Why not? Because in the mind a subtle ghost and a clever worm play tricks, and so in many matters we miss our chances—facing Avalokiteshvara, yet failing to recognize him. Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva stands right before us, yet we go searching everywhere. That is precisely being ruled by upside-down discursive thoughts.

The word "investigate" in investigating Chan means to contemplate and observe. Contemplate what? Contemplate prajna. That is, in every thought, at every moment, observe yourselves right here (abiding at ease in yourselves), not others (abiding in others). Observe whether you are present here—if you are here, you can investigate Chan and apply effort; if you are not here, you are giving rise to scattered discursive thoughts and idle fancies. The body sits in the Chan Hall, but the mind races off to New York or Italy. Reaching everywhere, climbing on conditions—no longer at ease.

Contemplating at ease is being a Bodhisattva. Contemplating uneasily is being a common being. Contemplating at ease is heaven. Contemplating uneasily is hell. If we contemplate at ease, the mind not running outward, then we can "practice the profound prajna paramita." In investigating Chan, the body sits in the Chan Hall while the mind continuously, unbrokenly investigates—only that is truly practicing profound prajna, finding wisdom. Attaining great wisdom, we reach the other shore, the shore of liberation.

The secret of investigating Chan is "by day reflect, by night reflect" (investigating by day, investigating by night). Investigate what? Investigate "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" Investigate today, investigate tomorrow. Day after day in the Chan Hall, "practice the profound prajna paramita"—but do not expect to taste the savor of Chan after only a short time. You must pass through a long, long time. Only with skill in "practicing the profound prajna paramita" can you "see that the five skandhas are all empty."

The five skandhas are also called the five coverings. "Skandha" means accumulation; "covering" means veiling and shrouding. Why are we not at ease, not liberated? Because we are shrouded by the five coverings! The five skandhas are form, feeling, cognition, formation, and consciousness.

The form skandha: what has obstruction is called form; what has shape is also form. If the form skandha is not empty, then seeing forms you are deluded by the dust of forms, hearing sounds you are deluded by the dust of sounds, smelling scents you are deluded by the dust of scents, tasting flavors you are deluded by the dust of flavors, touching things you are deluded by the dust of touch. If the form skandha were empty, then within there would be no mind, without no shapes, near and far no things. "Form" also means all kinds of beauty, looks that confuse the eyes so you cannot see clearly—hazy, like the blind. In the Daodejing it is said:

The five colors blind the eye;

The five sounds deafen the ear;

The five flavors numb the palate.

Meaning:

Five colors blind people's eyes,

Five sounds deafen people's ears,

Five flavors dull people's mouths.

All these come from delusion by the form skandha. Once the form skandha is smashed, mountains and rivers, lands, cities, houses are all empty—no more trouble. So while the form skandha is not empty, we remain attached to form. Attached to form, the delusions of views (the delusion of seeing) cannot be removed.

Delusions of views arise when, meeting states, craving and fondness start. States are form. Facing whatever state, giving rise to greed or fondness—that is attachment. Delusions of views have eighty-eight grades; sever them all and you realize the First Fruit of Arhatship. We who cultivate the Way must first sever the eighty-eight grades of view-delusions existing in the Three Realms, then sever the eighty-one grades of thought-delusions in the Three Realms.

Thought-delusions come from delusion about truth, giving rise to discrimination—failing to see all principles clearly. Severing all eighty-one grades of thought-delusions, you realize the Fourth Fruit of Arhatship.

The feeling skandha. "Feeling" is receiving and accepting, giving rise to sensation. When states come, with no thinking at all, you at once take them in and produce a sensation. Eating something, sensing it delicious—that is "feeling." Wearing fine clothes, feeling pleased—also "feeling." Living in a fine house, feeling delight—that is "feeling." Riding in a fine car, feeling comfortable—also "feeling." Whatever the body receives, however it senses it—all is called "feeling."

The cognition skandha: that is thought, ideas. Because the five senses contact and receive the states of the five dusts, all kinds of discursive thoughts and ideas arise. They flash into being and vanish, producing reflection upon form and feeling.

The formation skandha. Formation means shifting flow—moving and changing, now coming now going, now going now coming, never pausing, drifting on without stop. The impulse to do evil or good lies in the mind, yet ruled by discursive thought and reflection, it shows through the acts and gestures of body, mouth, and mind (all such acts belong to the formation skandha).

The consciousness skandha. Consciousness means discrimination; when states come, a discriminating mind arises. For example: seeing beauty, delight arises; hearing harsh words, dislike arises, and so on.

Smashing through the five skandhas, you cross beyond all suffering and hardship—no more calamity at all. Why do we suffer calamity? Because we have not yet cast off the two attachments: attachment to self and attachment to dharmas (all things and matters).

In Great Master Xuanjue's Song of Enlightenment it is said:

The five skandhas, floating clouds, empty in coming and going;

The three poisons, water bubbles, hollow in appearing and vanishing.

Meaning:

The five skandhas like drifting clouds, neither coming nor going; The three poisons like water bubbles, falsely appearing and vanishing.

The five skandhas never had any own-nature—like drifting clouds, suddenly there, suddenly gone. Not penetrating this principle, we remain forever shrouded by the five skandhas, unable to be at ease, unable to be liberated. The cultivator must smash the five skandhas. As clouds drift by, let them drift by; as they drift away, let them drift away. Pay them no heed, cling to them not. The three poisons—greed, anger, delusion—are like water bubbles, with no real substance. They arise of themselves and vanish of themselves, so do not cling to them. The "Song of Enlightenment" also says:

Realize True Suchness—no person, no dharmas;

In an instant, wipe out Avici karma.

If I used false words to deceive beings,

May I have my tongue pulled out for dust-mote kalpas.

Meaning:

Realize True Suchness—no person, no dharmas;

In an instant, shake off Avici karma.

If with lying words I deceived beings,

May I suffer tongue-cutting for Ganges-sand kalpas.

"True Suchness" is "no marks, yet nothing that is not marked" (no shape at all, yet nothing that is not it). It also means "sweep away all dharmas and matters; leave behind all marks and notions." It may be called "returning to the origin, realizing the pure own-nature." Reaching this state, there is neither person nor dharmas. Person and dharmas both forgotten. No more clinging to people, no more clinging to dharmas (things and matters) either. That is realizing the principle and substance of True Suchness. Then, in a single instant, all the karma leading to the Uninterrupted Hells, created through limitless kalpas past, at once wholly dissolves. Great Master Yongjia said: "If I used false words to deceive beings, I willingly go down to the tongue-pulling hells, suffering through kalpas as countless as dust motes."

In the Chan Hall, cultivate genuinely. Like reeling silk from cocoons, you must be patient, drawing each thread slowly, or it tangles. Do not fancy yourselves clever, seeking shortcuts, wanting to use science to become enlightened—that is idle fancy. If science could bring enlightenment, scientists would long ago have cornered it for themselves, enlightened long since, leaving no share for anyone else! Put away hazy notions; sincerely and properly investigate "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" Though your back aches, bear it; though your legs hurt, endure; enduring on and on, the moment will come when you become enlightened. As it is said:

Without one bout of bone-piercing cold,

How could plum blossoms fill the nose with fragrance?

Meaning:

Never passing through bone-chilling cold,

How could plum blossoms release their scent?

Take heed! Do not be too clever, only to be fooled by your own cleverness. Remember: a share of effort in cultivation is a share of skill. Cultivation is true skill, not "mouth Chan" (Chan in words only). Mere talk without practice does no good. "Mouth Chan" not only fails to help enlightenment—on the contrary, it obstructs. Hence:

"Not speaking—that is Chan."

A single thought of spiritual light can shine through heaven and earth—you are in no way different from the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods. Why can we not realize the Three Bodies, Four Wisdoms, Five Eyes, and Six Spiritual Powers? Because we common beings have too many discursive thoughts, and so wisdom is veiled, lightless—becoming ignorance. All day raising delusion, creating karma, and so undergoing bitter retribution in the round of birth and death.

The Three Bodies are the Dharma body, the reward body, and the response body (or transformation body).

The Four Wisdoms are the All-Accomplishing Wisdom, the Wonderful Contemplating Wisdom, the Wisdom of Equality-Nature, and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.

The Five Eyes are the flesh eye, the heavenly eye, the Dharma eye, the wisdom eye, and the Buddha eye.

The Six Spiritual Powers are the heavenly-eye penetration, the heavenly-ear penetration, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of past lives, spiritual travel, and the ending of outflows.

Only with no discursive thoughts at all can you realize these states. This is no abstruse philosophy or theory—just a natural phenomenon, realized through true skill. Nothing strange about it; most ordinary.

From beginningless kalpas past we have been veiled by ignorance, never meeting a Good Knowing Advisor to guide us, never knowing what understanding the mind and seeing the nature (awakening to one's own mind, thoroughly seeing the fundamental nature) is, never knowing what returning to the origin (going back to the source) is. We practice Chan precisely to understand the mind and see the nature, to return to the origin. Once liberated, there are no more obstacles or hindrances—far apart from all upside-down dream-like thinking—at last reaching Nirvana.

Chan Session, 12/1980

tieu_de: Without Eliminating Discursive Thoughts, There Can Be No Enlightenment
tom_tat: The purpose of investigating Chan is to open wisdom and seek liberation. We must focus mind and will on investigating “Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?” Investigating to the extreme, you will forget every discursive thought—forget food, clothing, sleep…
noi_dung:
Without Eliminating Discursive Thoughts, There Can Be No Enlightenment

The purpose of investigating Chan is to open wisdom and seek liberation. We must focus mind and will on investigating the phrase "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" Investigating to the extreme, you will forget every discursive thought—forget food and drink, clothing, sleep, and even great and small needs! Then, "wind cannot blow through, rain cannot seep in"—you only unbrokenly investigate the word "Who"! This single thought is firm as vajra, indestructible. Then, "above, you do not know there is sky; below, you do not know there is earth; in between, you do not know there are people"—reaching the state of "no others, no self, no living beings, no life"; and that is also when you experience "within, no body or mind; without, no world"—yourself and the universe merged into one.

In ancient times, many virtuous high monks could reach the level of "not a single thought arising" (giving rise to no discursive thoughts):

"Though eating rice all day, never eating a single grain. Though wearing clothes all day, never putting on a single thread."

Reaching the state of "no others, no self," with no more clinging to self and others, where would there be time to give rise to discursive thoughts? They held that wasting a minute could forfeit the chance of enlightenment, and so focused on investigating "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?"—not resting until the word "who" was found. Seeking the word "Who" is the finest method of controlling discursive thoughts.

At Gaomin Monastery in Yangzhou there was a monk named Miaodu. Investigating Chan to the level of "walking without knowing he was walking, standing without knowing he was standing, sitting without knowing he was sitting, lying down without knowing he was lying down," he thought of nothing at all, focusing only on "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" One day he needed to urinate, but so unbroken was his wholehearted investigation of the word "Who" that he walked into the Hall of Heavenly Kings by mistake, taking the area before Wei Tuo Bodhisattva's altar for the restroom! Just as he was about to urinate, he suddenly raised his head and saw Wei Tuo Bodhisattva glaring down at him, jeweled pestle raised high—frightening him wide awake! Realizing he had come to the wrong place, he hastily prostrated before Wei Tuo Bodhisattva, repenting his offense and begging forgiveness.

How could such a thing happen? Because Chan Master Miaodu focused so single-heartedly, investigating the word "Who" with his whole being, paying no heed to anything else, that he mistook the Hall of Heavenly Kings for the restroom!

Someone idly thinks: "I'll imitate Chan Master Miaodu—I'll go to the Avalokiteshvara altar instead of the restroom!" If you deliberately did so, you would be a hundred and eight thousand miles from the Way! Know that Chan Master Miaodu imitated no one—he only single-mindedly investigated "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?", wholly absorbed in a single question, and so it came about. Deliberately imitating him and going astray is utterly wrong; you should not harbor even the thought of imitating! Remember:

"Off by an inch, off by a mile."

Many sit in the Chan Hall yet refuse to apply effort, idly wondering: "Why hasn't anyone struck the bell yet? Hurry and sound the rest so I can stretch my arms and legs and ease this ache!" Or their discursive thoughts turn to food: "Isn't mealtime here yet? I'm starving!" Some even calculate: "Twelve days gone—nine more days till merit is perfected. If only it would hurry up and end, so this torment stops!" People join a Chan Session hoping the longer the better, for more chances at enlightenment—yet these sit on the bench as if on a bed of nails, fidgety and restless, shifting legs or stretching—never still. Others enter samadhi, while they enter "gossip-samadhi," chattering discursive thoughts unceasing. If that is how it is, why join a Chan Session at all? What use putting on airs of cultivation? Better not to come, and spare yourselves the suffering!?

But know that to end birth and death, you must hang the two words "birth and death" before your brows, so that opening your eyes you see the question of birth and death, closing your eyes you never forget life and death. At all times applying effort—only then can birth and death be ended. If in the Chan Hall you never think of "ending birth and escaping death," but instead idle away in scattered thoughts, as if fearing your discursive thoughts too few—how pitiful!

The cultivator of the Way must not give rise to discursive thoughts even for a second. There is a saying:

"The great matter unclear—like burying one's parents."

(The great matter not yet understood—as mournful as a parent's funeral.)

Until we understand the "great matter of birth and death," it is as grievous and lamentable as a parent's death. So in investigating Chan, always apply effort—waste not a second or minute, and never be lax. Applying effort until "the furnace fire turns pure blue," the skill ripened—sympathetic response comes of itself. With sympathetic response, skill corresponds. Even after enlightenment, you must still keep striving forward. Never be lazy, never lock yourselves in the "conjured city"; never suppose the journey ends here, unwilling to advance further. Such notions are stumbling blocks in cultivation.

Knowing clearly that discursive thoughts will never bring you enlightenment, why still give rise to them? Knowing clearly they are discursive thoughts, why not sweep them away? That is most people's failing—knowing, yet deliberately offending. Plainly put, you still "cannot see through, cannot let go," still clinging to this, haggling over that, attached to male and female...—wasting all your precious time.

Chan Session time is supremely precious, for such fine affinities are not easily met. During this time, fling all discursive thoughts beyond the ninth cloud, keep the mind pure, and focus on "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" Do not slacken! Everyone, strive in investigating Chan! Investigate! Investigate! Investigate!

(Chan Session, 12/1980)

tieu_de: Enlightenment Must Be Certified to Accord with the Dharma
tom_tat: Before the time of King Awesome Sound Buddha, anyone could become enlightened without needing anyone's certification. From the time of King Awesome Sound Buddha onward, all who awakened on their own must be approved by a Patriarch or a Good Knowing Advisor (already…
noi_dung:
Enlightenment Must Be Certified to Accord with the Dharma

Before the time of King Awesome Sound Buddha, anyone could become enlightened without needing anyone's certification. From the time of King Awesome Sound Buddha onward, all who awakened on their own must be approved and certified by a Patriarch or a Good Knowing Advisor (already enlightened) to accord with the rules. Just as at the Shurangama Dharma assembly, twenty-five sages recounted their perfect-penetration realizations and requested Shakyamuni Buddha's certification.

Now I shall tell you a gongan about certification.

In the Tang dynasty (China), there was Great Master Yongjia. He was born in Yongjia county, Zhejiang province. Because all his life he never left Yongjia county, people of the time called him Great Master Yongjia. After leaving home, he studied the doctrines of the Tiantai school and loved practicing Chan contemplation; through reading the Vimalakirti Sutra he was suddenly greatly enlightened. Later, meeting Chan Master Xuan Ce (a disciple of the Sixth Patriarch Huineng), Yongjia recounted his own story. Chan Master Xuan Ce advised him to visit the Sixth Patriarch at Caoxi and request certification—otherwise, enlightened without a teacher, he would be a "naturalist heretic."

When Yongjia arrived at Nanhua Monastery in Caoxi, the Sixth Patriarch happened to be sitting in Chan. Yongjia was most arrogant—coming beside the Sixth Patriarch's bench, he neither bowed nor prostrated, but circled the bench three times holding his staff, then stood leaning on it.

The Sixth Patriarch asked: "A Shramana must be complete in three thousand dignified manners and eighty thousand subtle conducts. Lacking not a single conduct may one be called a Shramana (translated as Diligence-and-Extinction—diligent in morality, samadhi, and wisdom; extincting greed, anger, and delusion—diligent in morality, samadhi, and wisdom, ending greed, anger, and delusion). Venerable One, from where do you come, giving rise to such great arrogance?"

Yongjia replied: "Birth and death is the great matter; impermanence is swift."

The Sixth Patriarch asked: "Why not embody the unborn? Why not comprehend the unswift?"

Yongjia replied: "Embodying is itself the unborn. Comprehending is originally the unswift."

The Sixth Patriarch said: "You truly understand the meaning of the unborn."

Yongjia retorted: "Is there still meaning in the unborn?"

The Sixth Patriarch answered: "Without meaning, who is discriminating?"

Yongjia replied: "Discrimination is itself not meaning!"

The Sixth Patriarch said: "So it is! So it is!"

Then Yongjia received approval and certification, becoming a Dharma heir of the Sixth Patriarch.

After receiving the Sixth Patriarch's certification, Yongjia wished to return at once to Kaiyuan Monastery in Yongjia. But the Sixth Patriarch kept him for one night, and only the next day did he descend the mountain for home. Because in a single night he had awakened to the true principle of the Buddhadharma, people of the time called him "the One-Night Enlightened Monk" (the Master enlightened within one night). Later he vigorously proclaimed the Sudden Enlightenment dharma of the Chan school, writing the Song of Enlightenment expounding the state of sudden enlightenment. It is an immortal work, a required text in Buddhism.

Sitting in the Chan Hall, outwardly we look as if applying effort in cultivation, yet in fact we only sit thinking, scattered discursive thoughts—not cultivating at all. Someone thinks: "This is the scientific age; enlightenment must use scientific methods"—yet thinks back and forth, nothing scientific about it—truly "a fool talking dreams."

Whoever is enlightened must pass every test—or else commit the offense of great false speech and fall into the Uninterrupted Hells. As a rule, all who trumpet themselves—"I am enlightened! I have realized fruition!"—must undergo retribution (falling into the hells). I hope you are all most careful, never speaking recklessly, lest retribution come hereafter!

Here you rise very early and sleep very late. Why cultivate so bitterly? Because one more minute of Chan investigation is one more chance at awakening. Now you sit in the Chan Hall focusing the mind, investigating "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?"—not that none applies effort single-mindedly, but those truly wishing to awaken and gain its use are very few. Most do not clearly understand Chan investigation, nor are they earnest; they cultivate perfunctorily, muddling through the days. With such an attitude toward the Session, though they sat till "the end of future kalpas," they could never become enlightened. I hope every country will have many awakened ones, to aid the future of Buddhism.

During the Session, do not chat, do not think scattered thoughts. Truly apply effort—only then is there sympathetic response, only then does wisdom open. With wisdom, no longer upside down. No longer upside down, you can teach beings. If you yourself do not clearly understand the truth, with what standing do you teach others? Is that not "the blind leading the blind"? Most dangerous indeed!

Chan investigation is like a farmer sowing grain in spring; in summer tilling, watering, weeding, manuring; in autumn reaping a fine harvest; and when winter comes, food and warmth. A farmer's hope through the year is enough to eat and wear. Chan investigation is the same. Carefully guard your thoughts, always keeping watch over yourselves. In the Chan Hall—walking, are you applying effort? Sitting, are you applying effort? In short, walking, standing, lying, sitting—all must be effort in cultivation. Whatever effort suits you, apply effort so—no restrictions. For example, if investigating the hua-tou does not correspond for you, you may recite the Buddha's name, or practice stopping-and-contemplating. Whatever method suits and corresponds for you will bring your chance at accomplishment.

Whatever Dharma-door you apply effort in, the mind must be single—no discursive thoughts. Applying effort to the extreme, good news will come. With discursive, scattered thinking always, no Dharma-door will correspond. One who truly applies effort—walking, not knowing walking; sitting, not knowing sitting—heeding neither walking nor sitting, how could discursive thoughts arise? You need only know "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name? Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" Just this one phrase, thought after thought unbroken, always investigating within. Then, thirsty, you know no thirst; hungry, you know no hunger; hot, you know no heat; cold, you know no cold. Why not? Because the mind is single. Aching back—the ache forgotten; hurting legs—the hurt unknown; all thoughts dying away. Only one thought remains: "Who recites the Buddha's name?" Always raising it up, then letting it go. Let go, then raise it up again. At all times unbroken, effort continuous, unpaused. Applying effort to the extreme, any chance encounter can suddenly bring you enlightenment.

Why are you not suddenly enlightened? Because you are not yet focused in will, do not yet understand the principle of understanding the mind and seeing the nature, do not know the state of returning to the origin, and do not know where your homeland is—and so wander in foreign lands like a beggar.

In closing I leave you with this: investigate "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" until "mountains end and waters run dry, the road of doubt exhausted"; then you will see "dark willows, bright flowers—another village ahead."

(Chan Session, 12/1980)

tieu_de: Good and Evil Never Leave the Single Thought in Our Minds
tom_tat: This is the true principle of Buddhism. Everyone understands this truth, yet no one can practice it—and so the world is in great…
noi_dung:
Good and Evil Never Leave the Single Thought in Our Minds

"Commit no evil,

Do all good deeds,

Purify your own mind—

That is the Buddhas' teaching."

This is the true principle of Buddhism. Everyone understands this truth, yet no one can practice it—and so the world is in great turmoil.

A Chan Session is the finest chance for us to "reform evil toward good, correct faults and renew ourselves." With a single evil thought, heaven and earth can breed wild winds and storms, creating every calamity. If all humankind across the globe knew to receive and uphold the Five Precepts and practice the Ten Good Deeds, then heaven and earth would send timely wind and rain, and the world everywhere would be at peace. In short, if from the head of state down to the common folk all kept the Five Precepts and did the Ten Good Deeds, that nation would surely enjoy ample food and clothing, everyone dwelling in peace and work. If all violated the Five Precepts and committed the Ten Evils, then no doubt—in that nation, families would know no harmony, society no security, the country no wealth or strength, and the people a life of misery and toil.

Investigating Chan is itself no killing, no stealing, no sexual misconduct, no false speech, no intoxicants. In the Chan Hall, focus on investigating Chan—raising the hua-tou, letting go of all matters, concentrating on the word "Who." At all times shining the search, halting every other discursive thought—that is upholding the Five Precepts, and also practicing the Ten Good Deeds. Thus, sitting in Chan in the Chan Hall fulfills the Five Precepts and Ten Good Deeds. So waste no time on idle fancies; seize the moment to investigate "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?"

In investigating Chan, we must strive vigorously and valiantly. We must return the light and reflect it inward (gathering in mind and thought, shining back upon the inner mind), questioning our own hearts: how many good thoughts have arisen, how many evil thoughts stirred, how many discursive thoughts started. Take stock.
