"Good thoughts unborn—bring them to birth;

Good thoughts born—make them grow.

Evil thoughts unborn—let them never arise;

Evil thoughts born—make them perish."

That is the first, fundamental step of cultivation.

Why is the world destroyed? Because people give rise to "few good thoughts, many evil thoughts." With one good thought, heaven and earth gain in righteous force. With one evil thought, heaven and earth pile up turbid force. So we must turn evil, turbid air into peaceful air. Turbid force is poisonous force: the moment we give rise to a greedy thought, poison in the universe increases a little; a hateful thought, and poison in the universe increases a little more; a deluded thought, and poison in the universe grows still more. If we handle all matters with greed, anger, and delusion, heaven and earth darken and calamities arise; but handling all matters with morality, samadhi, and wisdom, the sky is clear, the earth still, everywhere at peace. Hence: where evil people gather, calamities abound; where many good people dwell, blessings increase. In short, calamity or auspiciousness—both are made by people.

The ancients said: "Good and evil are two roads—who cultivates, cultivates; who creates (karma), creates." Who cultivates good transcends the Three Realms; who creates evil falls into the Three Evil Destinies. Good and evil differ by a single thought. Having wisdom is a good thought; having delusion is an evil thought.

All things in the world speak Dharma (reveal truth). Some speak wholesome Dharma, some unwholesome. Some speak the dharma of side doors and crooked paths, wrong views. Some speak the Middle Way, the definitive-meaning Dharma, right views. In other words, speaking wholesome Dharma teaches people to see through all appearances, let go of all attachments, and gain ease; speaking unwholesome Dharma teaches people not to see through, not to let go of attachments, never gaining ease. Why are people upside down? Because of attachment, refusing to let go. An ancient verse says:

Since ancient times, how many heroes—

North and south mountains, all lie in mud.

Meaning:

Since ancient times, so many heroes and stalwarts, Lying in muddy earth over every mountain.

Consider: of all the people in this dusty world, who can leap past the gate of birth and death? Alive, scheming for empty fame—dead, where is the fame? Coveting high office—dead, office ends too! All turns to emptiness. In China, Qin Shi Huang, wishing to protect his descendants so that age upon age would reign as emperors, had the Great Wall built. Who knew the throne would pass only to the second generation—his son Hu Hai (the Second Emperor of Qin), reigning less than three years before being killed by Chancellor Zhao Gao. Was that not wasted scheming?

Since ancient times, at home and abroad, the immensely rich, the high officials—all living lives deluded, scrambling for fame and gain, creating boundless karmic offenses; at death, empty-handed to meet King Yama. See then: in investigating Chan we must resolve to apply effort—no laxity, no indulgence—lest the chance slip by and later regret come too late.

As it is said:

"A moment of time, a moment of life."

Someone says: "Once I am famous, I shall let go of everything and focus on cultivating the Way." But time waits for no one—waiting till then is already too late.

Investigating Chan or reciting the Buddha's name—both are fine. Only cultivate genuinely, and you can escape the wheel of birth and death; at life's end you will surely "have a body free of sickness and suffering, a mind free of greed and attachment, as if entering samadhi, smiling to rebirth." That is truly holding birth and death in your own hands!

(Chan Session, 12/1980)

tieu_de: The Story of Master Xuanzang's Journey to India for Sutras
tom_tat: Dharma Master Xuanzang was born in the second year of Renshou under Emperor Wen of Sui—the year 601 C.E. He was a native of Chenliu, Henan, of the Chen family, and from childhood showed uncommon intelligence—at only seven he studied the Five…
noi_dung:
The Story of Master Xuanzang's Journey to India for Sutras

Dharma Master Xuanzang was born in the second year of Renshou under Emperor Wen of Sui—the year 601 C.E. He was a native of Chenliu, Henan, of the Chen family, and from childhood showed uncommon intelligence—at only seven he studied the Five Classics. At thirteen, he followed his second elder brother, Dharma Master Changjie, to Luoyang, leaving home at Jingtu Monastery, where he studied the Sutra canon. Under the Sui system, whoever wished to leave home and cultivate had to pass an examination. Those who qualified received a certificate called an ordination permit, and only then were fit to be novices. The Master reached Luoyang just as an examination was being held, but being too young, he was not allowed to sit it. Before the examination hall gate, he stood lingering, sighing with regret! The chief examiner, Zheng Shanguo, chanced to see him and at once recognized him as a dragon-elephant of Buddhism, specially admitting him to the examination.

At twenty, after receiving the Complete Precepts, the Master set out traveling to consult Good Knowing Advisors everywhere. He had occasion to notice that the teachings of various monks often disagreed with the Sutra canon, leaving cultivators not knowing what to rely on—especially regarding the Treatise on the Seventeen Stages, where views diverged on many points. He then vowed to go to India (present-day India) to study the Buddhadharma and resolve these doubts.

Because the road to India was grueling, crossing countless obstacles—peaks soaring high, passes perilous beyond measure—to prepare for this hazardous journey, Dharma Master Xuanzang trained himself in mountaineering.

Using tables, chairs, and the like, piling one upon another, heaped like an artificial hill, every day he practiced climbing up and down until adept, then went into real forests and mountains to practice. Such training lasted about a year.

The Master memorialized the throne, requesting leave to seek Sutras in India. At the time the Tang court forbade leaving the country, so the Master's memorial was not approved by Emperor Taizong. Yet, resolved beforehand, whether permitted or not, in the end he firmly set out.

Starting from Chang'an, alone, the Master headed straight west.

One day, passing a mountain cave, he saw much bat droppings before its mouth. He thought some cave must surely be uninhabited—for were anyone dwelling there, how could there be so much bat droppings! Moved by curiosity, the Master entered, and before going far he saw a strange shape, like a monster: hair matted atop its head, where birds had built a nest, nestlings chirping within! The monster's face was coated with thick dust, shaped like a stone statue. Drawing near to look closely, the Master found—an old cultivator, long in samadhi. The Master struck a hand bell lightly to bring him out of samadhi, and after a while the old monk began to stir.

The Master asked why he sat there. The old monk's jaw worked a while, then sound emerged as follows:

-"I await the Red-Yang Buddha (Shakyamuni Buddha) appearing in the world, that I may help him propagate the Buddhadharma."

Hearing the Master say that Shakyamuni Buddha had long since entered Nirvana, the old monk looked astonished and asked:

When was Shakyamuni born?

He was born over a thousand years ago, and long since passed away.

The old monk said:

Shakyamuni has entered Nirvana? Then I shall enter samadhi again and await the White-Yang Buddha (Maitreya Buddha) appearing, to help him propagate the Buddhadharma.

The Master said:

You need not enter samadhi awaiting Maitreya Buddha's advent. Thus you might miss your chance yet again. Better now to follow me to Zhendan (China). When I return home, you shall help me propagate the Buddhadharma.

The old monk thought it over and found it reasonable, agreeing to Dharma Master Xuanzang's proposal.

The Master instructed him: "This body of yours is too worn out—you should change into a new one. Reaching Chang'an, look for a house roofed with yellow glazed tiles and be reborn there. Later, when I return from India with the Sutras, I shall come for you."

With that, the two parted—one heading east, the other west.

Dharma Master Xuanzang climbed passes and forded streams, enduring countless perils, never once retreating. He had vowed:

Better to die one step in the Western Heaven

Than live, stepping back toward the Eastern Land.

Such a spirit—forgetting self for the Dharma—was truly great! Only thus could the Master complete an equally great enterprise, a magnificent contribution to Chinese Buddhism; he was also the founder of the Consciousness-Only school.

There is a saying, "seeing the worthy, think of equaling them." To accomplish our Way-karma, we must follow the bright example of Dharma Master Xuanzang, taking him as our model, so that our inherent wisdom appears and we contribute our share to Buddhism.

From then on, day after day, pillowing on earth under dew, he kept westward on his journey, patiently holding his resolve, single-hearted—not stopping short of the goal. The ancients said: "Where there's a will, there's a way." After myriad hardships, traveling three years, he reached India, and at Nalanda Buddhist University took Great Master Shilabhadra as teacher—then a high monk famed for Consciousness-Only studies. There he specialized in the Treatise on the Seventeen Stages and the Yogacara Treatise.

Finishing his studies, the Master returned home. Passing the city of Kanyakubja (Kanyakudja), he was invited by its king, Shiladitya (Shiladitya). When Kanyakubja held a great convocation—attended by eighteen kings together with Mahayana and Hinayana schools, Brahmins, and even outside paths, some six thousand in all, in short a Dharma assembly unprecedented—the Master was invited as its host. He also drafted a treatise proclaiming the Mahayana, posted before the assembly hall gate with a note: "Correct a single word, and I shall take you as teacher." The convocation lasted eighteen days, yet none corrected a word; in the end he stood invincible, his name resounding through the five regions of India—none ignorant of Dharma Master Xuanzang's great name.

In the 19th year of Zhenguan (645 C.E.), on the 24th of the first lunar month, he reached Chang'an, greeted by tens of thousands—monastics and laity alike. Emperor Taizong sent the prime minister, the Duke of Liang, Fang Xuanling, to receive him. Later he presided at Hongfu Monastery, translating Buddhist Sutras.

He studied in India twelve years, plus five years traveling to and fro—thus a veritable Patriarch among monk-scholars abroad. The Sutras brought back to China filled five hundred and twenty crates—over six hundred texts. He offered them all to the nation. The Tang Emperor summoned him to court and rewarded him.

Meeting the Tang Emperor, he offered congratulations: "Congratulations, Your Majesty!" The Emperor

not grasping his meaning, asked back: -"Congratulations on what?"

- On Your Majesty's new crown prince.

The Tang Emperor, most surprised, replied:

- No such thing.

The Master thought to himself: "I clearly told the old monk to be reborn here—why is he nowhere seen?" He entered samadhi to contemplate. Alas! The old monk, searching carelessly, had been reborn by mistake into General Yuchi Gong's household! The Master memorialized the Emperor with the whole affair. Taizong said:

So that is how it is. Master, take him across.

The Master visited Yuchi Gong and told the story. At first sight of this meritorious official's nephew, he rejoiced greatly—for the young man looked most handsome, the makings of a hero, surely a great Dharma vessel hereafter. So he opened straightaway: "Follow me and leave home!" Hearing this, the youth looked displeased and replied:

What does the Great Master say? Tell me to leave home? No such thing! With that, the youth turned on his heel and left.

Dharma Master Xuanzang could only memorialize the Tang Emperor again, asking him to complete this affinity. Taizong issued an edict ordering Yuchi Gong's nephew to leave home. The great minister received the edict and summoned his nephew, meeting flat refusal. He said:

How can this be! Why does the Emperor make me leave home? Let me see the Emperor and get this clear!

The next day, Yuchi Gong brought his nephew before the Emperor. The youth memorialized:

Your Majesty bids me leave home—very well! But I ask three conditions.

Taizong said:

As many conditions as you wish.

I have always loved wine and cannot do without it. So wherever I am, a cartload of wine must attend me.

The Emperor thought privately: "A monastic's precepts forbid wine. But Dharma Master Xuanzang instructed me to grant whatever conditions he asks." The Emperor replied:

Granted! What is the second condition?

I know monastics may not eat meat, but I love it. So wherever I am, a cart of fresh meat must follow me.

Granted. And the third condition?

Yuchi Gong's nephew, never imagining the Emperor would grant his first two demands, continued:

Monastics may not have wives, but I cannot do without women. So wherever I am, a cartload of girls must follow me.

The Tang Emperor thought: "Dear me! How can this be granted? But the Master instructed me to accept whatever conditions he asks." Thinking so, the Emperor replied:

Granted! I approve them all. Now you may leave home!

Seeing no further way to refuse, the youth reluctantly agreed to leave home. So, on the appointed day, when he walked to Great Xingshan Monastery for the ceremony, behind him trailed a cart of wine, a cart of fresh meat, a cart of beauties. Meanwhile the monastery, forewarned, at news of the party's approach sounded drums and bells together. At the first sound of bell and drum, the youth awoke: "Oh! I am that old monk of years past, come here to help Dharma Master Xuanzang propagate the Buddhadharma." At once he sent all three carts back, wanting nothing more.

That youth later became Great Master Kuiji, styled by his contemporaries the Three-Carts Patriarch.

Among the Treatises on the Thirty Verses on Consciousness-Only that Dharma Master Xuanzang brought back to China were ten commentators' works in all. The Master translated them all into Chinese, closely following the originals—not a word added, not a word omitted. At the time Great Master Kuiji served as polisher. When all ten Treatises were translated, Great Master Kuiji proposed: "Among the ten commentators' works, each has its strengths and each its differences. Without unification, scholars now and hereafter may be confused, not knowing what to rely on. Better to strip away the redundant husk, keep only the kernel, and cast it into a single treatise, so that students of Consciousness-Only now and hereafter may reach one conclusion, without wasting time, grasping the dharma's essence."

Dharma Master Xuanzang found the proposal sound, and so all were merged into one treatise—today's "Treatise on the Thirty Verses on Consciousness-Only."

The Master further personally transmitted to Great Master Kuiji the Hetuvidya Treatise (logic), making Great Master Kuiji thereafter a specialist in Consciousness-Only studies. Devoting his whole mind to spreading Consciousness-Only thought, the Great Master is regarded as the Second Patriarch of the Consciousness-Only school.

Two years after returning home, Dharma Master Xuanzang was commanded to compose the "Great Tang Records on the Western Regions" in 12 fascicles. In the first year of Xianqing under the Tang—6460 C.E.—at fifty-nine, he began translating the Great Prajna Sutra. In the Sanskrit original, the Great Prajna Sutra comprises two hundred thousand (200,000) verses. He translated it entire, omitting not a passage, closely following the original, completing six hundred fascicles in four years. The next year he planned to translate the Great Jewel-Accumulation Sutra, but falling ill, translation halted.

The Master passed away in the second month of the first year of Linde,

at sixty-four, buried at Beiyuan by the Fan River. The Master's Sutra-translation work totals 75 texts in 1335 fascicles. Thus he ranks among China's four great Sutra translators. His disciples were many—among them Great Master Kuiji and Woncheuk inheriting Consciousness-Only, while Puguang and Shentai inherited the Kosha school.

The Sui and Tang dynasties were Buddhism's golden age—the age of "a hundred schools contending"—Patriarchs appearing in turn to found schools. At the time there were ten schools: two of the Hinayana, eight of the Mahayana.

Of these ten, the Three Treatise school and the Consciousness-Only school wholly preserved India's original thought—the teaching transmitted to new soil, its essence kept intact. As for the Tiantai school—taking the Lotus Sutra as its basis—and the Xianshou school—taking the Avatamsaka Sutra as its basis—their content had merged with Chinese thought. The four schools just named are classed as the Teachings gate. Down to today, through time's changes, the present categories divide into five great houses: Teachings, Chan, Pure Land, Vinaya, Esoteric.

In truth all share one ultimate goal—reaching Nirvana—differing only in methods of practice.

Chan Session talks, December 1980

tieu_de: Investigating Chan Requires Returning the Light Inward
tom_tat: What is “it”? It is the hua-tou we use to apply effort in Chan investigation. Cultivate the Way with the true mind: raise up the hua-tou and investigate unbrokenly, unceasingly. Hour after hour, minute after minute…
noi_dung:
Investigating Chan Requires Returning the Light Inward

Walking, standing, lying, sitting,

Never apart from it;

Apart from it—

At once a mistake.

What is "it"? It is the hua-tou we use to apply effort in Chan investigation. Cultivate the Way with the true mind: raise up the hua-tou and investigate unbrokenly, unceasingly. Hour after hour, minute after minute, second after second—not a stray thought, not a discursive thought intruding; in short, in thought after thought, only the single hua-tou as the topic of investigation. Then where is there time to chat with one another and disturb others? No chance either to laze and rest, still less to gossip about rights and wrongs—single-heartedly holding the hua-tou to awaken. There is a verse:

All matters pass smoothly by;

Hard to cast off is temper.

If truly never angered—

That is a precious jewel.

Harboring no hatred,

All matters flow.

Afflictions never arise—

Whence grievances?

Ever blaming others,

Suffering without end.

Only with such an attitude can the Chan investigator hope one day to "enter the gate." In the Chan Hall, everyone must return the light and reflect it inward—turning back upon themselves, asking: am I applying effort, or letting my mind run after discursive thoughts? Look at yourselves: am I shining the light to illumine myself—not shining outward? This demands our utmost heed.

Applying effort in the Chan Hall, remember these two lines:

Mahasattvas pay others no mind;

With Amitabha, each looks to himself!

Moment after moment, manage yourselves—no need to mind anyone else, still less to trouble others, for that obstructs everyone's effort and may cost them their chance at enlightenment—unacceptable. As I often tell you:

Sincerely admit your own faults;

Never discuss the faults of others.

Others' faults are my own faults;

Same substance is called Great Compassion.

If everyone held this thought, all would cultivate single-heartedly, thinking of nothing else—no more busy gossip disturbing others.

The Chan investigator must squarely face one fundamental issue. What issue? That is habitual tendencies. Sitting in Chan removes habitual tendencies and bad habits, purifies the mind, and undoes the ugly habit of envying those better than ourselves. Cast off envious minds, afflicted and ignorant minds—all of them. Only then will the True Mind show, wisdom appear, and the meditator have hope of good news.

Why do people love gossip about rights and wrongs? Precisely from delusion. Why does jealousy arise? Also from delusion. Why the wish to harm others? Delusion, all of it. Whatever is unreasonable springs from delusion. Then whence delusion? Precisely from refusing to practice samadhi, and so lacking wisdom—and so we circle forever in self and others, right and wrong, never getting out. Therefore we must return the light inward, facing our past faults, resolving to reform, instead of stubbornly clutching ugly habits and refusing to let go.

Why do you doze when sitting in Chan? Because in seeking the Dharma your hearts are not true. If you sincerely sought the Way, you would never doze. Try it and see—am I right or not?

Chan Session talks, December 1980

tieu_de: The Chan Hall Is the Way-Place That Selects Buddhas
tom_tat: Everyone coming to the Chan Hall to apply effort may be seen as sitting for an examination—testing who will win the fruition of Buddhahood. How can one pass? The crux is reaching the state “within, no body or mind; without…
noi_dung:
The Chan Hall Is the Way-Place That Selects Buddhas

Everyone coming to the Chan Hall to apply effort may be seen as sitting for an examination—testing who will win the fruition of Buddhahood. How can one pass? The crux is reaching the state "within, no body or mind; without, no world"—in other words, this state:

Seeing, yet not seeing;

Hearing, yet not hearing;

Smelling, yet no scent.

Whoever has such skill has hope of passing.

Why seeing, yet not seeing? Through "returning the light and reflecting it inward." Why hearing, yet not hearing? Through "turning the hearing around to listen to oneself." Why smelling, yet no scent? Because body and mind are gathered in, so scents cause no clinging. This is the state where the eyes see forms yet see no forms, the ears hear sounds as if no sounds, the nose smells scents yet senses no scent, the tongue tastes yet no flavor, the body touches yet feels nothing, the mind meets dharmas yet clings to no dharmas. Only reaching this state is there hope of passing and becoming a Buddha. Only when "in the blazing furnace, still fresh and green" (the furnace fire all blue), standing on the "lofty mountain peak," at the "hundred-foot pole's tip" yet leaping further—only then is there hope. So in the Chan Hall we cannot waste time. The ancients said:

An inch of time, an inch of gold;

An inch of gold cannot buy an inch of time.

Gold lost may yet be found;

Time lost—where to seek?

We must seize the moment and strive in cultivation. Many are the Dharma-doors, but "investigating Chan" alone is supreme. In this Dharma-door, applying effort to ripeness can work a total turnaround—can "turn the back on dust to unite with awakening"—and pass to become a Buddha.

The Bodhisattva-Way cultivator can give up country, home, wife and children. Within the body, he can even give up head, eyes, brains and marrow—wholeheartedly for beings, giving all without regret. Equipped with such a spirit, at the "Buddha-selecting school" there is hope of passing. Know that this is the Buddhas' selection—utterly impartial, won by no luck but only by your own true skill.

Buddhas select Buddhas—not demons selecting Buddhas—yet demons aid Buddhas. Buddhas teach beings directly, while demons teach indirectly, teaching from the reverse side, spurring us to great vows and aiding our vigorous cultivation. So demons are the other face of Good Knowing Advisors. I often say:

Demons whet the path of the Way;

The True Way always has demons.

The more whet, the brighter;

The brighter, the more whetting.

Whet like the bright moon

Shining mid-sky upon the demon host;

Its light scattering demons—

The original Buddha appears.

So we should not treat demons as enemies, but regard demons as Good Knowing Advisors too. Contemplating thus, we rest at ease and avoid afflictions. For example, someone speaking ill of us is our Good Knowing Advisor. Doing a thing rightly, yet told we did it wrong—we strive to do it still more rightly, as in the saying: "Atop the hundred-foot pole, step one step further." "Whoever shows me my faults is my teacher"—we must regard whoever finds our faults as our teacher, thanking them, not taking them for enemies.

The Buddhas are not as muddled as we are; so while we keep wearing our false faces, we can never be selected as Buddhas. We must sincerely seek what is true—and true, yet truer still—we must be "true, true, true, true, true, true, true!" seven times true, to hope for selection. That is "seven trues, eighth right"—in the seven-day Chan Session, genuinely cultivate; on the eighth day, reform from wrong to right. Then all foul habits are swept away at once, reaching utter purity!

Chan Session talks, December 1980 What Is a "No-Mind Cultivator"?

In the Sutra in Forty-Two Chapters there is a line: "Feeding the Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions cannot match feeding a no-mind cultivator." What is a no-mind cultivator? It means the Chan investigator in the Chan Hall who has no mind seeking fame or gain—who has cut off the five roots of the hells: wealth, sex, fame, food, and sleep—with no mind, no other thoughts, while sitting investigating Chan. Such a one is called a no-mind cultivator.

To truly propagate the Dharma in this West, we must follow the "no-mind cultivator" Dharma-door. This is not hoping for offerings for "no-mind cultivators"—for a mind set on offerings is already having a mind. So Chan Hall time is time we truly practice Chan and samadhi—never letting discursive thoughts surge one after another, like film frames flickering past—that is a hundred and eight thousand miles from the Way. The further you walk, the farther from home; you become a wandering vagrant—how pitiable!

We must strive genuinely in cultivation, relying only on our own true skill. Crave no fame or gain; avoid advertising yourselves. Cultivate in the spirit of Manjushri, Samantabhadra, Avalokiteshvara, Ksitigarbha, and the Bodhisattvas—protecting the Way-place and teaching beings. The Bodhisattvas ever take the accomplishment of beings as their own accomplishment, with no distinction of self and others. Bodhisattvas ever hear of people's merit and rejoice in praising it.

The proverb says: "With musk, fragrance comes of itself—what need to fan it with a great wind?" The cultivator mindless to a high degree naturally wins sympathetic response. Doing the Buddha's work is being a Buddha; doing a Bodhisattva's work is being a Bodhisattva; doing an Arhat's work is being an Arhat; doing a ghost's work is being a ghost—that is only natural. The cultivator of the Way cannot take shortcuts or rely on luck. Only truly committing, step by steady step, sincerely cultivating, may one hope one day to accomplish the Way-karma.

Chan Session talks, December 1980

tieu_de: Investigating Chan Is Practicing the Six Paramitas
tom_tat: Serving as verger, note this: when rest comes, the verger must strike the bell once as a signal, so everyone prepares to rise; when all are ready, strike the bell a second time—at once all rise together…
noi_dung:
Investigating Chan Is Practicing the Six Paramitas

Serving as verger, note this: when rest comes, the verger must strike the bell once as a signal, so everyone prepares to rise; seeing all ready, strike the bell a second time—at once all rise together—followed by two beats of the wooden fish signaling to start walking. When running incense, divide into two rings—the outer ring for fast runners, the inner for slow runners. This is a harmonizing arrangement, so all may follow with ease, fast or slow alike. It is said: "Too tight and it snaps; too loose and it sags; neither tight nor loose, and the work succeeds"—meaning cling to no fixed dharma, but stay supple.

In the Diamond Sutra there is a line: "There is no fixed dharma called anuttara-samyak-sambodhi." To want something fixed is to make problems.

The Diamond Sutra also says: "All dharmas are equal, without high or low." So cultivators too must be equal. Though the Buddha has the Three Bodies, Four Wisdoms, Five Eyes, and Six Spiritual Powers, the Buddha still regards himself as no different from beings—hence the saying: "Mind, Buddha, and beings—all three without distinction"—mind is Buddha, Buddha is beings; beings are Buddha, Buddha is mind.

Running fast is also investigating Chan; running slow is also investigating Chan—follow your own strength. The point is naturalness, no artifice, nothing forced—apply effort so, patiently. Back aching, legs hurting—pay them no mind. Wanting nothing at all is called giving. The body doing no evil is purity of bodily karma; the mouth speaking no gossip is purity of verbal karma; the mind free of discursive thoughts is purity of mental karma. The three karmas pure is called moral discipline. Able to bear pain is called patience; able to apply effort unbroken, through all hardships without retreat, is called vigor. Able to sit peacefully unmoved, ever clearly aware, is called samadhi. From samadhi, wisdom arises—that is prajna. All six paramitas perfected—that is reaching the other shore, the shore of awakening.

When stillness begins, the verger must watch: when the row leader reaches his own seat, strike the wooden fish once. When all have reached their seats, strike once more. Everyone sits at once, back straight, head not drooping, back not hunching. It is said, "sit like a bell"—sitting shaped like a bell, head straight, back upright, posture settled and firm.

Investigating "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name" does not mean reciting (recite) this hua-tou. This is investigating—studying the word "who." Someone says: "I know—the one reciting the Buddha's name is me." That is wrong! If we truly answered this hua-tou clearly, we would have seen the nature, found the Dharma's source, and returned home. In fact it is not so simple and easy as we think: "It's me! I'm reciting the Buddha's name." You recite the Buddha's name? Then when you die, can you still recite? You will say "no." If not, how can you claim the one reciting is you? Remember: the one reciting the Buddha's name does not die—if you must die, the one reciting is not you. Reciting the Buddha, one becomes a Buddha—but who becomes a Buddha? Who reaches Buddhahood? You are already dead!

So right here you must investigate—investigating unrelenting, until "seas run dry and rocks crumble," until the day "waters flow, rocks appear"—and in an instant you suddenly awaken: "Ah! So that is how it is!"

Chan Session talks, December 1980

Practicing Formless Merit

The Chan Hall is where Buddhas are selected—here is the field of blessings for sowing merit. There is a saying:

Sitting still for but an instant

Surpasses building seven-jeweled stupas as many as the Ganges' sands.

Why say so? Because building monasteries and stupas is merit with shape and marks.

In the Diamond Sutra there is a line:

All conditioned marks are false and illusory;

Seeing all marks as no marks, one sees the Tathagata.

A rough translation:

Whatever has marks is all false;

Seeing all marks as no marks—that is seeing the Tathagata.

Merit from sitting still, even for a moment, is never lost. Someone says: "Then I'll skip outer merit—I'll do inner merit only." Thinking so is wrong. Do both—cultivate merit and virtue together—until merit is complete, blessings and wisdom both full, becoming the "Honored One of Two Perfections."

Remember: monasteries built, in time decay; stupas raised, in fire burn. Only sitting still can carry the own-nature of

the Triple Jewel—Buddha, Dharma, Sangha—to accomplishment. That is merit without outflows, defying wind and rain, fire and flood, never lost through ages—so formless merit outweighs merit with marks ten thousandfold.

Sitting investigating in the Chan Hall, casting off all discursive thoughts, cultivating with a true mind—that merit is limitless. Otherwise, no benefit at all—hence the saying: "Merit from sitting still for an instant outweighs building stupas as many as the Ganges' sands."

All of you joining this Chan Session already have good roots, meeting this affinity to investigate Chan together. Now keep the mind pure—not following "monkey mind, horse thoughts," letting ideas run outward. That runs counter to the Way—wasting seven days in vain, benefiting nothing, betraying the resolve you brought. Find a way to subdue idle thoughts and settle the mind. There is a saying:

Mind pure—the moon appears in the water's depths;

Settled—the sky without a wisp of cloud.

To this end, next year (1982), a ten-week Chan Session—seventy days of sitting—will be held. Nowhere in the whole world today can you find a Way-place where people investigate Chan for seventy straight days.

The City of Ten Thousand Buddhas vows to turn the Dharma-ending Age into the Right-Dharma Age, and so gives body and life to cultivation, applying effort for the Way. If anyone truly cultivates, only coming to the City of Ten Thousand

Buddhas will they find such a chance. Elsewhere cultivation is perfunctory—skill merely going through the motions. In name also Chan Sessions, but in fact the schedules differ. At the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas, each session day starts circling at two-thirty in the morning and rests only at midnight—and within that span only one hour's break. This is our Chan Session rule.

Chan Session talks, December 1980

tieu_de: The Story of Venerable Master Hsu Yun's Leaving Home
tom_tat: Master Hsu Yun was a native of Xiang, Hunan province, of the Xiao family. His father Yutang once served as prefect of Quanzhou in Fujian—an upright official beloved by the people. At forty, still childless, one day he and his wife…
noi_dung:
The Story of Venerable Master Hsu Yun's Leaving Home

Master Hsu Yun was a native of Xiang, Hunan province, of the Xiao family. His father Yutang once served as prefect of Quanzhou in Fujian—an upright official beloved by the people. At forty, still childless, one day he and his wife went to Avalokiteshvara Monastery to pray for an heir. Their sincerity won sympathetic response, and after returning home, his wife conceived. Ten months to term, both dreamed the same night of a long-bearded old man in blue, wearing an image of Avalokiteshvara on his head, riding a tiger toward them. Waking, the womb delivered a lump of flesh (only an Eighth-Ground Bodhisattva manifests this state). His mother died of fright.

The next day, an old medicine peddler passing by cut the flesh open with a knife, revealing a baby boy inside. The infant was raised by his stepmother.

Endowed with good roots, Master Hsu Yun found Confucian books dull, fame and rank uninteresting—only Buddhist Sutras delighted him—and so from childhood the thought of leaving home to cultivate sprouted. Once he ran off to Gushan Monastery in Fuzhou meaning to leave home, but was caught and brought back. His father sent him home to Hunan under his second uncle's watch, hoping to end all thoughts of leaving home.

He was an only son, while his third uncle had died heirless—and so he became heir to two family branches. By the custom of the day, he might wed two wives—one a daughter-in-law for his birth father, one in place of a daughter-in-law for his uncle—keeping both lines' ancestral rites hereafter. A case of killing two birds with one stone, the envy of the world—yet to him a great nuisance.

To carry on both family lines, at eighteen he wed two ladies, of the Tian and Tan families, in a single ceremony. Both were daughters of genteel houses, well versed in principle. On the wedding night, Master Hsu Yun reached an understanding with both: in name husband and wife, in fact not—chastity kept whole, all three dwelling together, inviolate, living so in peace.

The next year, with both ladies' consent, Venerable Hsu Yun resolved to go (both ladies later left home too). Bidding farewell to warm family life, he went to Yongquan Monastery on Gushan in Fuzhou to leave home. There he bowed to Elder Miaolian as teacher, receiving the Dharma name Yanche, styled Deqing. Fearing his family would find him, he went deep into the mountains to practice asceticism—hungry, eating pine nuts and leaves; thirsty, drinking spring water. Such bitter asceticism truly surpassed human capacity, as in the saying:

Wear what no one can wear;

Eat what no one can eat;

Endure what no one can endure;

Bear what no one can bear.

Through countless trials and hardships, Venerable Hsu Yun never faltered—on the contrary, he rejoiced.

Three years later, to draw near Good Knowing Advisors and further study the Buddhadharma, he traveled everywhere consulting, crossing mountains and forests, tasting every hardship. Wherever a high monk or great worthy dwelled, however distant, however cut off by rivers and mountains, he had to reach them to study the Way. Along the road of study he met many setbacks, yet with inborn patience, an iron will, forgetting self to seek the Dharma, he never retreated—his original resolve unchanged, ever pressing eagerly forward, vigorously studying. Such a spirit truly commands admiration—a model for all to follow.

Later, to repay his kind mother, he vowed the "three steps, one bow" pilgrimage from Mount Putuo to Mount Wutai. Three whole years, his merit perfected, his vow fulfilled.

Now a tale of sympathetic resonance from that pilgrimage.

Bowing his way to the Yellow River's banks, he met snowfall falling three days and nights unceasing. Sheltering in a grass hut, hungry and cold, his body numbed senseless, he lapsed unconscious. Waking, he found in the hut a beggar cooking porridge for him. Eating, his strength returned, and he continued his bowing journey toward Mount Wutai. Only upon reaching Mount Wutai did he learn that the beggar was an incarnation of Manjushri.

While Venerable Hsu Yun was in seclusion on Mount Jiuhua, word came that Gaomin Monastery in Yangzhou would hold a Chan Session of eight weeks. He resolved to join. From Mount Jiuhua he traveled along the river. In heavy rains the river overflowed its banks; slipping, he fell in and was swept away, drifting with the current some twenty-four hours. Near Caishi Rock dam, tangled in a fishing net, he was hauled out—barely breathing. The fishermen reported to nearby Baoji Monastery, which took him in for rescue. He revived, but bled from all seven orifices—a most critical state. Resting only a few days, he pressed on to Gaomin for the Session, heedless of his life, his resolve unchanged.

Gaomin's rules were most strict, and strictly enforced. Violators were punished without favor. Then, the abbot, Chan Master Yuelang, appointed him to stand in for an office—which he declined—and declining violated the rules, so he was beaten with the fragrant board. He took the punishment without complaint; but after the beating his illness turned grave, bleeding unstaunched, past saving.

Someone wonders: "Venerable Hsu Yun applied effort so—could the Dharma-protecting spirits have failed to guard him, letting him fall in the river?" In fact the spirits did protect him—else how would fishermen have known to haul him out? Clearly, in the unseen, the spirits ever blessed him.

This too was a test—of how he faced his own life and death through these disasters. Facing such trials, did he flinch? Did he ever think: "I have cultivated so many years—reciting Sutras, bowing repentances, burning fingers, secluding, practicing austerities, giving everything my all—yet never a sympathetic response in return? Enough! I'll quit cultivating, return to lay life and its five desires!" Had he thought so, how could he have become Patriarch of all five schools!

Gaomin Monastery honored its rules to the utmost. None spoke together—even roommates knew not each other's names. Venerable Hsu Yun kept discipline strictly; gravely ill, he never mentioned it, and none knew he had just been fished from the river—he only poured his whole heart into Chan investigation. Twenty days later his illness eased—through the blessings of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

One day, Dharma Master Deyan, abbot of Baoji Monastery at Caishi Rock, visited Gaomin. Glimpsing Venerable Hsu Yun sitting upright on the bench, radiant and bright, the Master was amazed and told everyone how the Venerable had been swept away and rescued. All marveled, and to aid his effort toward results, the Chan Hall officers assigned him no further duties. From then he focused on samadhi until reaching the state where not a thought arises.

In the eighth week, on the third night, at the call to stillness, the attendant brought hot water and carelessly splashed boiling water on his hand—the teacup fell to the floor. Hearing the cup shatter, he was at once enlightened (Chan Master Zibo was likewise enlightened hearing a bowl break). On the occasion he composed this verse:

The cup fell crashing to the ground;

Its ringing rang out clear.

Empty space shattered to pieces;

The mad mind came to rest.

Translation:

The teacup fell;

The crash rang out.

Empty space burst apart;

The mad mind at once ceased.

Another verse says:

Scalded hand,

shattered cup;

Home broken, man gone—words fail to speak.

Spring comes, flowers fragrant, everywhere in bloom;

Mountains, rivers, earth—all are the Tathagata.

Translation:

Hand splashed with water,

Cup smashed to pieces.

Home ruined, man gone, speech impossible;

Spring arrives, fragrant blossoms everywhere;

Rivers, mountains, earth—all the Tathagata.

Enlightened, he left Gaomin, wandering far and wide, ever more vigorous in study and consulting Good Knowing Advisors. Later he reached Yunnan, restoring monasteries on Jizu Mountain. Short of funds, he traveled to the Southern Seas to raise donations. Aboard ship bound for Singapore, the Master fell ill—and landing, he had no passport. British officials, finding him infectious, placed him in the infectious-disease hospital—no different from sending him to die. Later he was moved to Jile Monastery, housed apart, in seclusion—yet before long his illness eased. He traveled on to Thailand to raise funds, lodging at a monastery. He entered samadhi for nine days—outwardly like a dead man, yet not dead—startling all Bangkok. Then, from the king and high officials down to the people, all came to take refuge with him. The faithful's pure donations were all gathered and sent to Yunnan for monastery building.

In spring 1947, Nanhua Monastery held a precept platform, and there I met Venerable Hsu Yun for the first time. I still remember: after the transmission, the Venerable developed a swollen throat and could not speak, and so I could not consult him. Through a doctor's treatment, he gradually recovered.

The hardships of Venerable Hsu Yun's whole life truly beggar words! I doubt anyone could be found to bear what the Venerable endured. His conduct—through all this century, saving self and others, benefiting self and others, with miraculous transformations and auspicious signs—cannot all be told here. Now I relate only his life in brief, hoping you will model his patience and endurance.

Today, monastics sit investigating Chan for a few days yet hope for sympathetic response, hope to awaken to great wisdom. Such greed is excessive! Venerable Hsu Yun, a lifetime giving body to the Way, heedless of his own life and death, only then recognized his original face—while we, what hardships have we met? What merit made? Yet nursing idle fancies of enlightenment—truly childish!

For the cultivator of the Way, resolve must never retreat, vows never retreat, conduct never retreat—single-heartedly, vigorously advancing, as in the saying: "atop the hundred-foot pole, step one step further." No matter the accomplishment, only resolve on Bodhi, strive in cultivation, entertaining no other schemes—neither the Five Eyes and Six Powers, nor miraculous functions—those are not cultivation's ultimate fruit. Remember well! Morning to night, think not of spiritual powers, think not of enlightenment—those are stones hobbling the cultivator's feet.

Talks during the 1981 Chan Session,

July 16 to 23,

at the Ten Thousand Buddhas Hall of the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas.

tieu_de: The Story of Venerable Master Hsuan Hua's Leaving Home
tom_tat: Editor's note: The Venerable Hsuan Hua was a native of Shuangcheng county, Jilin province, of the Bai family. His father Fuhai was a farmer, thrifty all his life. His mother, née Hu, ate vegetarian and recited the Buddha's name every day…
noi_dung:
The Story of Venerable Master Hsuan Hua's Leaving Home

Editor's note: The Venerable Hsuan Hua was a native of Shuangcheng county, Jilin province, of the Bai family. His father Fuhai was a farmer, thrifty all his life. His mother, née Hu, ate vegetarian and recited the Buddha's name every day of her life, loved giving and doing good—helping whoever needed help—so the village praised her as a living Bodhisattva. On the night of the 16th day of the 3rd lunar month in the Wuwu year, she dreamed that Amitabha Buddha descended, his body radiating light, illumining the world, shaking heaven and earth. Startling awake, she noticed a strange fragrance, wondrously sweet, filling her whole body, down into liver and lungs, bringing an inconceivable state. In a moment Duke Xuan was born, crying three days and three nights before stopping—as if already knowing the suffering beings must bear in this Saha world. Below are excerpted the Duke's own account of his leaving-home affinities.

As a child, before I turned twelve, I was a most stubborn child. How stubborn? If anyone teased me, I cried—and once crying, no one knew when I would stop. My parents' words did no good; I would not listen, doing only as I pleased. Often I refused food and drink, just wailing on—my parents gave up, helpless to make me obey. Then I knew my parents loved me dearly; seeing me refuse food, their hearts melted and they yielded to me. So unfilial was I then, heedless of my parents' suffering—thinking back now, I was truly rotten!

Once, a neighbor child came to play. Then I had just learned to crawl, and that child was also learning to crawl. We crawled on a platform, the two of us racing to see who crawled fastest. Seeing me crawl ahead of him, crawling behind, he bit my leg. What a fool I was! Instead of fighting back, I only knew how to cry. Remembering it now makes me laugh!

That year, when I was eleven, out playing with village children, I chanced to see the corpse of a small child. Never having seen such a sight since birth, I thought the child was sleeping—but calling, it would not wake; eyes closed, breath gone. Understanding nothing, home I asked my mother:

Why is that child sleeping out in the field? My mother said:

That child is dead.

Why must one die? I asked again.

- Why couldn't one die? My mother answered so.

Just then a relative said:

Only those who leave home to cultivate never die.

From then on, thinking of death I was afraid—I did not want to die. I felt living-then-dying was no good at all, and the thought of leaving home sprouted in my head—I wanted to cultivate to end birth and death.

One day I said to my mother:

- I wish to leave home to cultivate—I wonder if Mother approves?

My mother said:

- Leaving home is a fine thing—Mother cannot stop you. Yet Mother thinks: when Mother is gone, leaving home will still not be too late.

So my mother consented to my leaving home. I was overjoyed, though I could not yet go. At once I felt remorse for my past unfilial acts that had grieved my parents and taxed their hearts for me. How to repay such kindness? Thinking back and forth, I hit upon a way—a foolish way—bowing to my parents in repentance. Decided, I carried it out.

The moment I bowed down before my parents, they were most astonished, asking:

- What is this bowing about?

Because before I did unfilial things toward Father and Mother, angering you—now I know it was wrong, so from today I shall bow to Father and Mother.

My father said:

- Knowing your faults and repenting is good—no need to bow.

I replied:

I have always been stubborn—what I say, I must see through to the end.

My parents, knowing my nature well, said no more, letting me follow my wish—and so, morning and evening, they received my bows.

From that day, each morning at dawn, while the household still slept, I went to the yard and bowed three times to my father, three to my mother. Each night, after all had slept, I went to the yard again and bowed three times to each parent. After a while, feeling it not enough, I added bows to heaven and earth. Then I had never heard terms like king of heaven, king of earth, or king of men—knowing only heaven, earth, sovereign, father, mother, and teacher—so morning and evening I bowed three times to heaven, three to earth, three to the head of state, three to father, three to mother, three to my future teacher. Bowing so for a time, still feeling it not enough, I added bows to the greatly filial of the world, the greatly good of the world, the great worthies and great sages. Later I added bows to the good people of the whole world, as well as the not-good people of the world. Bowing to heaven, I prayed that great evildoers, the very worst, would reform from evil to good—all becoming good people.

The bows grew daily, reaching eight hundred and thirty (830) bows. Each session lasted two and a half hours, morning once, evening once—five hours a day in all. Whether gales blew or rains poured, I bowed the full count in the yard. Even in winter snow and rain, still in the yard. I also bowed to heaven praying for timely wind and rain, nation at peace, people secure.

Bowing so for several years, when my mother passed away I stayed by her grave, bowing on for three years. Afterward I left home and began studying the Sutra canon. I found Buddhist Sutras truly the richest, most complete treasury, which other religions lack—no canon compares.

Before leaving home, I had also joined other religions' activities—attending Protestant and Catholic services, even other Ways' Dharma assemblies—but on the whole, studying to the end to find the method ending birth and escaping death, it was truly disappointing, for those religions' doctrines never reach the ultimate. Yet people find Protestantism and Catholicism widely known and followed. Why? Because the New and Old Testaments are translated into many languages, their meaning simple and easy to grasp.

Buddhism's meaning, though perfect, has Sutra texts too lofty, beyond ordinary reach—so few follow it. So I vowed to translate the entire Tripitaka in twelve divisions into plain vernacular, then into every nation's tongue. A reckless vow—for I knew no foreign tongues, had no chance to learn them, lacked the wisdom to complete it—who knew if I could do it?

In 1962 I came to America to propagate the Buddhadharma. When affinities ripened, my disciples began translating to fulfill my vow. After years of effort, results are fairly fine, but the goal is still far—may everyone strive harder. Translating Sutras is sages' work—a supremely noble task. Rendering the whole Tripitaka in twelve divisions into English—no merit compares.

Today, a disciple has vowed to translate Buddhist Sutras into English, recalling my vow of years past. I hope my disciples will join hearts and forces to fulfill that vow.

Editor's note: At Nanhua Monastery, during his time with Venerable Hsu Yun, Duke Xuan was valued by Venerable Hsu Yun and appointed Dean of Studies of the Vinaya Academy, and shortly after Director of Education. At the precept-transmission ceremony Duke Xuan was appointed Witnessing Acharya. Later Duke Xuan received from Venerable Hsu Yun the transmission of the Guiyang lineage, becoming its 9th-generation Dharma heir.

On the road of propagating the Dharma, Venerable Hsuan Hua traveled from Hong Kong to America, where Duke Xuan lectured dozens of

Sutras, promoting all five schools—Chan, Teachings, Vinaya, Esoteric, Pure Land—tearing down the fences between schools, taking Buddhism's revival as his own duty, urging his disciples daily to investigate Chan, recite the Buddha's name, repent, study Sutras, and truly cultivate—upholding the Right Teaching, hoping the Right Dharma forever endures.

Venerable Hsuan Hua was born with transcendent wisdom and a marvelous memory—read once, remembered forever; lecturing Sutras or Dharma never from a prepared draft, but according to time and audience. With unobstructed eloquence, words flowing like water, everywhere the Way, meaning perfectly interfused—commanding all admiration.

Duke Xuan lecturing the Avatamsaka Sutra could close his eyes and recite the text, not a word wrong—a thing never seen. This writer saw with his own eyes, heard with his own ears—boundless admiration. His disciples were all educated university youth, each in awe before Duke Xuan's virtue and vast learning—all prostrating in full reverence.

At the Venerable's urging, young men and women—Chinese, American, Vietnamese—came seeking refuge and the Complete Precepts to leave home and cultivate. Among them were Ph.D.'s, master's and bachelor's graduates, daring to leave bright futures behind to enter the Buddha's gate seeking truth. Some practiced asceticism—fasting a week, or twenty-one days, thirty-six days, up to seventy-two days. Such asceticism is unprecedented in American Buddhist history—rare indeed through the ages. Others, praying for world peace, vowed the three-steps- one-bow pilgrimage, two years and six months unbroken, through wind and rain, offering their bodies as an example before the assembly. This happened precisely because the Venerable's transcendent virtue so moved them that they resolved to follow his self-forgetting, other-saving spirit in walking the Bodhisattva Way.

The Venerable teaches disciples methodically. Disciples keep the rules strictly, practice earnestly, always wearing the precept sash per the Buddha's rules, eating one meal daily at noon, sleeping without lying down. Nowhere in today's world is there another such place—so the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas may be called the world's Buddhist center, an inconceivable beacon for all Buddhist faithful.

In 1962 the Venerable brought the Right Dharma to the West, then founded the Dharma Realm Buddhist Association (its predecessor the Sino-American Buddhist Association), then the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas with branch Way-places in America, Canada, Taiwan, Malaysia. To train the world's pillar talent, at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas the Venerable established Dharma Realm Buddhist University, Instilling Virtue Secondary School, Nurturing Virtue Elementary School. For the Right Dharma's eternal endurance, uniting theory with practice, the Venerable further founded a program training Sangha and laity.

The Venerable also founded the International Translation Institute, aimed at spreading Buddhist Sutras worldwide. Today, a great many monks, nuns, and laity labor head-down translating Buddhist Sutras into English. To date, over a hundred Sutras and books in English and other Western tongues have been published and circulate.

The Venerable's devoted life is an offering to the Dharma, forgetting self. To this day, though the Dharma Realm Buddhist Association's branch Way-places scatter across America, Canada, and Asian countries, the Venerable ever keeps a humble, simple bearing, calling himself a "little ant," a lowly creature beneath all people, daring to contend with none. The Venerable once said:

"The City of Ten Thousand Buddhas is no private enterprise, but belongs to all Buddhist faithful of the world—even to faithful of all other religions worldwide. All now dwelling at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas labor devotedly, while I am only the gatekeeper—a cultivator of the Way, here awaiting those with affinities, come to cultivate together. Do not merely stand outside the gate. You are all members of the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas—in the future you will all become Buddhas."

Talks at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas, Ten Thousand Buddhas Hall Chan Session, July 16 to 23, 1981.

tieu_de: Novice Guo Zuo's Affinity for Leaving Home
tom_tat: When I was abbot of Three Conditions Monastery at Pingfang station, about 30 miles south of Harbin, one day in meditation I knew that the next day a young boy would come seeking to leave home. The next morning…
noi_dung:
Novice Guo Zuo's Affinity for Leaving Home

When I was abbot of Three Conditions Monastery at Pingfang station, about 30 miles south of Harbin, one day in meditation I knew that the next day a young boy would come seeking to leave home. The next morning I told my disciple Guo Neng: "Today a young boy is coming to leave home—when he arrives, let me know."

That noon, Guo Neng came to my room reporting in a Shandong accent: "Master! That young boy you spoke of—he has indeed come!" Going out front, I saw a small boy of twelve or thirteen, handsome and sturdy—plainly the makings of a Bhikshu. Seeing me, he felt as if meeting kin long parted—unable to contain himself, he wept for utter joy.

I asked: "Why do you wish to leave home?" The boy replied: "Because I am ill (at five he could cure others' illnesses, but not his own). Doctors examined me but found no cause, and knew no medicine to cure it. My parents worried greatly, seeking doctors and medicines everywhere, to no avail. One night, in three dreams I saw the same dream-scene. I saw a monk, fat, telling me my illness held no hope of cure—unless I went to Three Conditions Monastery in Harbin, found Dharma Master Anci, and left home under him to cultivate—then the illness would end without medicine. Remembering this clearly, I told my parents and asked leave, then came here to beg Dharma Master Anci in compassion to accept me as disciple."

I smiled and asked on:

Do you know Dharma Master Anci?

I do not know him.

Not knowing him, how will you find him? There is no one here called Dharma Master Anci.

The boy said with utter faith:

There is! The moment I entered the monastery gate, I recognized the fat monk from my dream—and now he sits right here (he pointed at the statue of Maitreya Bodhisattva). He did not lie to me. He told me to come here—no mistake!

I asked on:

What proof is there for anyone to believe your dream? Or is it that you lack clothes, lack food, lack shelter—and so wish to leave home?

The boy insisted:

Not so! I follow exactly this fat Master's guidance (he pointed at Maitreya's statue), telling me to find Dharma Master Anci—for only he can cure my illness. So for over a month I walked more than a thousand miles (then Japan had just surrendered unconditionally, and Manchuria's railways had not yet reopened). Sometimes passing inns, then ahead no villages at all—I had to sleep in open fields. To save time, I only knew to walk on, heedless of all else. One night, sleeping in a field, a pack of wolves suddenly ringed me—but I was not afraid. I told them: "Clear off at once! Refuse, and I'll show no mercy—you'll taste this fruit (a hand grenade)!" Hearing this, the wolves obediently left.

Finishing his tale, the boy looked at me pleadingly. Wishing to test his sincerity, I took a piece of bread, chewed it to mush in my mouth, and spat it on the ground. I told him: "Pick it up and eat it! Eaten, then we'll talk." Without a moment's hesitation or disgust, the boy picked up the saliva-soaked mush and swallowed it down. Such a test sufficed to prove his sincerity and good will toward leaving home—so I consented to his receiving the novice precepts.

After receiving the novice precepts, he applied effort in cultivation, studying eagerly—never lazy, never lax—and within half a year realized the Five Eyes and Six Spiritual Powers, his powers most high—vast spiritual powers indeed. This is no exaggeration—utter fact. Everyone there knew that little novice had spiritual powers. Pity that later he grew proud (arrogant and conceited), inwardly smug, fancying himself most fine—and his powers took wing without a trace; try as he might, he could display them no more.

We cultivators must heed this point. Having spiritual powers is fine, and lacking them is fine too—never grow proud, never cling, still less use them to advertise yourselves. Chiefly, be content with yourselves, vigorous and truly cultivating—toiling with all your might is true skill. With shallow skill yet clinging—to these sounds, those states—deeming them tremendous! Never fall into this—for that is a hundred and eight thousand miles from the Way!

Talks at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas, Ten Thousand Buddhas Hall,

Chan Session, July 16 to 23, 1981.

tieu_de: Novice Guo Shun's Affinity for Leaving Home
tom_tat: Guo Shun was a native of Harbin town, Jilin province, of the Yao family, farmers by trade. Blessed with good roots from past affinities, he early sensed the dusty world's many sufferings, and the thought of leaving home sprouted…
noi_dung:
Novice Guo Shun's Affinity for Leaving Home

Guo Shun was a native of Harbin town, Jilin province, of the Yao family, farmers by trade. Blessed with good roots from past affinities, he early sensed the dusty world's many sufferings and the world's evils, and the thought of leaving home sprouted. He traveled everywhere seeking a wise teacher. One day on the road, Japanese soldiers seized him (then Japan occupied Manchuria). Judging him a jobless vagrant, they sent him to forced labor on the frontier.

That place was a labor camp at Heihe. Day after day he dreamed of escaping, yet never found the chance. For around the camp ran an electric fence—escapees, if not gunned down by guards, were mauled by guard dogs—and past those two barriers, electrocuted at the fence. The labor camp was truly a hell on earth, suffering beyond words.

One night, Guo Shun dreamed of a long-bearded old man telling him: "Tonight is your chance to flee this cage. Outside the gate is a white dog—follow it out!" Startling awake, he crept to the gate and looked out—sure enough, a white dog waited there. He followed the dog, slipping safely past the electric fence, fleeing all the way home.

Snatched from death, Guo Shun saw the red dust's true face clearly, and resolved to leave home and cultivate the Way.

In 1944, I went to Da Nan Gou village to heal the mother of a layman named Gao. The next day, word spread that she had wondrously recovered. Hearing this, Guo Shun came to bow to me as teacher. He knelt, refusing to rise; seeing his sincerity, I consented to his leaving home, granting his wish. I instructed him thus:

"To cultivate at home is not easy; to leave home is harder still. There is a saying: 'The great matter unclear—like burying your mother; the great matter clear—all the more like burying your mother.' The cultivator must further endure what others cannot endure, bear what others cannot bear, eat what others cannot eat, wear what others cannot wear. Diligently practice morality, samadhi, and wisdom to utterly end greed, anger, and delusion—that is a Shramana's duty." I read him these verses:

Thought after thought, never forget birth-and-death's suffering;

Heart after heart, long to escape transmigration's realm.

Empty space shattered—see the Buddha-nature;

The whole fallen away—recognize the source.

Further instructing:

"Now is the Dharma-ending Age—many leave home, few cultivate; many believe in the Buddha, few become Buddhas. Having vowed to leave home, the crux is resolving on Bodhi—vowing to be a bright lamp standing before the wind, like true gold in the furnace—betray not your original resolve. Be careful!"

Guo Shun bowed in reverence, then followed me back to Three Conditions Monastery to receive the novice precepts, with the Dharma name Guo Shun. Afterward, Guo Shun cultivated vigorously, strictly upholding the precepts—never lax, never indulgent—wholeheartedly investigating Chan. Each samadhi lasted over a day and night before emerging, and in samadhi he further knew the whole stream of cause and effect from past to present to future. His state was truly inconceivable.

In September 1945, Guo Shun built a grass hut for cultivation, left of the Dragon King Temple, at the foot of West Mountain, within Da Nan Gou. Finished, I led disciples Guo Neng, Guo Zuo, Guo Shi, and others for its consecration. That very night, ten dragon spirits came seeking refuge. I told them:

Your duty is making rain, for which the world makes offerings. Now in such drought, why make no rain?

The dragon spirits answered together:

Without the Jade Emperor's decree, we lesser spirits dare not make rain!

Convey for me a memorial to King Shakra (the Jade Emperor) to send rain tomorrow—then I shall grant you refuge.

The next day, sure enough, heavy rain fell, ending the drought—farmers overjoyed, feasting to thank the dragon spirits in merry celebration.

From this consecration of Guo Shun's grass hut comes the tale above—so I named the hut "Dragon-Rain Thatched Hut" as a keepsake.

In this grass hut, three cultivated together—all fellow villagers. One surnamed Liu, one surnamed Yang—both following Guo Shun in effort morning and evening, reciting the Great Compassion Mantra as their main practice. Later, Mr. Liu left home as a monk, while Mr. Yang was drafted, joining the Eighth Route Army. In the ranks, Mr. Yang kept writing home—then fell wholly silent, grieving his family to fear him dead.

In 1948, one day Guo Shun and Mr. Gao were reciting the Great Compassion Mantra in the grass hut when suddenly knocking sounded—and opening, there stood layman Yang. Returned, he said nothing, walking behind the house. Guo Shun went back inside to finish the Mantra. Done, he went behind to meet Mr. Yang, meaning to ask where he had been these two years. But stepping into the back room, no one was there—only a weasel flicking its tail and dashing off.

Guo Shun recited the Great Compassion Mantra with full awesome virtue, and so was never deluded by fox-kind (foxes, weasels)—thus it resumed its true weasel form. The story, roughly: Mr. Yang had died on the battlefield, his brain eaten by the weasel, which then took his shape to delude others. Little did it know Guo Shun's samadhi power had reached a high level—not easily shaken, the deviant never overcoming the right—so the weasel spirit, helpless, withdrew. Thus cultivators need such encounters for experience, ever alert lest outer states shake them.

In 1945, at the Ullambana festival on the 15th of the 7th lunar month, my disciples and I offered incense before the Buddha altar. I vowed: "If I live to a hundred, I vow to burn this body as an offering to the Buddha, seeking the unsurpassed Way." Then all disciples vowed likewise. Guo Shun alone vowed: "Your disciple Guo Shun, meeting fitting occasion, vows to follow Medicine King Bodhisattva's example, burning this body for the Buddha, not waiting till a hundred." In meditation I had known that in a past life Guo Shun had made that vow, so I accepted his vow above.

Guo Shun saw the world's impermanence and Buddhism's decline, his heart boundlessly grieved beyond words—and so on April 18, 1949, he vowed self-immolation, offering his body to Buddhism. He prepared oil-soaked firewood, sat atop it, and burned his own body. The next day the villagers learned of it—coming to see Guo Shun's whole body turned to ash, only the heart unburnt. The villagers, reverent, buried the ashes with the heart on the spot.

Talks at the Ten Thousand Buddhas Hall, City of Ten Thousand Buddhas, Chan Session, July 16 to 23, 1981.

tieu_de: The Six Great Principles of Cultivators
tom_tat: Cultivators must have a Dharma-selecting eye (“Dharma-selecting vision”) to discern what is right Dharma and what is deviant dharma. Right Dharma is: no fighting, no greed, no seeking, no selfishness, no…
noi_dung:
The Six Great Principles of Cultivators

Cultivators must have a Dharma-selecting eye ("Dharma-selecting vision") to discern what is right Dharma and what is deviant dharma. What is right Dharma? No fighting, no greed, no seeking, no selfishness, no self-benefit, no lying. These are the six great principles—cultivators following them will gain right knowledge and right views. Conversely, deviant dharma is fighting, greed, seeking, selfishness, self-benefit, lying. With these six come deviant knowledge and views. This is the crux, the dividing line between the two sides—forward is Right Dharma, backward deviant dharma. We must see this clearly.

Given no deviant knowledge or views, one need only hold samadhi power firm—and demon kings can find no way to disturb us, unable to shake our minds. There is a saying: "Kill the Buddha when a Buddha comes; kill the demon when a demon comes." What does this mean? It only advises us not to cling overmuch to states. Seeing a Buddha come, yet not accepting the image—let alone seeing a demon! Though in many cases such states are previews, most efficacious, still we should not believe in them. What we must believe is precisely the six great principles—no fighting, no greed, no seeking, no selfishness, no self-benefit, no lying. That is the demon-slaying sword, the demon-quelling club.

With right knowledge and views complete, though gods appeared to make offerings and bow in reverence, the cultivator's mind would stay unmoved. Should the mind stir, giving rise to delight, then delight-demons seize the chance to break in, driving the cultivator mad. Should gloom arise, then gloom-demons come to stain the mind with afflictions, or sometimes giving rise to clinging, to arrogance. All these are demons' mischief, robbing the mind of purity.

So meeting any bizarre state, the cultivator should not believe, nor let the mind stir. Believe only in your own wisdom—believing the own-nature can give rise to the myriad dharmas, the own-nature fundamentally pure, fundamentally undefiled, fundamentally not upside down. Then what remains to seek? Wherever there is seeking, there is defilement; having fighting, greed, selfishness, self-benefit, lying is having defilement. Meeting any dharma, we can take those six great principles as our measure—observing: what accords is Right Dharma, what accords not is deviant dharma.

The six great principles can smash the deviant knowledge and views of heavenly demons and outside ways. All the contrivings of heavenly demons and outside ways are of a seeking nature—aimed at fighting, greed, seeking, selfishness, self-benefit, lying—for themselves, not for others. Those are the thoughts of side doors and crooked paths.

The cultivator of the Way must gather merit and foster virtue, yet never cling to what has been done—as the saying goes: "sweep away all dharmas, leave behind all marks"—never saying: "I did this merit, I cultivated thus" or "I reached this state, I have such spiritual powers." Supposing such things exist—examined closely, all are hollow—never believe them, never be caught. Believing in marvels and psychic dharmas, the cultivator can never enter right concentration, right reception (samadhi). Understand: right concentration, right reception are not gained from outside—they must arise from the own-nature. How does the cultivator attain them? Through the skill of returning the light inward, seeking back within oneself (seeking from oneself)—only then are right concentration and right reception accomplished.

The City of Ten Thousand Buddhas is where myriads of sages gather. Yet on all four sides, demon kings wait their chance to slip in. If the cultivator's mind is impure, the head full of discursive thoughts, demon kings seize the opening to sneak in and incite—for instance, making the cultivator predict this and that. If the cultivator then believes these are powers he has gained, he has walked into the trap—becoming the Demon King's kin.

Likewise, hearing some sound, you hastily take it for a voice from empty space. In fact empty space holds no speech—know that: "apart from the mark of speech, apart from the mark of mind following conditions." Suppose you hear empty space's voice—that is only a demonic state, not brought by "Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom." What worth is a trifling scrap of news!

The cultivator's mind must be pure. Crave no power of foresight. Foresight brings nothing good—on the contrary, only trouble, distracting us, scattering focus—and so discursive thoughts tangle and afflictions pile up. Without foresight, you will have no afflictions, the mind unobstructed. The Heart Sutra says: "Because there is no obstruction, there is no fear—far apart from all upside-down dream-like thinking: Ultimate Nirvana." This is precisely the practitioner's goal on the Way of cultivation.

tieu_de: Unrelenting Investigation Naturally Brings Enlightenment
tom_tat: The rule for sitting in Chan investigation is: eyes gazing down at the nose, nose contemplating the mouth, mouth contemplating the mind; this checks the scattered mind described as “monkey mind, horse thoughts,” keeping the mind from seeking outward…
noi_dung:
Unrelenting Investigation Naturally Brings Enlightenment

The rule for sitting in Chan investigation is: eyes gazing down at the nose, nose contemplating the mouth, mouth contemplating the mind; this checks the scattered mind described as "monkey mind, horse thoughts," keeping the mind from seeking outward. In the Chan Hall, practitioners must not glance east and west—for then the mind chases outer states and no investigation is possible. This demands your special heed! Chan Session time is supremely precious—not a minute or second to waste. Seize the chance to grow wisdom.

Cultivators must not cherish this stinking skin bag. Only parting from that thought can you apply effort; unable to part from it, you become its slave, serving it morning to night. So the true cultivator must regard it as a stinking skin bag—that is, refuse to prize it. Prizing it obstructs the Way. We must "borrow the false to cultivate the true"—treating it only as a means.

In investigating, the great taboo is dozing. Most meditators suffer two common ills: restlessness and sinking—if the mind is not caught in discursive thoughts, it falls into stupor. So in applying effort, throw your whole spirit into investigating—never allowing drowsiness. Once in samadhi, that is another matter.

Chan investigation skill leads to right concentration, right reception—also called samadhi. Realized, this is the state "thus, thus unmoving; clear, ever bright." How to reach it? It takes a bout of bitter effort, transcendent vigor, the mind free of a single discursive thought—until "not a thought arises, the whole appears"—at last seeing your "original face, the homeland scenery."

The key to Chan investigation is the hua-tou. Thought after thought, investigate the hua-tou. Investigate unrelentingly and enlightenment comes of itself—investigating until "mountains end and waters run dry," good news comes of itself, and the state of "bright flowers beneath the willows" appears before your eyes. Someone says: "I have joined so many Chan Sessions—why am I not enlightened?" Because you refuse bitter effort yet keep craving enlightenment. Understand: enlightenment is the fruit of accumulated skill. In time, merit perfected, the moment come—enlightenment comes of itself. With no skill at all, yet wanting enlightenment—that is a deluded idle fancy, no different from "toads craving swan meat"—impossible.

tieu_de: In Cultivating the Way, Do Not Compete
tom_tat: Now in the Chan Session, practitioners apply effort—but a shallow skill. People treat Chan like a race, vying for first. You can sit three hours—I'll sit five, a cut above you. With such a mind in Chan, how could you awaken…
noi_dung:
In Cultivating the Way, Do Not Compete

Now in the Chan Session, practitioners apply effort—but a shallow skill. People treat Chan like a race, vying for first. You can sit three hours—I'll sit five, a cut above you. With such a mind in Chan, how could you awaken? Though you sat for eighty thousand great kalpas, you could never understand the mind and see the nature. Why? Only because you harbor a winning-losing mind. There is a saying:

Fighting comes from a winning-losing mind;

It runs counter to the Way.

Four marks arising in the mind—

How attain samadhi?

These four verses warn cultivators never to give rise to contention. When skill is complete, wisdom appears—and others will naturally rank you first. That is true first place. But craving first place in your heart—that is a winning-losing mind, running counter to the Way.

Cultivators must be like water. Water's nature is yielding—claiming no merit, grasping no virtue—giving what is good to others, keeping what is bad for itself. Laozi said: Supreme good is like water. Water benefits the myriad things without contending. Water dwells where all disdain to dwell—hence it accords with the Way."

Supreme good describes supreme practitioners. They are likened to water. Water flows to low places, benefiting all things without contending for merit or virtue. Toward every kind—birds, fish and shrimp, beasts or plants, whether womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, or transformation-born—water treats all alike, giving equally to all. Cultivators are the same—toward all beings as past parents, as future Buddhas. Cultivators must spread kind hearts, finding means to rescue beings from the sea of suffering—dwelling where beings refuse to dwell. With such thoughts, the practitioner nears the Way. But a winning-losing mind runs counter to the cultivator's principles—against the Way.

Cultivators must be free of the four marks.

Who cultivates? Sensing no one cultivating—that is no mark of self.

Sensing no winning or losing with anyone—that is no mark of others.

Seeing neither self's mark nor others' mark—naturally the mark of living beings is also gone.

With no mark of living beings, whence a mark of life? Thus no mark of a life.

Harboring thoughts of vying to win, the four marks surely follow; with the four marks, samadhi can never be reached. This principle we must practice and polish well. In short, whoever retains the four marks is a common being; whoever is free of the four marks is a Bodhisattva.

Cultivators must remember the four verses in the Diamond Sutra:

All conditioned dharmas

Are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows;

Like dew and lightning—

Contemplate them thus.

Whatever has shape and marks is a conditioned dharma. Conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a water bubble, a shadow, a lightning flash—all hollow, without substance. Contemplate all things thus—only then can the true principle be clearly understood, clinging ended, discursive thoughts no longer troubling us.

The Diamond Sutra further says: "The past mind cannot be grasped, the present mind cannot be grasped, the future mind cannot be grasped." Why cannot the past mind be grasped? Because the past is gone—why mind it? Why cannot the present mind be grasped? Because in the present, thoughts succeed unbroken. You call this the present—but spoken, that present is already gone; time never pauses. Why cannot the future mind be grasped? Because the future has not yet come. So past, present, future—these three minds cannot be grasped. Practicing per the Buddha's teaching, you may at once reach the state of Nirvana.

Cultivators of the Way must take right knowledge and views as their model for vigorous practice. In practice, "apart from the mark of speech"—for nothing remains to say; "apart from the mark of mind's conditions"—for no conditions remain for the mind to chase; "apart from the mark of words"—for no words remain to describe. Unspeakable—what remains to remember? What can we still not let go? What remains to concern us? Friends! Apply effort right there—instead of shallow effort on the outer shell!
