Someone thinks: "Today in Chan, my legs didn't hurt, my back didn't ache—I didn't even hear the rest bell." That means he dozed off—of course knowing nothing. Do not mistake that state, lest you go astray and fall under demonic influence!

Take heed! Meeting strange states in Chan investigation, pay them no mind, no attention—let them be naturally, unmoved by strange states. The Shurangama Sutra explains this most clearly. May practitioners study its "Fifty Skandha-Demons" thoroughly.

The Shurangama Sutra is a precious mirror for Chan investigators—so all cultivators must ponder this Sutra deeply.

tieu_de: The Cultivator's Goal Is Buddhahood
tom_tat: Why cultivate? To become a Buddha. How does one become a Buddha? The first step is “doing no evil, vowing to do all good.” The next step is “diligently practicing morality, samadhi, and wisdom; ending greed, anger, and delusion.” A step further…
noi_dung:
The Cultivator's Goal Is Buddhahood

Why cultivate? To become a Buddha. How does one become a Buddha? The first step is "doing no evil, vowing to do all good." The next step is "diligently practicing morality, samadhi, and wisdom; ending greed, anger, and delusion." A step further, "bringing forth the Bodhi mind, walking the Bodhisattva Way." For these reasons, before Buddhahood the cultivator must choose the bright, open road to walk. Never scheme crookedly, seeking rugged shortcuts, going astray. Take heed! Be careful!

The true cultivator practices per the Dharma—fearing no suffering, fearing no hardship—boldly pressing straight to Buddhahood. There is a saying:

Grind a steel rod into a needle;

Merit complete, it comes of itself.

Applying effort to the utmost, Buddhahood comes of itself. But boasting of your own talent and merit—never will you become a Buddha.

When the Five Eyes open, you will see how the Buddhas of the ten directions cultivated to realize Buddhahood; you will see how the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions cultivated to win Bodhisattvahood; you will see how the Arhats of the ten directions applied effort to reach Arhatship. In a flash, you directly perceive those states.

One with the spiritual power of the Five Eyes needs but a thought-instant to thoroughly penetrate all the Buddha's teachings recorded in the Tripitaka, as well as the True Suchness of all dharmas.

The refuge vows say:

I take refuge with the Buddha. May all living beings understand the Great Way and bring forth the unsurpassed mind.

I take refuge with the Dharma. May all living beings deeply enter the Sutra Treasury, their wisdom like the sea.

I take refuge with the Sangha. May all living beings lead the great assembly, in all things unobstructed.

If you can "deeply enter the Sutra Treasury, with wisdom like the sea," then nowhere is unpenetrated, nowhere unclear, nowhere unknown, nowhere unseen—that is thorough enlightenment. Do not keep the small and lose the great; do not crave petty states that cloud the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom. That way, you can never deeply enter the Sutra Treasury, never gain wisdom like the sea.

One of great wisdom never craves petty states—for whoever craves such states cannot tell true from false. They mix brass with gold, taking brass for true gold—even crystal seems mere rock to them. Why? They cannot tell real from fake.

Cultivators of the Way must have right knowledge and views—never inverting right and wrong, clearly distinguishing black from white—never passing off fish eyes as pearls, never blurring to fool others. Otherwise, with deviant knowledge and views, in ten thousand lives never a Buddha.

What are right knowledge and views? Simply put, we must cast off the three poisons—greed, anger, delusion—keeping body and mind pure; wisdom will appear and shine, scattering ignorance's darkness, ending afflictions. Reaching this state is realizing fruition—may you strive toward that goal in cultivation.

End Discursive Thoughts!

Sitting in the Chan Hall, outwardly you seem to investigate Chan—but within you chase discursive thoughts. These thoughts lead you now up to the heavens, now down to earth, now as hungry ghosts, now as beasts. All spring from the roots of greed, anger, delusion. Claiming diligence in morality, samadhi, wisdom—yet in fact not practicing them; claiming to end greed, anger, delusion—yet in fact not ending them. So strange! And not only in this life—life after life we follow that road, and so rise and fall, circling the six paths of transmigration, never stopping. As a dog, feeling supreme; as a cat, also feeling supreme—in short, in whatever birth, counting yourself number one. Why? Through clinging born of ignorance. Only truly cultivating the Way, striving in Chan investigation, can we escape transmigration and realize blissful Nirvana.

Some unserious cultivators let time slip by in vain. Others sit, they sit; others walk, they walk—whatever others do, they do. Such people fling their own birth-and-death beyond the ninth cloud, counting it nothing—no resolve to cultivate, unwilling to end discursive thoughts. They sit there, minds flitting from thought to thought—eighty-four thousand discursive thoughts a day, yet still too few. Discursive thoughts! More discursive thoughts! Discursive thoughts throw the mind into turmoil, the soul upside down—truly lamentable!

Then how to end discursive thoughts? Investigate the hua-tou—no other way. Though the hua-tou is also a discursive thought, it gathers your spirit, never letting the mind roam outward. This is precisely countering poison with poison—using one discursive thought to control all others, taking one discursive thought as the topic—investigating over and over, until no other discursive thoughts remain. When the practitioner reaches the level of no more discursive thoughts—that is enlightenment's moment. Then a word, a gesture, a deed can open for you enlightenment's gate.

tieu_de: Entering Samadhi Is Not Sleeping
tom_tat: Someone asked me: “How do entering samadhi and sleeping differ?” Briefly: entering samadhi, the practitioner sits upright, back straight; breathing may stop, the pulse sometimes ceasing—outwardly like a dead person, yet awareness fully present…
noi_dung:
Entering Samadhi Is Not Sleeping

Someone asked me: "How do entering samadhi and sleeping differ?" Briefly: entering samadhi, the practitioner sits upright, back straight; breathing may stop, the pulse sometimes ceasing—outwardly like a dead person, yet awareness fully present. In samadhi, sitting still and unmoving—sometimes a day, or ten days, up to a whole month. But one asleep—body listing, head lolling, breath puffing in and out, sometimes snoring like thunder. That is the difference.

Chan practice is like schooling—from elementary through secondary, college, then graduate research, before the doctorate is granted. Chan investigation likewise divides into four stages, called the four dhyanas. A brief explanation follows:

The first dhyana, also called "the Ground of Joy and Bliss Born of Separation." This state carries the practitioner wholly apart from beings' realm, attaining a state of bliss. This bliss differs from commoners' pleasure, for it is skill brought by the own-nature. Entering the first dhyana, breathing stills. This means outer breathing stops, while inner breathing begins—like the hibernation of animals. Then the mind is clear as water, bright as a mirror, shining upon the own-nature's substance—yet still aware of sitting in Chan.

The second dhyana is called "the Ground of Joy and Bliss Born of Samadhi." In this samadhi, the practitioner tastes a bliss beyond compare—precisely "Chan bliss as food, replete with Dharma joy"—for in this state bliss makes hunger forgotten; one may forgo food and drink for days with no ill effect. Yet never cling to that attainment. With such a thought, the work may dissolve, easily straying into demonic states—so we must be careful. In this samadhi, not only does breathing stop, the pulse ceases too. Leaving samadhi, the body functions normally again.

The third dhyana is called "the Ground of Wondrous Bliss Apart from Joy." The practitioner leaves the second dhyana's joy behind, reaching a wondrous bliss beyond words—feeling all things the Buddhadharma, all things bliss. In the third dhyana's state, breath and pulse both still, thought also halts. Then—thinking neither good nor evil, neither right nor wrong—not a thought arises. Yet never be proud, for this is but a station on the road. Far yet to ending birth and escaping death—a full eighty-four thousand miles more.

The fourth dhyana is called "the Ground of Purity through Renouncing Thought." In this state, even the thought of bliss is gone—all renounced—and the practitioner reaches a pure state, with nothing left to contrive. This is also called the state "of non-action, leaving nothing undone." The fourth-dhyana stage is still but a station on Chan investigation's road—never mistake yourselves realized, lest you repeat the Unlearned Bhikshu's error and fall into the hells.

The fourth dhyana still lies within common beings' scope. Strive further—to the state of "the Five Heavens of No Return" is called realizing sage fruition. Yet even there birth-and-death is unresolved, for the Three Realms are not yet transcended. See this clearly—no vagueness allowed.

Is the Shurangama Sutra a Forged Sutra?

Great Master Hanshan once said: "Without reading the Lotus, one cannot know the Tathagata's painstaking heart in saving the world; without reading the Shurangama, one cannot grasp the crux of delusion and awakening in cultivating the mind." Exactly so—for the Shurangama Sutra embraces all dharmas, gathers in every capacity—the quintessential Dharma-door of the ages, the true seal of becoming Buddhas and Patriarchs. Hence Chan practitioners must study this Sutra thoroughly, penetrating the state of the "fifty kinds of skandha-demons" to avoid falling to the Demon King. Otherwise, without clear recognition, whatever state is met breeds clinging—the practitioner easily enters demonic states, becoming the Demon King's kin. Most dangerous!

Not only must the Shurangama Mantra be memorized—the Shurangama Sutra too the meditator must know by heart. It is said "memorized, its wonders sprout"—when the moment comes, great benefit, inconceivable sympathetic response. Whoever studies Chinese literature must read the Shurangama Sutra—its prose exquisite, its meaning rich—in short, an ideal Sutra.

Some self-styled ranking scholars, never deeply studying Buddhism, call themselves Buddhist experts, claiming authority—yet understanding Buddhism not at all—rashly deeming the Shurangama Sutra forged. Then others, with other motives, chime in echoing. Truly the blind leading the blind—piteous!

Why do people say the Shurangama Sutra was not spoken by Shakyamuni Buddha? Only because the Sutra's meaning is all too true. The Sutra lays bare all the world's ills—whereby demons, ghosts, ox-ghosts, snake-ghosts can no longer run rampant, forced to show their true shapes. So they seek every means to destroy it—they must trumpet the Shurangama as false Sutra to survive. Admitting it the Buddha's spoken Dharma would finish them. First, they cannot keep the "Teaching on the Four Kinds of Purity"; second, they cannot practice the "Perfect-Penetration Dharmas of the Twenty-five Sages"; third, they dare not face the states of the "Fifty Kinds of Skandha-Demons."

If everyone read the Shurangama Sutra and understood it, outside-ways' powers would lose their magic, rendered useless—none believing in their powers anymore. That is why heavenly demons and outside ways can only slander, trumpeting the Shurangama a forged Sutra.

Nor is it only laypeople slandering the Shurangama as false Sutra—even monastics parrot along. Why? Because some monastics study little—sometimes illiterate, unable to read Sutra texts—while the Shurangama's prose runs deep, its meaning recondite—beyond their grasp, unable to tell true from false. Hearing people call this Sutra false, that Sutra forged, they never reflect—repeating whatever others say. Naturally the Shurangama bears this wrongful name for that reason.

Long ago in India, the Shurangama Sutra ranked a national treasure, forbidden to leave the country. All leaving were strictly searched—and to keep the Sutra in, customs officers watched departing monks with special care.

Then in India—China then in the Tang—a high monk named Paramiti labored by every means to carry the Shurangama Sutra to China. Fearing discovery at checkpoints, he devised concealment—hiding the Sutra deep within his arm—and at last landed in Guangzhou territory. Then Chancellor Fang Rong had been demoted by Wu Zetian to governor of Guangzhou. Paramiti was invited by Fang Rong to translate this Sutra, with Fang Rong himself polishing the translation. So the Shurangama Sutra became a work of literary worth, then presented to Wu Zetian. At the time, rumor held the Great Cloud Sutra forged—so Empress Wu Zetian barred this Sutra from circulation.

When Chan Master Shenxiu was honored as National Master, receiving offerings in the palace, one day the Chan Master saw this Sutra—finding it most beneficial to Chan practitioners—and had it circulated. From then the Shurangama Sutra circulated in China. By legend, the Shurangama Sutra was the last Sutra transmitted to China—yet also the first destroyed in the Dharma-ending Age, followed by the other Sutras—at the very last, one Amitabha Sutra remaining.

Note: Venerable Duke Xuan firmly held that the Shurangama Sutra is the mind-seal of the Buddhas—a thousand myriad times certain. So the moment he reached America, Duke Xuan lectured the Shurangama Sutra. Why? The Buddhadharma spreading to American soil—the Dharma-ending becomes the Right Dharma—and that was the Venerable's resolve in continuing the Buddha's wisdom-life. The "Shallow Explanation of the Shurangama Sutra" will appear serially in the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas' Vajra Bodhi Sea magazine, in Chinese and English. Readers, please note.

tieu_de: We Must Practice Prajna Paramita
tom_tat: “The Bodhisattva Who Contemplates at Ease, practicing the profound prajna paramita, illumined the five skandhas, seeing they are all empty, and crossed beyond all suffering…
noi_dung:
We Must Practice Prajna Paramita

"The Bodhisattva Who Contemplates at Ease, practicing the profound prajna paramita, illumined the five skandhas, seeing they are all empty, and crossed beyond all suffering and difficulty."

These four lines are the Heart Sutra's essence. A brief explanation follows:

Who Contemplates at Ease means returning the light and reflecting it inward—contemplating whether you are at ease or not at ease. In other words, are you here or not here? At ease, here—the mind not running off to roam, not chasing after conditions. Uneasy, not here—the mind scattered, discursive thoughts tangled—in extreme cases leading to nervous breakdown, the mind ever seeking chances, hoping people come bearing offerings. With such discursive thoughts, you are not at ease.

As for "Bodhisattva"—every act aims at beings' benefit as its sole goal, never for self-benefit. We common beings' intent is exactly reversed—all thinking of our own benefit, never others'. Whatever we do, first calculating whether it profits us—acting only when profitable. That is precisely selfish self-benefit. Why is the world not at peace? For precisely this reason.

You fight, I snatch—no yielding to one another—and so wars arise, nations fall, homes break.

This Bodhisattva "practices the profound prajna paramita"—from beginningless time until now, life after life practicing this profound dharma, never pausing. Practicing profound prajna means:

No arrogant mind—for arrogance is delusion.

No smug mind—for smugness is delusion.

Ever a mind of shame (shame and remorse); lacking a mind of shame is delusion.

No mind chasing conditions (climbing mind)—for letting the mind roam after conditions is delusion.

No angry mind—for anger is delusion.

No upside-down mind—for the upside-down mind is the deluded mind.

We cultivators must take these six minds as standards to judge whether our acts accord with the Dharma. Accordant—our acts are wisdom; contrary—delusion. It may also be said: diligently practicing morality, samadhi, wisdom, ending greed, anger, delusion is wisdom; not practicing them, not ending them, is delusion. Wisdom and delusion differ in just these points.

Only practicing profound prajna can illumine the fifty kinds of skandha-demon states within the five skandhas. In the form skandha ten kinds of skandha-demons, in the feeling skandha ten kinds, in the cognition skandha ten kinds, in the formation skandha ten kinds, in the consciousness skandha ten kinds—fifty kinds in all. Broken down further, countless, limitless—if the cultivator is careless, easily straying into demonic states. In general, deviant knowledge and views belong to the demons' clan; right knowledge and views belong to the Buddhas' clan.

Practicing the profound prajna paramita, demonic states are seen through clearly—no longer shaken by demons. Then, beyond illumining the five skandhas as empty, you cross beyond all suffering and difficulty. The five skandhas empty means True Emptiness. There is a saying:

True Emptiness: no person, no self;

The Great Way: no shape, no marks.

Translation:

True Emptiness—no person, no self; The Great Way—no shape, no marks.

"All suffering and difficulty" means the sufferings of the three calamities and eight difficulties.

Practicing per the four Sutra lines above to the ultimate, the practitioner reaches the level of mastering the eight winds. What are the eight winds? Eight: praise, scorn, suffering, joy, gain, loss, slander, and honor. These are like eight winds that stir and whirl whoever lacks samadhi power. A brief explanation:

Praise: praise or acclaim. Someone praises you one line—you taste a sweetness sweeter than honey, most comfortable.

Scorn: scorn or blame. Someone blames you—you dislike it, inwardly uncomfortable.

Suffering: this is affliction. Meeting troubles, you feel miserable. Meeting afflictions, test yourself—can you bear them?

Joy: joy or pleasure. Meeting joyful things, take them not as success.

When pleasures come, regard them as a test—to see how your mind fares.

Gain: this is benefit. Gaining benefit, you feel glad; suffering loss, you feel sad—the mark of weak samadhi power.

Loss: loss means decline. Whatever hardships come, unwavering—failing, yet the mind unmoved.

Slander: say someone speaks ill of you—you take no offense! Counting it nothing, the storm passes of itself.

Honor: say someone praises you, honors you—still be unmoved. Count all fame and rank floating clouds.

These eight winds are a Dharma-door for testing the cultivator's mind. Favorable or adverse states—the mind unmoved. Moved—practice awry, samadhi power weak; unmoved—the cultivator has skill. Yet never be smug—as in boasting: "The eight winds cannot shake me—my samadhi power is firm as vajra!"

That attitude is already wrong.

Long ago in the Song dynasty, the layman Su Dongpo had studied the Buddhadharma somewhat—but his samadhi skill was still weak. Yet he fancied his samadhi power already fine. One day, brimming with inspiration, he composed these four verses:

I bow my head to the God among gods;

His light shines upon the great chiliocosm.

The eight winds cannot move him;

Seated upright upon the purple-golden lotus.

A rough translation:

Bowing to the gods of gods;

Light shining on the great chiliocosm.

Eight winds blowing, unmoved;

On the golden lotus, sitting straight.

Then thinking himself enlightened, he sought Chan Master Fo Yin's certification. He sent a man across the river carrying the verse to Gold Mountain Monastery.

The Chan Master read it and inscribed four words—"Fart! Fart!"—right on the verse paper, sending it back by attendant. Su Dongpo read it, and the fire of ignorance blazed sky-high. Furious: "How can this be? This is an enlightenment verse! What does 'fart' mean?" With that, he crossed the river to confront Chan Master Fo Yin.

But arriving at the monastery gate, Chan Master Fo Yin stood waiting—seeing him come, laughing loudly: "Oh! Welcome, Great Scholar Su—unmoved by eight winds, yet a single fart blows you across the river! Welcome!" (The two were close friends, often joking together.) Su Dongpo, fury bursting, hearing the Master's words, on reflection found them sound—admitting his skill still green, and bowed thanks to the Chan Master. From then on he dropped "mouth Chan."

Chan is practice, not empty talk. Talking without doing—meaningless.

tieu_de: Cultivators Must Not Lie
tom_tat: In the Chan Hall, we must follow the Chan Hall's rules—no maverick acts of our own. Remember: the Chan Hall trains sages—never wreck the Way-place, costing others their chance at enlightenment…
noi_dung:
Cultivators Must Not Lie

In the Chan Hall, we must follow the Chan Hall's rules—no maverick acts of our own. Remember: the Chan Hall trains sages—never wreck the Way-place, costing others their chance at enlightenment. On this point, Session participants must take special heed—guarding the precepts strictly, never lightly.

Joining a Chan Session is a rare affinity—a thousand myriads of times not to be wasted. Now we gather here investigating Chan together through good roots of past lives, leading to today's affinity. The cultivator of the Way, meeting this chance, must seize enlightenment's moment—wasting no time, not a second or minute. Never for momentary pleasure seek comfort in laziness—for that wastes enlightenment's chance and may plunge you into the three evil destinies. Then regret comes too late. Hence my two lines:

Do not wait for suffering to study the Way; the three evil destinies are all lazy people.

These two lines mean: do not wait for suffering to seek the Way. Beings in the three evil destinies (hells, hungry ghosts, animals) are all lazy people.

So the meditator must apply effort hour after hour, ever vigorous. The hua-tou ever in mind—walking also investigating, sitting also investigating—investigating back and forth, investigating penetratingly—and the original face appears. Why? Because the hua-tou can smash discursive thoughts. Investigate until above, you know no sky; below, you know no earth; between, you know no people—then when would discursive thoughts arise? Understand that discursive thoughts are precisely false speech—that is, we fail the five basic precepts: through rivalry we lie, through greed we lie, through seeking we lie, through selfishness we lie, through self-benefit we lie. Lying to deceive others, erring yet never admitting, finding excuses for ourselves—with such thoughts and acts, how cultivate the Way?

Why does our effort show no progress? Precisely because we have lied too much. One lie breeds a hundred discursive thoughts. Then sitting—sitting unseated; standing—standing unsteady—the illness of restlessness, not knowing how to bear oneself—advance or retreat? Which is right? Which is wrong? No peace to be found—wholly against the Dharma.

The true cultivator, everywhere follows the rules, ever vigorous—never speaking falsehood, never drifting with whatever comes. May we imitate no liars, follow none who flout the rules—for following them brings no benefit but harm. Take care on this point, take heed—lest infection bring great calamity.

The true cultivator fears no suffering, shrinks from no hardship—hour after hour, minute after minute strictly cultivating, unmoved by outer states.

Investigate! Investigate! Investigate! Investigate until waters recede and rocks appear—seeing clearly the original face.

tieu_de: Cultivators Must Bear Suffering
tom_tat: There is a saying: “Bear suffering and suffering ends; enjoy blessings and blessings dissolve.” Why must we in cultivating the Way practice asceticism? Each day we eat but one meal because we wish to end suffering. Suffering ended…
noi_dung:
Cultivators Must Bear Suffering

There is a saying: "Bear suffering and suffering ends; enjoy blessings and blessings dissolve." Why must we in cultivating the Way practice asceticism? Each day we eat but one meal because we wish to end suffering. Suffering ended—there will be joy.

As for blessings, some should be enjoyed and some not. Blessings to enjoy are those our own hands have made—like a fine house, fine clothes, fine food, a fine car. Yet remember: once those are enjoyed out, blessings dissolve too—and in the blessings-bank ledger, the balance stands empty.

Blessings not to be enjoyed are those not of our own making. They come to us by tricks—like money stolen from others. Spending such gains unlawfully, the law will surely punish. Thus you have overdrawn—running a deficit in the blessings-bank ledger.

Enjoying blessings, once enjoyed out, blessings are gone—let alone deliberately enjoying blessings not to be enjoyed. Then not only are blessings spent, you go bankrupt besides. Hence blessings must never be enjoyed out—enjoyed out, blessings end; suffering may be borne out—borne out, suffering ends. As people, remember this. Meeting hardship and adversity, gladly accept adversity. Then no resentment—you harbor no discontent.

One who has studied the Buddhadharma thinks and acts unlike worldly people. One way follows birth-and-death's current, creating karma; the cultivator goes against birth-and-death's current, dissolving karma. In every circumstance, such people keep the mind at peace, feeling no suffering. There is a saying: "Only tasting the utmost suffering can one become supreme." Truly a maxim of truth.

Now I tell a gongan for your reference. The last emperor of the Ming was the Chongzhen Emperor. As a sovereign, he had wisdom enough, but lacked the blessings for the throne. Why? Because meeting suffering, he never bore it out to the end. In a past life he was a novice, dying before receiving the Complete Precepts—so he remained a little novice. As a novice, he took on all heavy chores—hauling water, chopping wood. He bore it, swallowing resentment, toiling daily to guard the Way-place. One day, climbing the roof to mend it, he slipped and fell to his death. Fellow cultivators hurried to tell the Abbot. The Abbot, knowing this little novice's karma, sought to help his disciple bear suffering out—and before the assembly declared: "This little novice worked carelessly, slipped and died, harming the Way-place. He has committed the offense of damaging the permanent dwelling—deserving punishment. Tie his corpse to a team of horses and drag it till it falls apart. No coffin burial needed." The fellow cultivators, hearing the Abbot, could not bear it—moved by fellow-cultivator friendship to pity. Disobeying the Abbot's order, they conferred: "We are Dharma brothers, cultivating in one Way-place—how let him be horse-dragged? We must bury him properly." Agreed, they pooled money for a coffin and buried him in the mountains.

Through bitter toil serving the monastery, the little novice had gathered merit—and so was reborn as emperor—the Chongzhen Emperor. But he reigned only sixteen years, meeting a world in great turmoil—within, Li Zicheng rebelling; without, the Qing invading. Through those years, never a single peaceful day—unceasing pressure and worry. Precisely his Dharma brothers' kindness harmed him—not letting him bear suffering out. Had those friends heeded the Abbot sooner, horse-dragging the corpse, his suffering would have ended—and the later scene of Chongzhen hanging himself on Coal Hill, dying for his country, would never have come.

Cast Off the False Mind, Keep the True Mind

The Avatamsaka Sutra says:

If one wishes to fully understand

All Buddhas of the three periods,

Contemplate the Dharma Realm's nature:

All is made from mind alone.

(If one wishes to understand,

All Buddhas of the three periods,

Contemplate the Dharma Realm's nature:

All is made by mind alone.)

Acting with a Buddha's mind, you are a Buddha; acting with a Bodhisattva's mind, you are a Bodhisattva; acting with a Pratyekabuddha's mind, you are a Pratyekabuddha; acting with a Shravaka's mind, you are a Shravaka; acting with a heaven's mind, you are a heaven; acting with a human's mind, you are a human; acting with an asura's mind, you are an asura; acting with a beast's mind, you are a beast; acting with a hungry ghost's mind, you are a hungry ghost; acting with a hell's mind, you are a hell-ghost.

Hence the saying: "The Ten Dharma Realms never leave a single present thought of mind." Then we know all things are made by mind. A verse on the mind, full of meaning, says:

Three dots like scattered stars;

A curving hook like the crescent moon.

Wearing fur starts from here;

Becoming a Buddha also through it.

A rough translation:

Three dots like a starry host;

A hook curving like the newborn moon.

Growing fur comes from here;

Becoming a Buddha also from here.

Reflect well—the verse is most true.

People in the world must keep the Right Mind, never harboring the deviant mind. What is the Right Mind? The Bodhi mind, the equal mind, the kind mind, the pitying mind, the giving mind, the mind of shame. What is the deviant mind? Selfish minds, self-benefiting, jealous, hateful, arrogant, idle-fancying minds. In cultivation we must aim to cast off the false mind and keep the True Mind—that is, casting off the deviant mind, giving rise to the Right Mind.

If every act of ours holds right mindfulness, that is right knowledge and views; with deviant thoughts come deviant knowledge and views. One with deviant thoughts calls wrong right and right wrong, takes white for black and black for white—upside-down right and wrong, black and white undistinguished. Every act he deems right—yet the fruit is offense; fallen into the hells, still not knowing why. Hence the Buddhas painstakingly exhorted, tirelessly admonishing: "Walk not the wrong road! Enter no dead end!" This also reminds us cultivators never to create evil karma in the Way-place. There is a saying:

Neglect no small good deed; commit no small evil deed.

Hour after hour, minute after minute alert, examining ourselves—trembling as on a deep abyss's edge, as treading thin ice—slowly shedding foul habits, bettering bad conduct, sly tendencies, ghostly cleverness. Examine yourselves in all things clearly—not muddling through the days like the blind leading the blind, deceiving one another, driving the world daily toward crisis—toward the final age, all to destruction.

Those with right mindfulness can lead humankind along the open, upright road. All of one heart, helping one another—you helping me, I helping you—all in mutual aid. There is a saying: "Helping others is the fount of joy," or "doing good is the greatest joy." Resolving on good deeds, the joy no pen describes—only doers of good know its full savor. Try tasting good deeds—how does it feel? That joy is truly wondrous. We must at all costs avoid crooked roads—tripping not only ourselves, but leading others into dead ends. For these reasons, our minds must be upright and bright to shine through and smash all darkness.

tieu_de: When Deluded, the Master Saves; When Enlightened, Save Yourself
tom_tat: Now is Chan Session time (December 15, 1977). Raise up the hua-tou to investigate, applying effort hour after hour, minute after minute. Cultivators must cultivate by themselves—never leaning on others, still less leaning on their own teacher…
noi_dung:
When Deluded, the Master Saves; When Enlightened, Save Yourself

Now is Chan Session time (December 15, 1977). Raise up the hua-tou to investigate, applying effort hour after hour, minute after minute. Cultivators must cultivate by themselves—never leaning on others, still less leaning on their own teacher. At the Session, we cultivate—not our teacher—see this clearly. Someone thinks: "While the Master is at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas, I apply effort; when the Master is away, I needn't strive." Thinking so will not do. Whether the teacher is at the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas or not, we still strive vigorously in cultivation—thorough before and after—only then is there hope of accomplishment. Otherwise you merely cultivate outwardly—deceiving yourselves and others—never to be liberated.

Investigating the hua-tou means investigating "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?"—asking who is reciting the Buddha's name. Saying: "I am reciting the Buddha's name"—then when I die, where does this "I" run off to? Clearly not this "I." Investigating so, no "I" can be found. If there is no "I," then while alive need we cultivate at all? Thinking so is also wrong. Then what is right? Investigate our original face (the fundamental face)—what was it before our parents gave birth to us? Investigate penetratingly—and you will become enlightened.

Who is it that recites the Buddha's name? Pursue it hour after hour, minute after minute, second after second, unrelenting. In fact this is the skill of countering poison with poison. Who recites the Buddha's name? Though it too is a thought, take one thought to control all other thoughts—take one discursive thought to halt all discursive thoughts. Halting to the extreme, the moment comes when waters recede and rocks appear, true features show, and you are enlightened.

What is enlightenment? Truly seeing what you are, realizing the principle of emptiness, understanding all is hollow—and that is true understanding. Then you know what state "Fundamentally not a single thing—where can dust alight?" is. That too is the state of understanding the mind and seeing the nature. There is a saying, "With the mind understood, nothing is hard; with the nature seen, sorrow unknown"—meaning that reaching mind-understanding, whatever befalls brings no sorrow. Another saying goes:

Since ancient times, immortals have no special magic;

Vastly giving rise to joy, giving rise to no sorrow.

This means immortals of old had nothing unusual—for giving rise to vast joy, they had no sorrow. That marks those who cultivate the Way.

Whoever cultivates the Way—meeting adverse or favorable states, the mind stays unmoved. With samadhi power at that level, states no longer shake you—instead you can turn states around. That is the true skill of the cultivator of the Way. Another saying:

Mount Tai crumbling before you, unstartled;

Beauty before your eyes, unmoved.

A rough translation:

Mount Tai collapsing, yet unafraid;

Beauty before your eyes, the mind unmoved.

A young man before a beauty like Xi Shi, say—contemplating the "skull," his mind naturally stills. A young woman meeting a handsome youth like Pan An of old—contemplating "white bones," likewise unmoved. Without that dharma, meeting pretty girls or handsome boys, the mind scampers—like gibbons climbing, like horses galloping—never knowing what is right. Only through samadhi power too weak—and so the Way-karma wasted in vain. How regrettable!

Today I received a letter from two pilgrims on the "three steps, one bow" journey, and I understand the inconceivable things they have just been through, sheltered by dragon spirits and Dharma protectors. "Sympathetic response in the Way" is just this. Those two bowed sincerely, recited truly—moving the heavenly dragons of the eightfold division to ever stand beside them guarding. So wherever they go, all goes smoothly—peril turned to safety. Take them as bright mirrors, reflecting on yourselves—are you so pure? So clear, so wise, so free of discursive thoughts?

Friends! Hearing Sutras and Dharma, you must awaken to your own nature—awaken yourselves and save yourselves. You cannot lean on the Master! You must rely on yourselves. It is said, "The master leads you to the gate; practice is your own affair." Trust your own wisdom—never trust your own delusion. This point is of utmost weight. We join the Session aiming that our own natures save themselves. Of old the Sixth Patriarch said: "When deluded, the master saves; when enlightened, save yourself."

Now as we investigate Chan, use every second—wasting no time. Hence during Chan investigation we do not bow to the Buddhas, take formal meals, or make noon offerings—why? To help you focus on effort. One more minute investigating—enlightenment's chance one minute nearer. Where is spare time for other things—for chatter, for gathering? Clustering in twos and threes, gossiping rights and wrongs—all meaningless—truly squandering enlightenment's chance. Though you investigated for eighty thousand great kalpas, no hope at all. In the Session, investigate honestly! Investigate "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" Investigate "What was my original face before my parents gave birth to me?" That is wisdom's key.

In Chan Investigation, Conquer the "Gate of Pain"

Today, the New Year, I wish you a "Happy New Year." Such is worldly custom. We world-leavers should not follow that custom—yet we remain people in the world; too far from the world, we leave people behind. So I follow custom, wishing everyone "a happy new year." I add this verse:

Now meets the year nineteen-eighty-two;

From ten directions gather to investigate Chan.

Returning the light, contemplating at ease;

In the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas, sages are selected.

A rough translation:

This year, nineteen-eighty-two;

Gathered at Ten Thousand Buddhas to investigate Chan.

Returning the light, contemplating at ease;

Right here, sages are selected.

A happy New Year! For us Chan investigators, we must reach "taking Chan bliss as food"—the true Chan investigator, eaten or not, does not remember; dressed or not, slept or not, does not remember. Investigating to the ultimate—above, no sky known; below, no earth known; between, no people seen—merged into one with empty space, dwelling in a state of no others, no self, no beings, no life. In that state, aching legs matter nothing—aching back, no fear—for patient effort carries the meditator past all. For with no people, no self, no beings, no life—who is it that aches? Moreover, past the "gate of pain," pain passes too; unpassed, pain remains. Past the gate of pain, the meditator is not only pain-free but at ease, joyful beyond measure.

No Dharma-door is more wondrous than Chan investigation—for Chan investigation alone leads to taking Chan bliss as food, replete with Dharma joy. Hence since ancient times Chan adepts could sit days on end without rising. Did their legs ache? Of course they ached! But they could bear pain—bearing what others cannot bear. With valiant, vigorous energy, knowing only to press forward, never to retreat—and so they succeeded.

Chan investigation demands patience—for patience is enlightenment's capital. Like merchants in trade—capital is needed for business to grow and profit much. In Chan investigation we must conquer the gate of pain; past the gate of pain, the road opens bright and wide, leading straight to understanding the mind and seeing the nature. Unpassed this barrier, still "mountains ending, waters exhausted, the road blocked"—passed, it is "beneath the willows, bright flowers—another village." There are sayings:

Unable to cast off death, no life gained;

Unable to cast off the false, no truth realized;

Unable to cast off suffering, no bliss attained.

In Chan investigation we must hold such a spirit to hope for success. Smash through hardship's gate to see another (true) state. Hence we must be single in Chan investigation. Take heed! We come here to investigate Chan—not to kill time. Bring forth your truest resolve to apply effort, with truest patience to sit in Chan. Remember one thing: in this world, nothing is reaped without labor. Reaping without sowing—can things be so easy? That is hollow dreaming, never real. Only your own strength given promises the day of accomplishment. Now, the New Year come, you hold new hopes—hoping this year for enlightenment. May we all press toward this goal—unenlightened, never halting.

Talks at the Ten Thousand Buddhas Hall, City of Ten Thousand Buddhas, Chan Session, January 1 to 8, 1982.

tieu_de: What Qualifies One to Investigate Chan?
tom_tat: Whatever work you undertake, only through a stage of tempering comes success. The Chan investigation Dharma-door is harder still. The meditator must taste every bitterness and tempering to advance. Joining a Chan Session…
noi_dung:
What Qualifies One to Investigate Chan?

Whatever work you undertake, only through a stage of tempering comes success. The Chan investigation Dharma-door is harder still. The meditator must taste every bitterness and tempering to advance. Joining a Chan Session, most important is a patient mind—patience to do what you dislike, patience to bear what cannot be borne. Only with such a spirit are you qualified to investigate Chan—otherwise, say no more. Body in the Chan Hall, mind elsewhere—investigate as you may, all wasted, nothing accomplished.

Investigating Chan tempers this body into vajra—never to decay. Willing to temper this body, meeting suffering you must bear with all your might—for: "Bear suffering and suffering ends; enjoy blessings and blessings dissolve."

Toward what you delight to do, strive harder still—lest you betray the original resolve that brought you to the Session. On this point, take special heed!

Why Does the Body Bear Sickness and Suffering?

Dharma Realm Buddhist University, under the Dharma Realm Buddhist Association, once organized a Southeast Asia tour to propagate the Buddhadharma. Before going, I knew beforehand we would meet obstacles—for wherever I propagate the Dharma, I meet hindrance and jealousy. Why? Because I am too blunt—refusing to fawn along with others—and so jealousy arises. Yet my faith is: the deviant can never overcome the right—demons and ghosts can do no harm.

I trust the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas ever guard my Dharma. Where I go, though meeting many obstacles, they avail nothing—no mishaps occur, perils turn to safety, everywhere peaceful and sound. All through the Buddhas' and Bodhisattvas' blessings.

Wherever I go, I regularly meet sick sufferers seeking cure. Sickness comes from heavy karma of past lives—otherwise, one would never catch strange ills. Those who seek me all bear strange illnesses—Western and Eastern medicine both helpless, no cure at all. Most bearers of strange ills, in past lives, loved exploiting others, never willing to lose out; or they were misers, grudging others a cent, never aiding the poor—thinking only of themselves, never of others—ever selfish and self-benefiting, forgetting duty at the sight of gain, sinking ever deeper in karmic obstacles—and so strange illnesses in this life.

Bearers of strange ills include also those who slandered the Triple Jewel in past lives—even slandering Mahayana Sutras—an offense that can plunge one into the hells to suffer, and leaving the hells, turning as beasts, birds, or animals. When such beings rise to human birth, the six senses are incomplete—maimed, or blind, deaf, mute or stammering, lame—in short, an imperfect human body. Because in past lives they created evil karma, in this life they undergo retribution.

Meeting such retribution, they should earnestly repent and make much merit. Pity—not only unawakened, they prize money like life itself—and even scheme to exploit this monastic. Begging me to cure them, they will spend no money yet be cured. Cured, they grandly produce a red envelope as offering—yet inside the red packet, one, two, up to five dollars at most (Singapore or Malaysian dollars). Their karmic obstacles so heavy, yet still scheming to exploit—truly pitiable!

Why do I tell you these tales? To put you on high alert—carefully guarding against creating evil karma. In Buddhism, never slander the Triple Jewel, never slander Mahayana Sutras, never doubt yet refuse to cultivate, never lie to fool people. Creating such evil karma, in the future you will surely fall into the hells. Then, though the teacher pities you, nothing can be done to help. I warn you beforehand—so later blame me not for refusing to save you.

tieu_de: Clinging to States Invites Demonic Obstruction
tom_tat: In Chan investigation, the cultivator must truly press forward—toiling bitterly and diligently, valiantly advancing, absolutely never retreating. With such constant resolve is one a true Chan…
noi_dung:
Clinging to States Invites Demonic Obstruction

In Chan investigation, the cultivator must truly press forward—toiling bitterly and diligently, valiantly advancing, absolutely never retreating. Only with such constant resolve is one a true Chan cultivator.

While investigating, conquer every pain with patience—aching legs or back, ignore them. To reach enlightenment requires patience—otherwise, no enlightenment. Patience here embraces every patience—bearing hunger, bearing thirst, bearing pain, bearing all things. Bearing them, the clinging to self is smashed. With no self-clinging, contemplating the mind, no mind is seen either; contemplating outer forms, forms are gone too; reaching further, the myriad existences vanish as well. That is the moment: within, no body or mind; without, no world—all empty.

This "emptiness" too must never be clung to—for clinging to "emptiness" is itself a clinging. So "emptiness" too must be cast off—only then can you merge with the world into one, you and empty space no longer distinct. Carrying this state to the ultimate, there will be samadhi. Samadhi is no hazy state—on the contrary, most lucid, as in the saying: thus, thus unmoving; clear, ever aware—meaning unmoving, yet never once unaware of anything. Investigating Chan is no occasion for sitting and scheming, nor for craving some state. With such discursive thoughts, demons come to disturb.

In the Diamond Sutra there is a line:

All conditioned marks are false and illusory;

Seeing all marks as no marks, one sees the Tathagata.

So the Chan investigator must never cling to states, nor seek spiritual powers. Investigating so, you may go astray and fall under demonic influence. Nor crave fame and gain—lest you fall into deviant paths, becoming the Demon King's kin. How dreadful! The Chan investigator must be free of clinging, free of craving—hence the saying: "Kill the Buddha when a Buddha comes; kill the demon when a demon comes"—and wield the Vajra King's jeweled sword (wisdom) to sever all things. Fine states—never crave them; foul states—ignore them. A thousand myriads of times, crave no petty attainments—those are but skill's by-products; craving mind arising, you stray onto deviant roads. We must be most alert!

During the Session, the "self" must be forgotten, others forgotten too—time and space forgotten. There is a saying: "Sweep away all dharmas, leave behind all marks"—clinging to nothing at all, letting go of everything—then you may enter the state of the Fourth Dhyana heaven.

tieu_de: The State of the Fourth Dhyana Heaven
tom_tat: When the Chan investigator reaches the state of no self, no others, he enters the First Dhyana, also called “the Ground of Joy and Bliss Born of Separation.” At this stage, the meditator smashes clinging to beings, realizing “Chan bliss as…
noi_dung:
The State of the Fourth Dhyana Heaven

When the Chan investigator reaches the state of no self, no others, he enters the First Dhyana, also called "the Ground of Joy and Bliss Born of Separation." At this stage, the meditator smashes clinging to beings, realizing "Chan bliss as food" and feeling a joy in the Dharma replete. In this samadhi state, breathing ceases—no breathing out, no breathing in—and the meditator rejoices with a special joy. Such bliss is wondrous beyond words—in short, ordinary people never taste such bliss.

In the Second Dhyana, also called "the Ground of Joy and Bliss Born of Samadhi," the meditator feels an utmost joy and bliss. Sitting in place—neither eating nor drinking—the pulse beats no more—like one dead—yet thought remains, aware of sitting in stillness.

In the Third Dhyana's samadhi, also called "the Ground of Wondrous Bliss Apart from Joy," the meditator leaves behind Chan bliss as food, leaves behind even replete Dharma joy—realizing a subtle bliss beyond all telling, wholly inconceivable. In this state, all thoughts halt—not a thought arises. There is a saying:

When not a single thought arises, the whole appears;

When the six senses suddenly stir, it is covered by clouds.

A rough translation:

Not a thought arising, the whole appears; Six senses stirring, covered by clouds.

The Fourth Dhyana, also called "the Ground of Purity through Renouncing Thought," is a state where thoughts not only halt but are wholly cast off. Then the meditator reaches an extraordinary purity, and bliss extraordinary and wondrous. Yet the Fourth Dhyana's state remains a common beings' state—not yet realizing fruition. Never be too proud. Fruition's stage is still far—the meditator must strive investigating, keep investigating, press further still to reach the state of "the Five Heavens of No Return"—there first entering the sages' stream.

Of old, the Unlearned Bhikshu (the Unlearned Bhikshu being a Bhikshu without understanding, without study — Unlearned Bikshu), reaching this Fourth Dhyana state, mistook himself realized—and wherever he went, boasted so. Never penetrating the Buddhadharma, he spoke false words—and fell into the Uninterrupted Hells as the fruit.

tieu_de: The Secret of Chan Investigation
tom_tat: The word “Chan” translates as “still consideration,” also as “cultivation through reflection.” Reflection is precisely investigating; still consideration means “time and again, wipe it diligently; let no dust alight.” Practicing…
noi_dung:
The Secret of Chan Investigation

The word "Chan" translates as "still consideration," also as "cultivation through reflection." Reflection is precisely investigating; still consideration means "time and again, wipe it diligently; let no dust alight." Practicing cultivation through reflection means we must raise up the hua-tou, ever mindful, never apart for an instant. There is a saying: "Morning thus, evening thus." Apply effort through the own-nature; seek nothing outside. Meeting states then chasing states, you go astray. States born from the own-nature are true states. May you truly grasp this point—or you will fall to the Demon King, becoming his kin.

The still-consideration Dharma-door demands unbroken, close-woven effort, never pausing. Such effort may be likened to the mother hen wholeheartedly hatching her eggs, the dragon carefully nurturing its pearl, and the cat patiently stalking the mouse. Chan investigation requires a resolute mind, a sincere mind, and a constant mind. Never an arrogant mind, deeming yourself higher or finer than others. With such thoughts, madness demons enter, rendering skill fruitless.

In Chan investigation, give rise to no discursive thoughts. With discursive thoughts, no benefit at all—only wasted time and skill. Chan investigation requires a patient mind, a long-range mind—thinking long-term. The secret of Chan investigation is the word patience; what cannot be borne must still be borne; bearing to the extreme, suddenly penetrating, brightly enlightened. Without patience, unwilling to bear suffering and toil, meeting obstacles you will surely surrender. Such ways are unacceptable—most taboo in Chan investigation.

tieu_de: The Vajra King's Jeweled Sword Severs Discursive Thoughts
tom_tat: Discursive thoughts are the stumbling stones on enlightenment's road. Investigating “Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?” is wielding the Vajra King's jeweled sword, severing all discursive thoughts. When Shakyamuni Buddha had just realized Right…
noi_dung:
The Vajra King's Jeweled Sword Severs Discursive Thoughts

Discursive thoughts are the stumbling stones on enlightenment's road. Investigating "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?" is wielding the Vajra King's jeweled sword, severing all discursive thoughts. When Shakyamuni Buddha had just realized Right Enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, he said: "Strange indeed! Strange indeed! All beings, without exception, fully possess the Tathagata's virtuous marks and wisdom—but hindered by discursive thoughts and attachments, they cannot realize it." Thus the Buddha told us plainly why we do not become Buddhas: nothing but discursive thoughts and attachments—so we must smash these things. Smash them how? Precisely with the word "who"—like an auger boring down—boring until waters recede and rocks appear, and you will succeed.

Investigating Chan means investigating "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?"—in every moment studying this question, unbroken. In time, good news comes of itself—hence the saying: "Long sitting brings Chan; long dwelling brings affinities."

Sitting long, Chan comes of itself. Dwelling long in one place, affinities with neighbors come of themselves—you and all around blending in feeling, and so all live together in peace.

Investigating Chan to a subtle level, not only do discursive thoughts dissolve—temper softens, afflictions lessen, character rises, breadth widens. Then wisdom appears—knowing right from wrong, telling good from evil—greed, anger, delusion cleansed away—leaving only morality, samadhi, and wisdom's light shining, illumining the five skandhas as all empty.

A Brief Account of Venerable Master Hsuan Hua

Venerable Master Hsuan Hua was of the Bai family, his personal name Anci, his style Dulun. He was a native of Shuangcheng county, Songjiang province, in China's Northeast—that is, Manchuria.

His father, named Fuhai, farmed for a living. His mother, née Hu, bore eight children in all—five sons, three daughters—and he was the youngest.

The Venerable Lady Hu ate lifelong vegetarian and recited the Buddha's name without pause. One night she dreamed that Amitabha Buddha appeared, radiating great light that shone through the world, shaking heaven and earth. Startling awake, she smelled a wondrous fragrance filling the room—and soon after gave birth to him.

The moment he was born, he cried unbroken for three days and nights.

Precisely from grief at this Saha world's suffering.

He lived in a tiny country village of scattered homes. Thus, till eleven he had never once seen a dead person. One day, roaming the fields with village friends, he suddenly saw a small child—mouth closed, eyes shut, bundled lying in roadside straw. Calling, the child never answered; touched, no breath. Most puzzled, he asked his friends. One who knew said: "The child is dead!" But he was most astonished, not knowing what death was. Home, he asked his mother, who taught: "All people must die. Some die old, some of sickness, some by mishap. Rich or poor, scholar, farmer, artisan, merchant, or official—all in the end must die."

He asked again: "If truly so, is there any way to escape death?" Then a houseguest, once a cultivator of the Way, answered: "Only by cultivating the Way—awakening to your own mind, thoroughly seeing the fundamental nature—can birth and death be ended, transmigration transcended, Right Enlightenment realized, No Birth certified."

Though then still young, hearing the guest's words, he awakened deeply—and so set his resolve: to leave home and cultivate the Way.

Raising leaving home with his mother, she taught: "Leaving home is a fine thing indeed, but no easy matter. Good roots are needed, great vow power, bringing forth the great Bodhi mind—only then can the Unsurpassed Way be realized. Now that you hold such a heart, I most agree—truly matching my dream of old. Now I am old, my days few; your brothers and sisters stand on their own. Stay to serve your parents; when I am gone, leave home to cultivate—then will still not be too late."

Obeying his parents, thereafter daily he followed his mother bowing to the Buddhas. Done bowing to the Buddhas, he bowed to his parents.

Day after day, winter gone, spring come—he reverently served his parents as if Buddhas. Before long, his filial fame spread far—then all called him the Filial Son of the Bai family.

At nineteen his mother passed away; then bidding kin farewell, he went to the monastery, bowed to Venerable Master Changzhi as teacher, took refuge, formally left home, and received the precepts. Afterward, he returned to his mother's grave to observe filial mourning for three years. Throughout, he lived in a small thatched hut—daily sitting in Chan, reading and reciting Mahayana Sutra texts, reciting Amitabha Buddha's name. Many times he sat in Chan, entering samadhi for weeks on end, never leaving the bench.

One night, nearby villagers panicked to see his thatched hut ablaze with red fire. Flames rising straight into the sky, the hut bright as day. Many ran to the grave, shouting: "The Filial Son's house is burning!" A hundred villagers together grabbed dippers and buckets to fight the fire. But arriving, they found the hut calm—no fire burning—and him still peaceful, silent in samadhi!

Once as he sat in Chan, a visitor suddenly came. The visitor—wonder of wonders—was the Sixth Patriarch Huineng! The Patriarch told him that in the future he would go to America to save beings—that in the West he would meet many with affinities who could propagate the Buddhadharma, and he would save limitless, boundless beings. Not till the Patriarch bade farewell and left did he start awake—recalling that Huineng lived in the Tang, 1,200 years before. After World War II, he traveled everywhere. At last, over three thousand miles, he reached Nanhua Monastery, paying respects to that era's Great Good Knowing Advisor, Old Master Hsu Yun. The Old Master was then 109; the moment he saw him, the Old Master at once recognized his realization. Then the Old Master said: "So it is! So it is!" And he likewise replied: "So it is! So it is!"

Then Old Master Hsu Yun certified his attainment, and he formally became the Ninth Patriarch of the Guiyang Dharma lineage.

Afterward, the Old Master had him stay at the monastery as Dean of Nanhua Monastery's Vinaya Academy.

In 1950, he bid the monastery farewell for Hong Kong. There he lived in a remote mountain cave, untouched by worldly dust. Before long, countless Sangha members fled from mainland China to Hong Kong seeking refuge, needing his aid. At last, according with affinities, he left the cave, founding a lecture hall and two monasteries, and helped build many other Way-places.

Through twelve years in Hong Kong, he shone as a model—ascetic, vigorous in cultivating the Way, forgetting self for the Buddhadharma. He moved countless good men and believing women to bring forth the Bodhi mind, take refuge in the Triple Jewel, and support the Buddhadharma.

In 1962, he came to San Francisco, America. There, in a small warehouse, he persevered in silent cultivation, awaiting the ripe moment to propagate the Dharma. Then he called himself the "Grave-Dwelling Monk" (the monk in the grave), or the Living Dead Man (one dead yet alive). Buddhist laypeople who understood his true cultivation were deeply moved, reverently supporting him with offerings.

In 1968, he knew the moment had come; he said: "A single flower will blossom into five petals." That summer, he hosted the 96-day Shurangama Sutra lecture assembly. When the assembly ended, sure enough, the first five Americans sought to leave home under him.

From then on, he continued hosting many assemblies, explaining the Heart

Sutra, the Ksitigarbha Sutra, the Lotus Sutra, the Dharma Jewel Platform Sutra, and more.

In 1971, he lectured the Mahayana's supreme Sutra—the Avatamsaka Sutra.

Alongside lecturing Sutras and Dharma, he performed countless other merit-deeds saving beings. In 1976, he founded the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas—the base for propagating the Buddhadharma in America. At the Holy City, he built the monastery system, training monks, nuns, and students, creating supreme affinities for true cultivation.

The Eighteen Great Vows of Venerable Master Hsuan Hua

When Venerable Master Hsuan Hua was nineteen, his mother passed away. After the burial was complete, he went to Three Conditions Monastery in

Harbin, formally leaving home under Venerable Master Changzhi as teacher. Soon after, he went to his mother's grave to observe mourning. That year, on Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's birthday—the 19th of the 6th lunar month—before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he made eighteen great vows:

"Reverently bowing to the Buddhas of the ten directions,

And to the Tripitaka Dharma,

The Sangha of sages and worthies, past and present,

I pray you bear witness:

Your disciple Dulun,

Shi Anci,

Now brings forth this resolve:

Seeking not the blessings of gods or humans,

Nor of Shravakas or Pratyekabuddhas,

Nor even of provisional Bodhisattvas.

Relying solely on the Supreme Vehicle,

I bring forth the Bodhi mind.

Vowing that with the beings of the Dharma Realm,

Together at one time we shall attain

Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi."

I vow that if there is a single Bodhisattva in the ten directions and three periods of time, throughout the exhaustion of empty space and pervading the Dharma Realm, who has not yet become a Buddha, I vow not to attain Right Enlightenment.

I vow that if there is a single Pratyekabuddha in the ten directions and three periods of time, throughout the exhaustion of empty space and pervading the Dharma Realm, who has not yet become a Buddha, I vow not to attain Right Enlightenment.

I vow that if there is a single Shravaka in the ten directions and three periods of time, throughout the exhaustion of empty space and pervading the Dharma Realm, who has not yet become a Buddha, I vow not to attain Right Enlightenment.

I vow that if there is a single god or human within the Three Realms who has not yet become a Buddha, I vow not to attain Right Enlightenment.

I vow that if there is a single person in the worlds of the ten directions who has not yet become a Buddha, I vow not to attain Right Enlightenment.

I vow that if there is a single god, human, or asura who has not yet become a Buddha, I vow not to attain Right Enlightenment.

I vow that among the animal realm, if a single kind has not yet become a Buddha, I vow not to attain Right Enlightenment.

I vow that among the hungry ghost realm, if a single one has not yet become a Buddha, I vow not to attain Right Enlightenment.

I vow that among the hell realm, if a single one has not yet become a Buddha, I vow not to attain Right Enlightenment.

I vow that within the Three Realms, if any who have taken refuge with me—whether gods, humans, asuras, winged, swimming, moving, or planted beings, spirits, dragons, beasts, ghosts, or gods—have not yet become Buddhas, I vow not to attain Right Enlightenment.

I vow to dedicate all blessings and joys I deserve to all beings throughout the Dharma Realm.

I vow to take upon myself alone all the sufferings and hardships of beings throughout the Dharma Realm.

I vow to divide my spirit into countless bodies, universally entering the hearts of beings who do not believe in the Buddhadharma, leading them to abandon evil toward good, repent and reform, take refuge in the Triple Jewel, and at last become Buddhas.

I vow that all beings who see my face, even only hearing my name, shall bring forth the Bodhi mind and swiftly realize Buddhahood.

I vow to ever honor what the Buddha taught, and to practice eating one meal a day.

I vow to enlighten sentient beings, universally gathering in beings of every

disposition.

I vow that in this life I shall attain the Five Eyes, the Six Spiritual Powers, and free flight.

I vow that all my vows shall be fully realized.

And lastly:

"Beings without bounds, I vow to save. Afflictions without end, I vow to sever. Dharma-doors without measure, I vow to learn. The unsurpassed Buddha Way, I vow to realize."

Eight Rules of the Sutra Translation Institute

A translator must free himself from motives of self-seeking for fame and profit.

A translator must cultivate his own conduct, nourish his nature, and cease to be arrogant.

A translator must practice restraint, never praising himself while slandering others.

A translator must never take himself as the standard and measure, then disparage others by finding fault with their work.

A translator must take the Buddha-mind as his own mind.

A translator must use the Dharma-selecting Eye to discern what is

true principle.

A translator must respectfully request high monks and great worthies of the ten directions to certify his translation.

A translator must delight in propagating the Buddha's teachings by printing Sutras, Vinaya, and Shastras once his translation is certified correct.
